abstract: A central problem in connectionist modelling is the control of network and architectural resources during learning. In the present approach, weights reflect a coarse prediction history as coded by a distribution of values and parameterized in the mean and standard deviation of these weight distributions. Weight updates are a function of both the mean and standard deviation of each connection in the network and vary as a function of the error signal ("stochastic delta rule"; Hanson, 1990). Consequently, the weights their maintain in "uncertainty" establishing a policy concerning the size of the nodal complexity of the network and growth of new nodes. For example, during problem solving the present network can undergo "meiosis", producing two nodes where there was one "overtaxed" node as measured by its coefficient of variation. It is shown in a number of benchmark problems that meiosis networks can find minimal architectures, reduce computational complexity, and overall increase the efficiency of the representation learning interaction.

Weight updates are a function of both the mean and standard deviation of each connection in the network and vary as a function of the error signal ("stochastic delta rule"; Hanson, 1990). paragraphs: Meiosis networks address how a neural system should control its architectural resources while learning. Each connection represents a coarse history of predictions through a distribution of weight values, summarized by a mean and standard deviation. This gives the learning procedure information about uncertainty alongside the connection's central weight value.

The stochastic delta rule updates connections using both distribution summaries and the error signal. The retained uncertainty also informs decisions about network complexity. When a node is judged overtaxed according to its coefficient of variation, the network can split it into two nodes, a process the authors call meiosis.

This couples representation learning with architectural growth: evidence gathered during prediction helps determine when an existing node should become two. Across several benchmark problems, the authors report that the method can find minimal architectures, reduce computational complexity, and improve the efficiency of representation learning. The contribution is a mechanism for allocating additional nodes based on the uncertainty maintained during learning, giving network growth an explicit connection to learning history.
summary.tldr: Meiosis networks track weight uncertainty and split overtaxed nodes to adapt their architecture during learning.

title: Meiosis Networks

abstract: Recent work by Becker and Hinton (Becker and Hinton, 1992) shows a promising mechanism, based on maximizing mutual in(cid:173) formation assuming spatial coherence, by which a system can self(cid:173) organize itself to learn visual abilities such as binocular stereo. We introduce a more general criterion, based on Bayesian probability theory, and thereby demonstrate a connection to Bayesian theo(cid:173) ries of visual perception and to other organization principles for early vision (Atick and Redlich, 1990). Methods for implementa(cid:173) tion using variants of stochastic learning are described and, for the special case of linear filtering, we derive an analytic expression for the output.

We introduce a more general criterion, based on Bayesian probability theory, and thereby demonstrate a connection to Bayesian theo(cid:173) ries of visual perception and to other organization principles for early vision (Atick and Redlich, 1990). Methods for implementa(cid:173) tion using variants of stochastic learning are described and, for the special case of linear filtering, we derive an analytic expression for the output.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a visual system can organize itself through a probabilistic learning principle. It starts from earlier work in which maximizing mutual information, under an assumption of spatial coherence, supported learning visual abilities such as binocular stereo. The authors seek a more general criterion for this kind of self-organization.

Their proposed criterion is based on Bayesian probability theory. This connects the learning objective to Bayesian accounts of visual perception and to other organizing principles for early vision. The significance is conceptual as well as computational: a rule for learning visual representations can be related to a broader probabilistic account of how visual information is interpreted.

The paper also describes implementation methods using variants of stochastic learning. For linear filtering, a special case of the broader framework, the authors derive an analytic expression for the output. This gives the proposal both a general learning formulation and a case that can be treated explicitly. The contribution centers on the criterion, its theoretical connections, and ways of implementing it.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian criterion generalizes an information-based approach to visual self-organization and yields an analytic result for linear filtering.

title: Bayesian Self-Organization

abstract: In this paper we examine the practical use of hardware neural networks in an autonomous mobile robot. We have developed a hardware neural system based around a custom VLSI chip, EP(cid:173) SILON III, designed specifically for embedded hardware neural applications. We present here a demonstration application of an autonomous mobile robot that highlights the flexibility of this sys(cid:173) tem. This robot gains basic mobility competence in very few train(cid:173) ing epochs using an "instinct-rule" training methodology.

This robot gains basic mobility competence in very few train(cid:173) ing epochs using an "instinct-rule" training methodology.

paragraphs: This paper examines the practical use of neural network hardware in an autonomous mobile robot. The authors develop a system around EPSILON III, a custom VLSI chip intended specifically for embedded neural applications. The robot serves as a demonstration of how that hardware can support the acquisition of useful behavior.

The demonstration uses an approach the authors call instinct-rule training. With this methodology, the robot acquires basic mobility competence in very few training epochs, or passes through training. The reported outcome connects the learning procedure to an observable robotic capability: the hardware neural system supports the robot in learning how to move.

The authors present this application as evidence of the system's flexibility. Its significance lies in bringing the specialized chip, a training methodology, and an autonomous platform together in a working example. The stated achievement concerns basic mobility and rapid acquisition within that demonstration. It provides a practical account of embedded neural learning, with the robot's acquired competence serving as the central result.
summary.tldr: A mobile robot using the EPSILON III neural chip learns basic mobility in very few training epochs.

title: Competence Acquisition in an Autonomous Mobile Robot using Hardware Neural Techniques

abstract: The problem of assigning m points in the n-dimensional real space Rn to k clusters is formulated as that of determining k centers in Rn such that the sum of distances of each point to the nearest center is minimized. If a polyhedral distance is used, the problem can be formulated as that of minimizing a piecewise-linear concave function on a polyhedral set which is shown to be equivalent to a bilinear program: minimizing a bilinear function on a polyhe(cid:173) dral set. A fast finite k-Median Algorithm consisting of solving few linear programs in closed form leads to a stationary point of the bilinear program. Computational testing on a number of real(cid:173) world databases was carried out. On the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) database, k-Median training set correct(cid:173) ness was comparable to that of the k-Mean Algorithm, however its testing set correctness was better. Additionally, on the Wisconsin Prognostic Breast Cancer (WPBC) database, distinct and clini(cid:173) cally important survival curves were extracted by the k-Median Algorithm, whereas the k-Mean Algorithm failed to obtain such distinct survival curves for the same database.

paragraphs: The paper treats clustering as choosing a fixed number of centers so that the total distance from each point to its closest center is small. Its central move is to express this familiar grouping task in a mathematical form that supports a specific optimization procedure.

When distance has a polyhedral form, the objective can be represented as a piecewise-linear concave minimization problem and then as an equivalent bilinear program. The proposed k-Median algorithm solves a few linear programs in closed form and terminates at a stationary point. That guarantee describes a point where the procedure stops improving; it does not establish that the globally best clustering has been found.

Tests on real databases showed useful consequences. On the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer data, training correctness was comparable to k-Mean while test correctness was better. On the Wisconsin Prognostic Breast Cancer data, k-Median produced distinct, clinically important survival curves that k-Mean did not. The findings connect the optimization formulation to groupings with practical predictive and interpretive value.
summary.tldr: A concave optimization formulation yields a k-Median clustering algorithm with useful results on diagnostic and prognostic breast cancer data.

title: Clustering via Concave Minimization

abstract: Protein interactions typically arise from a physical interaction of one or more small sites on the surface of the two proteins. Identifying these sites is very important for drug and protein design. In this paper, we propose a computational method based on probabilistic relational model that attempts to address this task using high-throughput protein interaction data and a set of short sequence motifs. We learn the model using the EM algorithm, with a branch-and-bound algorithm as an approximate inference for the E-step. Our method searches for motifs whose presence in a pair of interacting proteins can explain their observed interaction. It also tries to determine which motif pairs have high affinity, and can therefore lead to an interaction. We show that our method is more accurate than others at predicting new protein-protein interactions. More importantly, by examining solved structures of protein complexes, we find that 2/3 of the predicted active motifs correspond to actual interaction sites.

paragraphs: Knowing that two proteins interact does not by itself identify the small surface sites responsible for their contact. This paper seeks those sites using high-throughput interaction observations and short sequence motifs. The goal matters for drug and protein design because it moves from predicting a relationship between proteins toward locating the components that may produce it.

The authors build a probabilistic relational model that searches for motifs capable of explaining observed interactions. It also estimates which pairs of motifs have high affinity and could therefore lead to an interaction. Learning uses expectation-maximization, with a branch-and-bound algorithm providing approximate inference during the expectation step.

The method is reported to predict new protein interactions more accurately than the alternatives considered. A separate structural check examines solved protein complexes and finds that two-thirds of predicted active motifs correspond to actual interaction sites. This connects the model's proposed explanations to physical contact locations. That fraction describes the examined predictions and structures, supporting the site's biological relevance without implying that every predicted motif is an interaction site.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic motif model predicts protein interactions and finds that two-thirds of examined predicted active motifs match actual interaction sites.

title: Identifying Protein-Protein Interaction Sites on a Genome-Wide Scale

abstract: The peristimulus time historgram (PSTH) and its more continuous cousin, the spike density function (SDF) are staples in the analytic toolkit of neurophysiologists. The former is usually obtained by binning spiketrains, whereas the standard method for the latter is smoothing with a Gaussian kernel. Selection of a bin with or a kernel size is often done in an relatively arbitrary fashion, even though there have been recent attempts to remedy this situation \cite{ShimazakiBinningNIPS2006,ShimazakiBinningNECO2007}. We develop an exact Bayesian, generative model approach to estimating PSHTs and demonstate its superiority to competing methods. Further advantages of our scheme include automatic complexity control and error bars on its predictions.
originalAbstract: The peristimulus time historgram (PSTH) and its more continuous cousin, the spike density function (SDF) are staples in the analytic toolkit of neurophysiologists. The former is usually obtained by binning spiketrains, whereas the standard method for the latter is smoothing with a Gaussian kernel. Selection of a bin with or a kernel size is often done in an relatively arbitrary fashion, even though there have been recent attempts to remedy this situation \cite{ShimazakiBinningNIPS2006,ShimazakiBinningNECO2007}. We develop an exact Bayesian, generative model approach to estimating PSHTs and demonstate its superiority to competing methods. Further advantages of our scheme include automatic complexity control and error bars on its predictions.

paragraphs: Neurophysiologists summarize spike activity around a stimulus using time histograms or smoother spike density functions. These summaries depend on choices about temporal resolution: histogram bin width or the width of a smoothing kernel. If those choices are relatively arbitrary, an important part of the resulting estimate rests on a manually chosen setting.

This paper develops an exact Bayesian generative approach to estimating peristimulus time histograms. A generative model provides a probabilistic account of the observed data, and Bayesian inference uses that account to estimate the response. The approach includes automatic complexity control, addressing how much detail the estimate should contain within the modeling procedure.

The authors report that their method outperforms competing approaches in their demonstration. It also supplies error bars on its predictions, so the output communicates uncertainty as well as an estimated response. These features make the contribution broader than an alternative way to divide time into bins: the method combines estimation, control of model complexity, and uncertainty reporting in one statistical framework.
summary.tldr: An exact Bayesian model estimates stimulus-aligned spike histograms with automatic complexity control and predictive error bars.

title: Bayesian binning beats approximate alternatives: estimating peri-stimulus time histograms

abstract: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) has become established as one of the key tools for dimensionality reduction when dealing with real valued data. Approaches such as exponential family PCA and non-negative matrix factorisation have successfully extended PCA to non-Gaussian data types, but these techniques fail to take advantage of Bayesian inference and can suffer from problems of overfitting and poor generalisation. This paper presents a fully probabilistic approach to PCA, which is generalised to the exponential family, based on Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling. We describe the model which is based on a factorisation of the observed data matrix, and show performance of the model on both synthetic and real data.
originalAbstract: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) has become established as one of the key tools for dimensionality reduction when dealing with real valued data. Approaches such as exponential family PCA and non-negative matrix factorisation have successfully extended PCA to non-Gaussian data types, but these techniques fail to take advantage of Bayesian inference and can suffer from problems of overfitting and poor generalisation. This paper presents a fully probabilistic approach to PCA, which is generalised to the exponential family, based on Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling. We describe the model which is based on a factorisation of the observed data matrix, and show performance of the model on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis provides compact representations of real-valued data. The paper addresses the broader problem of dimensionality reduction for data whose statistical behavior is not well described by Gaussian models. Existing extensions, including exponential family PCA and non-negative matrix factorisation, motivate the work but can suffer from overfitting and weak generalisation.

The authors introduce a fully probabilistic PCA approach generalized to the exponential family. Its structure comes from factorising the observed data matrix, connecting a compact representation to a probabilistic model of the observations. Bayesian inference is performed using Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling, making uncertainty part of the inference process rather than relying solely on a fitted factorisation.

The paper presents the model's performance on synthetic and real data. Its central contribution is the combination of exponential family modeling, matrix factorisation, and Bayesian inference within one dimensionality reduction approach. The stated motivation is to address weaknesses of existing methods; the abstract reports demonstrations without asserting a universal improvement over every alternative.
summary.tldr: The paper extends PCA to exponential family data using a probabilistic matrix factorisation and Bayesian sampling.

title: Bayesian Exponential Family PCA

abstract: Large networks of spiking neurons show abrupt changes in their collective dynamics resembling phase transitions studied in statistical physics. An example of this phenomenon is the transition from irregular, noise-driven dynamics to regular, self-sustained behavior observed in networks of integrate-and-fire neurons as the interaction strength between the neurons increases. In this work we show how a network of spiking neurons is able to self-organize towards a critical state for which the range of possible inter-spike-intervals (dynamic range) is maximized. Self-organization occurs via synaptic dynamics that we analytically derive. The resulting plasticity rule is defined locally so that global homeostasis near the critical state is achieved by local regulation of individual synapses.
originalAbstract: Large networks of spiking neurons show abrupt changes in their collective dynamics resembling phase transitions studied in statistical physics. An example of this phenomenon is the transition from irregular, noise-driven dynamics to regular, self-sustained behavior observed in networks of integrate-and-fire neurons as the interaction strength between the neurons increases. In this work we show how a network of spiking neurons is able to self-organize towards a critical state for which the range of possible inter-spike-intervals (dynamic range) is maximized. Self-organization occurs via synaptic dynamics that we analytically derive. The resulting plasticity rule is defined locally so that global homeostasis near the critical state is achieved by local regulation of individual synapses.

paragraphs: Networks of spiking neurons can change their collective behavior abruptly as the strength of their interactions increases. The paper considers a transition from irregular activity driven by noise to regular activity that sustains itself. This resembles a phase transition and raises the question of whether a network can organize itself near a critical state.

The authors show how synaptic dynamics can drive such self-organization. They derive the required dynamics analytically, obtaining a plasticity rule defined locally at individual synapses. In the resulting network, these local adjustments collectively maintain global behavior near the critical state. The connection between local regulation and network-wide homeostasis is the central mechanism.

At the critical state considered, the range of possible intervals between spikes is maximized. This is the specific meaning of dynamic range in the paper. The result connects an analytically derived learning rule to a property of collective neural timing: individual synapses can regulate themselves in a way that supports a broad range of inter-spike intervals across the modeled network.
summary.tldr: An analytically derived local plasticity rule lets a spiking network self-organize near a critical state with maximal inter-spike-interval range.

title: Self-organization using synaptic plasticity

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of designing binary codes for high-dimensional data such that vectors that are similar in the original space map to similar binary strings. We introduce a simple distribution-free encoding scheme based on random projections, such that the expected Hamming distance between the binary codes of two vectors is related to the value of a shift-invariant kernel (e.g., a Gaussian kernel) between the vectors. We present a full theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of the proposed scheme, and report favorable experimental performance as compared to a recent state-of-the-art method, spectral hashing.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the problem of designing binary codes for high-dimensional data such that vectors that are similar in the original space map to similar binary strings. We introduce a simple distribution-free encoding scheme based on random projections, such that the expected Hamming distance between the binary codes of two vectors is related to the value of a shift-invariant kernel (e.g., a Gaussian kernel) between the vectors. We present a full theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of the proposed scheme, and report favorable experimental performance as compared to a recent state-of-the-art method, spectral hashing.

paragraphs: The paper seeks binary representations of high-dimensional vectors that preserve useful similarity information. Similar vectors should receive similar strings of bits, so comparing the codes reflects relationships in the original space. The relevant code comparison is Hamming distance: the number of bit positions at which two strings differ.

The authors introduce a distribution-free encoding scheme based on random projections. Its central property links the expected Hamming distance between two codes to a shift-invariant kernel value for the original vectors, such as a Gaussian kernel. This makes the connection between binary similarity and the chosen kernel explicit, with the stated relationship expressed as an expectation over the randomized encoding.

The paper provides a theoretical analysis of convergence and reports favorable experimental performance compared with spectral hashing. The analysis supports understanding how the randomized codes behave, while the experiments examine their practical performance against an existing method. Together, these contributions establish a simple route from kernel-based similarity to binary representations without requiring a specified distribution for the data.
summary.tldr: Random projections produce binary codes whose expected Hamming distances relate to shift-invariant kernel similarities, with theory and favorable empirical comparisons.

title: Locality-sensitive binary codes from shift-invariant kernels

abstract: Hypothesis testing on point processes has several applications such as model fitting, plasticity detection, and non-stationarity detection. Standard tools for hypothesis testing include tests on mean firing rate and time varying rate function. However, these statistics do not fully describe a point process and thus the tests can be misleading. In this paper, we introduce a family of non-parametric divergence measures for hypothesis testing. We extend the traditional Kolmogorov--Smirnov and Cramer--von-Mises tests for point process via stratification. The proposed divergence measures compare the underlying probability structure and, thus, is zero if and only if the point processes are the same. This leads to a more robust test of hypothesis. We prove consistency and show that these measures can be efficiently estimated from data. We demonstrate an application of using the proposed divergence as a cost function to find optimally matched spike trains.

paragraphs: A point process describes events such as neural spikes occurring over time. Comparing only average firing rates or time-varying rates can miss differences in the underlying process, making hypothesis tests misleading. This paper develops comparison measures intended to capture the probability structure beyond those rate summaries, with applications including model fitting and detecting changes.

The proposed family of nonparametric divergences extends Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Cramér–von Mises testing ideas to point processes through stratification. A central property is that the divergence is zero exactly when the underlying point processes are the same. This makes the comparison sensitive to distinctions that rate-based descriptions alone need not capture.

The authors prove consistency and show that the measures can be estimated efficiently from observations. They also demonstrate an application in which a divergence serves as the objective for finding optimally matched spike trains. The work thus links a stronger statistical comparison of event processes to an optimization task, rather than treating the divergence only as a test statistic.
summary.tldr: New point-process divergences compare probability structure beyond firing rates and support consistent testing and spike-train matching.

title: A novel family of non-parametric cumulative based divergences for point processes

abstract: Variational Bayesian matrix factorization (VBMF) efficiently approximates the posterior distribution of factorized matrices by assuming matrix-wise independence of the two factors. A recent study on fully-observed VBMF showed that, under a stronger assumption that the two factorized matrices are column-wise independent, the global optimal solution can be analytically computed. However, it was not clear how restrictive the column-wise independence assumption is. In this paper, we prove that the global solution under matrix-wise independence is actually column-wise independent, implying that the column-wise independence assumption is harmless. A practical consequence of our theoretical finding is that the global solution under matrix-wise independence (which is a standard setup) can be obtained analytically in a computationally very efficient way without any iterative algorithms. We experimentally illustrate advantages of using our analytic solution in probabilistic principal component analysis.
originalAbstract: Variational Bayesian matrix factorization (VBMF) efficiently approximates the posterior distribution of factorized matrices by assuming matrix-wise independence of the two factors. A recent study on fully-observed VBMF showed that, under a stronger assumption that the two factorized matrices are column-wise independent, the global optimal solution can be analytically computed. However, it was not clear how restrictive the column-wise independence assumption is. In this paper, we prove that the global solution under matrix-wise independence is actually column-wise independent, implying that the column-wise independence assumption is harmless. A practical consequence of our theoretical finding is that the global solution under matrix-wise independence (which is a standard setup) can be obtained analytically in a computationally very efficient way without any iterative algorithms. We experimentally illustrate advantages of using our analytic solution in probabilistic principal component analysis.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian matrix factorization approximates uncertainty about two matrices whose product represents the data. A standard approximation treats the two factor matrices as independent. Earlier work showed that adding a stronger independence assumption across columns made the global optimum analytically computable, but it was unclear whether this sacrificed a better solution.

For fully observed data, this paper proves that the global solution under the standard matrix-wise independence assumption already has column-wise independence. The additional restriction therefore does not change the attainable global optimum in this setting. It exposes a property of the optimum rather than imposing a harmful simplification on it.

The practical consequence is that the standard variational problem can be solved analytically and efficiently without iterative algorithms. Experiments illustrate advantages of the analytic solution in probabilistic principal component analysis. The result is specifically about fully observed matrix factorization under the stated variational independence setup; within that scope, it turns an apparently stronger modeling assumption into a justification for direct computation.
summary.tldr: For fully observed VBMF, the standard global optimum already has column-wise independence, enabling an efficient analytic solution.

title: Global Solution of Fully-Observed Variational Bayesian Matrix Factorization is Column-Wise Independent

abstract: We propose maximum covariance unfolding (MCU), a manifold learning algorithm for simultaneous dimensionality reduction of data from different input modalities. Given high dimensional inputs from two different but naturally aligned sources, MCU computes a common low dimensional embedding that maximizes the cross-modal (inter-source) correlations while preserving the local (intra-source) distances. In this paper, we explore two applications of MCU. First we use MCU to analyze EEG-fMRI data, where an important goal is to visualize the fMRI voxels that are most strongly correlated with changes in EEG traces. To perform this visualization, we augment MCU with an additional step for metric learning in the high dimensional voxel space. Second, we use MCU to perform cross-modal retrieval of matched image and text samples from Wikipedia. To manage large applications of MCU, we develop a fast implementation based on ideas from spectral graph theory. These ideas transform the original problem for MCU, one of semidefinite programming, into a simpler problem in semidefinite quadratic linear programming.

paragraphs: Maximum covariance unfolding addresses dimensionality reduction when observations come from two naturally aligned sources. It constructs a common low-dimensional representation that strengthens correlations across the sources while preserving local distances within each one. The objective thus combines shared information between modalities with the neighborhood structure specific to each modality.

The paper explores two applications. For paired EEG and fMRI data, it seeks to visualize which fMRI voxels are most strongly associated with changes in EEG traces. An additional metric-learning step in the original voxel space supports this visualization. The second application retrieves corresponding image and text samples from Wikipedia across the two modalities.

The authors also develop a faster implementation for larger problems using ideas from spectral graph theory. This transforms the original semidefinite programming formulation into a simpler semidefinite quadratic linear programming problem. The work therefore combines a joint representation objective, applications that use cross-modal relationships, and a computational reformulation intended to make the approach manageable at larger scales.
summary.tldr: Maximum covariance unfolding jointly embeds two aligned modalities while maximizing cross-modal correlations and preserving local distances within each source.

title: Maximum Covariance Unfolding : Manifold Learning for Bimodal Data

abstract: We present and study a distributed optimization algorithm by employing a stochastic dual coordinate ascent method. Stochastic dual coordinate ascent methods enjoy strong theoretical guarantees and often have better performances than stochastic gradient descent methods in optimizing regularized loss minimization problems. It still lacks of efforts in studying them in a distributed framework. We make a progress along the line by presenting a distributed stochastic dual coordinate ascent algorithm in a star network, with an analysis of the tradeoff between computation and communication. We verify our analysis by experiments on real data sets. Moreover, we compare the proposed algorithm with distributed stochastic gradient descent methods and distributed alternating direction methods of multipliers for optimizing SVMs in the same distributed framework, and observe competitive performances.
originalAbstract: We present and study a distributed optimization algorithm by employing a stochastic dual coordinate ascent method. Stochastic dual coordinate ascent methods enjoy strong theoretical guarantees and often have better performances than stochastic gradient descent methods in optimizing regularized loss minimization problems. It still lacks of efforts in studying them in a distributed framework. We make a progress along the line by presenting a distributed stochastic dual coordinate ascent algorithm in a star network, with an analysis of the tradeoff between computation and communication. We verify our analysis by experiments on real data sets. Moreover, we compare the proposed algorithm with distributed stochastic gradient descent methods and distributed alternating direction methods of multipliers for optimizing SVMs in the same distributed framework, and observe competitive performances.

paragraphs: Distributing optimization across machines introduces a balance between computation and communication. This paper studies that balance for stochastic dual coordinate ascent, a method with strong theoretical guarantees for regularized loss minimization. Its focus is bringing the method into a distributed setting whose behavior can be analyzed.

The authors propose a distributed algorithm operating on a star network and analyze the tradeoff between computational work and communication. The network structure forms part of the setting for the result. The analysis gives a basis for understanding how these two resources interact, extending consideration beyond the performance of stochastic dual coordinate ascent on a single optimization system.

Experiments on real datasets verify the analysis. The authors also compare the proposed method with distributed stochastic gradient descent and distributed alternating direction methods of multipliers when optimizing support vector machines in the same framework. They observe competitive performance. The contribution is therefore an analyzed distributed algorithm with empirical support, rather than a claim that it uniformly surpasses the other distributed optimization methods.
summary.tldr: Distributed stochastic dual coordinate ascent offers an analyzed computation–communication tradeoff and competitive SVM optimization performance in a star network.

title: Trading Computation for Communication: Distributed Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent

abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of F-measures for binary, multiclass and multilabel classification. These performance measures are non-linear, but in many scenarios they are pseudo-linear functions of the per-class false negative/false positive rate. Based on this observation, we present a general reduction of F-measure maximization to cost-sensitive classification with unknown costs. We then propose an algorithm with provable guarantees to obtain an approximately optimal classifier for the F-measure by solving a series of cost-sensitive classification problems. The strength of our analysis is to be valid on any dataset and any class of classifiers, extending the existing theoretical results on F-measures, which are asymptotic in nature. We present numerical experiments to illustrate the relative importance of cost asymmetry and thresholding when learning linear classifiers on various F-measure optimization tasks.

Based on this observation, we present a general reduction of F-measure maximization to cost-sensitive classification with unknown costs. We then propose an algorithm with provable guarantees to obtain an approximately optimal classifier for the F-measure by solving a series of cost-sensitive classification problems. The strength of our analysis is to be valid on any dataset and any class of classifiers, extending the existing theoretical results on F-measures, which are asymptotic in nature. We present numerical experiments to illustrate the relative importance of cost asymmetry and thresholding when learning linear classifiers on various F-measure optimization tasks.

This paper analyzes F-measures in binary, multiclass, and multilabel settings. Its central observation is that, in many scenarios, these measures have a pseudo-linear structure in the rates of false positives and false negatives.

Using that structure, the authors reduce F-measure maximization to cost-sensitive classification with initially unknown costs. They propose an algorithm that solves a sequence of classification problems assigning different costs to errors. The algorithm has provable guarantees for obtaining a classifier that is approximately optimal for the F-measure.

The analysis applies to any dataset and any classifier class within the scope of the reduction, extending prior results described as asymptotic. Numerical experiments with linear classifiers examine the relative importance of asymmetric error costs and thresholding across F-measure tasks. The contribution explains how an objective with nonlinear error tradeoffs can be approached through a series of cost-sensitive learning problems.
summary.tldr: A structural analysis reduces supported F-measure optimization problems to sequences of cost-sensitive classification tasks with approximation guarantees.

title: Optimizing F-Measures by Cost-Sensitive Classification

abstract: The Jacobi metric introduced in mathematical physics can be used to analyze Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). In a geometrical setting, each step of HMC corresponds to a geodesic on a Riemannian manifold with a Jacobi metric. Our calculation of the sectional curvature of this HMC manifold allows us to see that it is positive in cases such as sampling from a high dimensional multivariate Gaussian. We show that positive curvature can be used to prove theoretical concentration results for HMC Markov chains.

A geodesic is the geometric path associated with the metric, so this viewpoint turns the sampler's movement into a question about the shape of its underlying space.

The curvature result therefore applies to identified sampling settings and provides a geometric property that can be brought into the theoretical analysis of the chain.

The contribution is a connection between the geometry of HMC trajectories and probabilistic guarantees about the resulting chain. This makes the Jacobi-metric viewpoint useful beyond a reinterpretation of the algorithm: its curvature supplies a tool for proving theoretical behavior in applicable cases.
summary.tldr: A Jacobi-metric formulation connects positive curvature in certain HMC settings to theoretical concentration results.

title: Positive Curvature and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: We study the best-arm identification problem in linear bandit, where the rewards of the arms depend linearly on an unknown parameter $\theta^*$ and the objective is to return the arm with the largest reward. We characterize the complexity of the problem and introduce sample allocation strategies that pull arms to identify the best arm with a fixed confidence, while minimizing the sample budget. In particular, we show the importance of exploiting the global linear structure to improve the estimate of the reward of near-optimal arms. We analyze the proposed strategies and compare their empirical performance. Finally, as a by-product of our analysis, we point out the connection to the $G$-optimality criterion used in optimal experimental design.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best option when the rewards of several options share an unknown linear parameter. Each option is an arm, and sampling an arm provides information for deciding which has the largest reward. The objective is to make that final selection at a fixed confidence level while using as few samples as possible.

The central insight is that sampling decisions should exploit the linear relationship across all arms. Because rewards share a parameter, evidence relevant to one arm can also improve estimates for others. The authors emphasize using this global structure to sharpen estimates for near-optimal arms, where distinguishing the best choice requires particular care.

They characterize the problem's complexity, propose sample allocation strategies, analyze them, and compare their empirical performance. Their analysis also reveals a connection to the G-optimality criterion from experimental design. This places the choice of which arms to sample within a broader question: how should observations be allocated to make the estimates needed for a decision sufficiently precise?
summary.tldr: The paper develops sampling strategies that exploit shared linear reward structure to identify the best arm with fixed confidence.

title: Best-Arm Identification in Linear Bandits

abstract: Influence maximization in social networks has typically been studied in the context of contagion models and irreversible processes. In this paper, we consider an alternate model that treats individual opinions as spins in an Ising system at dynamic equilibrium. We formalize the \textit{Ising influence maximization} problem, which has a natural physical interpretation as maximizing the magnetization given a budget of external magnetic field. Under the mean-field (MF) approximation, we present a gradient ascent algorithm that uses the susceptibility to efficiently calculate local maxima of the magnetization, and we develop a number of sufficient conditions for when the MF magnetization is concave and our algorithm converges to a global optimum. We apply our algorithm on random and real-world networks, demonstrating, remarkably, that the MF optimal external fields (i.e., the external fields which maximize the MF magnetization) exhibit a phase transition from focusing on high-degree individuals at high temperatures to focusing on low-degree individuals at low temperatures. We also establish a number of novel results about the structure of steady-states in the ferromagnetic MF Ising model on general graphs, which are of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper models social influence using an Ising system at dynamic equilibrium, with individual opinions represented as spins. Influence maximization becomes the problem of allocating a limited external magnetic field to maximize magnetization. This gives the allocation problem a physical formulation suited to opinions that remain part of an ongoing equilibrium process.

Under a mean-field approximation, the authors develop a gradient ascent algorithm that uses susceptibility to efficiently find local maxima. They also establish sufficient conditions under which mean-field magnetization is concave and the algorithm converges to a global optimum. Those global guarantees depend on the conditions and concern the mean-field formulation.

Experiments on random and real-world networks reveal a phase transition in the optimal mean-field allocations. At high temperatures, influence focuses on high-degree individuals; at low temperatures, it shifts toward low-degree individuals. This shows that the preferred targets can change with the model's regime. The paper also establishes structural results about steady states of ferromagnetic mean-field Ising systems on general graphs.
summary.tldr: A mean-field Ising influence algorithm has conditional global guarantees and reveals temperature-dependent shifts in whom to target.

title: Maximizing Influence in an Ising Network: A Mean-Field Optimal Solution

abstract: This paper puts forth a novel algorithm, termed \emph{truncated generalized gradient flow} (TGGF), to solve for $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{C}^n$ a system of $m$ quadratic equations $y_i=|\langle\bm{a}_i,\bm{x}\rangle|^2$, $i=1,2,\ldots,m$, which even for $\left\{\bm{a}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{C}^n\right\}_{i=1}^m$ random is known to be \emph{NP-hard} in general. We prove that as soon as the number of equations $m$ is on the order of the number of unknowns $n$, TGGF recovers the solution exactly (up to a global unimodular constant) with high probability and complexity growing linearly with the time required to read the data $\left\{\left(\bm{a}_i;\,y_i\right)\right\}_{i=1}^m$. Specifically, TGGF proceeds in two stages: s1) A novel \emph{orthogonality-promoting} initialization that is obtained with simple power iterations; and, s2) a refinement of the initial estimate by successive updates of scalable \emph{truncated generalized gradient iterations}. The former is in sharp contrast to the existing spectral initializations, while the latter handles the rather challenging nonconvex and nonsmooth \emph{amplitude-based} cost function. Numerical tests demonstrate that: i) The novel orthogonality-promoting initialization method returns more accurate and robust estimates relative to its spectral counterparts; and ii) even with the same initialization, our refinement/truncation outperforms Wirtinger-based alternatives, all corroborating the superior performance of TGGF over state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a real or complex vector from measurements that give squared magnitudes of inner products. These quadratic equations discard information about a global sign or phase, and solving such systems is NP-hard in general. The proposed algorithm, truncated generalized gradient flow, targets recovery in the random-system setting.

The algorithm has two stages. An orthogonality-promoting initialization uses simple power iterations to produce a starting estimate. Subsequent truncated generalized-gradient updates refine it using an amplitude-based objective that is both nonconvex and nonsmooth. The initialization and refinement are designed to work together while keeping the computation scalable.

The authors prove high-probability exact recovery, up to a global unit-magnitude factor, once the number of equations is on the order of the number of unknowns. The stated computational complexity scales linearly with the time needed to read the data. Numerical tests report more accurate and robust initialization than spectral alternatives and better refinement than Wirtinger-based methods even when initialization is held fixed.
summary.tldr: TGGF combines orthogonality-promoting initialization with truncated gradient refinement to recover vectors efficiently from random quadratic measurements.

title: Solving Random Systems of Quadratic Equations via Truncated Generalized Gradient Flow

abstract: We consider the problem of optimizing an expensive objective function when a finite budget of total evaluations is prescribed. In that context, the optimal solution strategy for Bayesian optimization can be formulated as a dynamic programming instance. This results in a complex problem with uncountable, dimension-increasing state space and an uncountable control space. We show how to approximate the solution of this dynamic programming problem using rollout, and propose rollout heuristics specifically designed for the Bayesian optimization setting. We present numerical experiments showing that the resulting algorithm for optimization with a finite budget outperforms several popular Bayesian optimization algorithms.

We show how to approximate the solution of this dynamic programming problem using rollout, and propose rollout heuristics specifically designed for the Bayesian optimization setting. We present numerical experiments showing that the resulting algorithm for optimization with a finite budget outperforms several popular Bayesian optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: When each evaluation of an objective is expensive, choosing where to sample depends on how many evaluations remain. This paper studies Bayesian optimization with a prescribed finite budget, treating the entire sequence of future sampling decisions as part of the optimization problem rather than considering only the next query.

The optimal strategy can be expressed through dynamic programming, but its state space is uncountable and grows in dimension, and its control space is also uncountable. The authors approximate this difficult planning problem with rollout and develop rollout heuristics tailored to Bayesian optimization.

Numerical experiments show that the resulting finite-budget optimizer outperforms several popular Bayesian-optimization algorithms. The abstract does not identify the tested objectives or report effect sizes, and the method is an approximation rather than an exact solution of the full dynamic program. Its main contribution is a practical route toward budget-aware planning of costly experiments.
summary.tldr: Rollout approximations make Bayesian optimization account for a fixed evaluation budget.

title: Bayesian Optimization with a Finite Budget: An Approximate Dynamic Programming Approach

abstract: Most real-world networks are too large to be measured or studied directly and there is substantial interest in estimating global network properties from smaller sub-samples. One of the most important global properties is the number of vertices/nodes in the network. Estimating the number of vertices in a large network is a major challenge in computer science, epidemiology, demography, and intelligence analysis. In this paper we consider a population random graph G = (V;E) from the stochastic block model (SBM) with K communities/blocks. A sample is obtained by randomly choosing a subset W and letting G(W) be the induced subgraph in G of the vertices in W. In addition to G(W), we observe the total degree of each sampled vertex and its block membership. Given this partial information, we propose an efficient PopULation Size Estimation algorithm, called PULSE, that accurately estimates the size of the whole population as well as the size of each community. To support our theoretical analysis, we perform an exhaustive set of experiments to study the effects of sample size, K, and SBM model parameters on the accuracy of the estimates. The experimental results also demonstrate that PULSE significantly outperforms a widely-used method called the network scale-up estimator in a wide variety of scenarios.

paragraphs: When a network is too large to observe directly, even estimating how many nodes it contains becomes difficult. This paper addresses both the total population size and the sizes of individual communities. It studies the problem under a stochastic block model, in which the population graph contains K communities.

The observed data comes from a randomly chosen subset of nodes. Researchers see the graph induced by those nodes, each sampled node's total degree in the population graph, and its community membership. These additional observations are part of the setup: the method is not presented as estimating population size from the sampled graph alone.

The authors propose PULSE, an efficient algorithm for estimating the overall and community populations from this information. They support their theoretical analysis with extensive experiments varying sample size, community count, and model parameters. Across a wide variety of tested scenarios, PULSE significantly outperforms the network scale-up estimator. The results support using community structure and sampled nodes' broader connectivity to estimate otherwise unobserved population sizes.
summary.tldr: PULSE estimates network and community sizes from sampled nodes, their total degrees, and known community memberships under a stochastic block model.

title: Estimating the Size of a Large Network and its Communities from a Random Sample

abstract: The exponential mechanism is a general method to construct a randomized estimator that satisfies $(\varepsilon, 0)$-differential privacy. Recently, Wang et al. showed that the Gibbs posterior, which is a data-dependent probability distribution that contains the Bayesian posterior, is essentially equivalent to the exponential mechanism under certain boundedness conditions on the loss function. While the exponential mechanism provides a way to build an $(\varepsilon, 0)$-differential private algorithm, it requires boundedness of the loss function, which is quite stringent for some learning problems. In this paper, we focus on $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy of Gibbs posteriors with convex and Lipschitz loss functions. Our result extends the classical exponential mechanism, allowing the loss functions to have an unbounded sensitivity.

paragraphs: The exponential mechanism provides a general route to randomized estimation with pure differential privacy, expressed as (ε, 0)-privacy. The abstract describes a connection between that mechanism and Gibbs posteriors, a class of data-dependent probability distributions that includes Bayesian posteriors. The earlier connection relies on boundedness conditions on the loss function.

Those conditions can be restrictive for learning problems whose losses do not fit the required bounds. This paper instead studies Gibbs posteriors under convex and Lipschitz losses and targets (ε, δ)-differential privacy. The additional δ changes the privacy guarantee being sought, so the extension should be understood together with that change rather than as the same pure-privacy result under weaker assumptions.

The stated result permits loss functions with unbounded sensitivity, extending the reach of the classical exponential-mechanism framework. The important distinction is between removing a bounded-sensitivity requirement and removing all restrictions on the loss: convexity and the Lipschitz condition remain part of the setting studied. The contribution is a theoretical route to privacy for a broader class of losses through Gibbs-posterior estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes approximate differential privacy for Gibbs posteriors with convex, Lipschitz losses that may have unbounded sensitivity.

title: Differential Privacy without Sensitivity

abstract: Deep networks trained on large-scale data can learn transferable features to promote learning multiple tasks. Since deep features eventually transition from general to specific along deep networks, a fundamental problem of multi-task learning is how to exploit the task relatedness underlying parameter tensors and improve feature transferability in the multiple task-specific layers. This paper presents Multilinear Relationship Networks (MRN) that discover the task relationships based on novel tensor normal priors over parameter tensors of multiple task-specific layers in deep convolutional networks. By jointly learning transferable features and multilinear relationships of tasks and features, MRN is able to alleviate the dilemma of negative-transfer in the feature layers and under-transfer in the classifier layer. Experiments show that MRN yields state-of-the-art results on three multi-task learning datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a deep network can share useful information across multiple tasks as its features become increasingly task-specific. Sharing can be unhelpful when it transfers unsuitable information, while insufficient sharing can leave useful relationships unused. The authors focus on exploiting task relationships within the parameter tensors of multiple task-specific layers.

Their Multilinear Relationship Networks place tensor normal priors over those parameter tensors in a deep convolutional network. The model jointly learns transferable features and multilinear relationships involving tasks and features. This makes the relationships between tasks part of what the network learns across its task-specific layers, rather than treating transferability as a property of the features alone.

The authors report that this joint treatment can alleviate negative transfer in feature layers and insufficient transfer in the classifier layer. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art results on three multi-task learning datasets. These findings support learning structured relationships across multiple layers as a way to improve task sharing, with the reported performance established on those evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Multilinear Relationship Networks learn structured task and feature relationships across task-specific layers to improve transfer in multi-task learning.

title: Learning Multiple Tasks with Multilinear Relationship Networks

abstract: Brain processes occur at various timescales, ranging from milliseconds (neurons) to minutes and hours (behavior). Characterizing functional coupling among brain regions at these diverse timescales is key to understanding how the brain produces behavior. Here, we apply instantaneous and lag-based measures of conditional linear dependence, based on Granger-Geweke causality (GC), to infer network connections at distinct timescales from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Due to the slow sampling rate of fMRI, it is widely held that GC produces spurious and unreliable estimates of functional connectivity when applied to fMRI data. We challenge this claim with simulations and a novel machine learning approach. First, we show, with simulated fMRI data, that instantaneous and lag-based GC identify distinct timescales and complementary patterns of functional connectivity. Next, we analyze fMRI scans from 500 subjects and show that a linear classifier trained on either instantaneous or lag-based GC connectivity reliably distinguishes task versus rest brain states, with ~80-85% cross-validation accuracy. Importantly, instantaneous and lag-based GC exploit markedly different spatial and temporal patterns of connectivity to achieve robust classification. Our approach enables identifying functionally connected networks that operate at distinct timescales in the brain.

paragraphs: Brain activity unfolds over many timescales, so understanding connections between regions requires attention to both timing and spatial organization. This paper examines whether instantaneous and lag-based Granger-Geweke measures can identify distinct functional interactions in fMRI data. It challenges the view that fMRI's slow sampling necessarily makes these measures unreliable.

The authors first use simulated fMRI data to examine what the two types of measure capture. Their results show distinct timescales and complementary connectivity patterns. Both types of connectivity support approximately 80–85% cross-validation accuracy. However, the classifiers draw on markedly different spatial and temporal patterns. This distinction matters because similar classification performance can reflect different information about brain networks. Together, the simulations and classification results support using the measures to identify functional networks operating at different timescales; the reported connections concern functional dependence in the analyzed data.
summary.tldr: Instantaneous and lag-based fMRI connectivity measures capture complementary patterns and distinguish task from rest with about 80–85% cross-validation accuracy.

title: Mapping distinct timescales of functional interactions among brain networks

abstract: We investigate the integration of a planning mechanism into sequence-to-sequence models using attention. We develop a model which can plan ahead in the future when it computes its alignments between input and output sequences, constructing a matrix of proposed future alignments and a commitment vector that governs whether to follow or recompute the plan. This mechanism is inspired by the recently proposed strategic attentive reader and writer (STRAW) model for Reinforcement Learning. Our proposed model is end-to-end trainable using primarily differentiable operations. We show that it outperforms a strong baseline on character-level translation tasks from WMT'15, the algorithmic task of finding Eulerian circuits of graphs, and question generation from the text. Our analysis demonstrates that the model computes qualitatively intuitive alignments, converges faster than the baselines, and achieves superior performance with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Attention connects parts of an input sequence with the output being generated. This paper adds a planning mechanism so that a sequence-to-sequence model can propose future alignments as well as use the current one. The aim is to make attention a process that can organize decisions across several future output steps.

The model constructs a matrix containing proposed future alignments. A commitment vector controls whether it continues following that plan or recomputes it. Inspired by the STRAW model from reinforcement learning, the mechanism uses primarily differentiable operations and can be trained end to end. Planning and decisions about revising the plan are therefore included within the trainable model.

The authors evaluate character-level translation, finding Eulerian circuits in graphs, and generating questions from text. The model outperforms a strong baseline on these tasks. Their analysis also finds intuitive alignment patterns, faster convergence than the baselines, and better performance with fewer parameters. These results support future attention planning as a useful addition across the sequence-generation problems studied.
summary.tldr: Planning future attention alignments improves tested sequence-to-sequence tasks while allowing the model to decide when to revise its plan.

title: Plan, Attend, Generate: Planning for Sequence-to-Sequence Models

abstract: In linear stochastic bandits, it is commonly assumed that payoffs are with sub-Gaussian noises. In this paper, under a weaker assumption on noises, we study the problem of \underline{lin}ear stochastic {\underline b}andits with h{\underline e}avy-{\underline t}ailed payoffs (LinBET), where the distributions have finite moments of order $1+\epsilon$, for some $\epsilon\in (0,1]$. We rigorously analyze the regret lower bound of LinBET as $\Omega(T^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}})$, implying that finite moments of order 2 (i.e., finite variances) yield the bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, with $T$ being the total number of rounds to play bandits. The provided lower bound also indicates that the state-of-the-art algorithms for LinBET are far from optimal. By adopting median of means with a well-designed allocation of decisions and truncation based on historical information, we develop two novel bandit algorithms, where the regret upper bounds match the lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to solve LinBET optimally in the sense of the polynomial order on $T$. Our proposed algorithms are evaluated based on synthetic datasets, and outperform the state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Linear stochastic bandits involve repeatedly choosing actions while learning how their features relate to rewards. This paper studies rewards with heavy tails, allowing unusually large observations under a weaker assumption than the commonly used sub-Gaussian noise condition. Specifically, it assumes finite moments of order 1+ε, with ε between zero and one.

The authors establish a regret lower bound of Ω(T^(1/(1+ε))), where T is the number of rounds. Regret measures the accumulated cost of making imperfect decisions while learning. When ε equals one, the assumption becomes finite variance and the bound becomes Ω(√T). The lower bound also shows that previous algorithms leave room for improvement in their dependence on the number of rounds.

Two proposed algorithms address that gap using median-of-means estimation with carefully allocated decisions and truncation informed by past observations. Their upper bounds match the lower bound apart from polylogarithmic factors, establishing optimal polynomial dependence on T. Synthetic experiments also report improvements over previous methods, complementing the theoretical characterization of what is achievable under heavy-tailed rewards.
summary.tldr: Two robust linear bandit algorithms match a heavy-tailed regret lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors under a finite-moment assumption.

title: Almost Optimal Algorithms for Linear Stochastic Bandits with Heavy-Tailed Payoffs

abstract: This paper addresses the mode collapse for generative adversarial networks (GANs). We view modes as a geometric structure of data distribution in a metric space. Under this geometric lens, we embed subsamples of the dataset from an arbitrary metric space into the L2 space, while preserving their pairwise distance distribution. Not only does this metric embedding determine the dimensionality of the latent space automatically, it also enables us to construct a mixture of Gaussians to draw latent space random vectors. We use the Gaussian mixture model in tandem with a simple augmentation of the objective function to train GANs. Every major step of our method is supported by theoretical analysis, and our experiments on real and synthetic data confirm that the generator is able to produce samples spreading over most of the modes while avoiding unwanted samples, outperforming several recent GAN variants on a number of metrics and offering new features.

Not only does this metric embedding determine the dimensionality of the latent space automatically, it also enables us to construct a mixture of Gaussians to draw latent space random vectors. We use the Gaussian mixture model in tandem with a simple augmentation of the objective function to train GANs. Every major step of our method is supported by theoretical analysis, and our experiments on real and synthetic data confirm that the generator is able to produce samples spreading over most of the modes while avoiding unwanted samples, outperforming several recent GAN variants on a number of metrics and offering new features.

paragraphs: Mode collapse occurs when a generative adversarial network fails to represent much of the variety in its target distribution. BourGAN approaches this problem geometrically: different modes are treated as structure in a space where distances between data points can be measured. That structure guides the design of the generator’s latent inputs.

The method embeds a subsample of the dataset from an arbitrary metric space into Euclidean space while preserving the distribution of pairwise distances. The embedding determines the latent dimension automatically and supports construction of a Gaussian mixture from which latent vectors are sampled. Training combines this mixture with an additional term in the GAN objective.

The paper supplies theoretical analysis for every major step and evaluates the method on real and synthetic data. In those experiments, generated samples cover most modes while avoiding unwanted samples, and the method outperforms several recent GAN variants on multiple metrics. The contribution is to connect latent-space construction directly to the geometry of the data, rather than treating the source of latent randomness as independent of the mode-collapse problem.
summary.tldr: BourGAN uses distance-preserving embeddings to construct a Gaussian-mixture latent space that improves empirical coverage of data modes.

title: BourGAN: Generative Networks with Metric Embeddings

abstract: For the task of generating complex outputs such as source code, editing existing outputs can be easier than generating complex outputs from scratch. With this motivation, we propose an approach that first retrieves a training example based on the input (e.g., natural language description) and then edits it to the desired output (e.g., code). Our contribution is a computationally efficient method for learning a retrieval model that embeds the input in a task-dependent way without relying on a hand-crafted metric or incurring the expense of jointly training the retriever with the editor. Our retrieve-and-edit framework can be applied on top of any base model. We show that on a new autocomplete task for GitHub Python code and the Hearthstone cards benchmark, retrieve-and-edit significantly boosts the performance of a vanilla sequence-to-sequence model on both tasks.

We show that on a new autocomplete task for GitHub Python code and the Hearthstone cards benchmark, retrieve-and-edit significantly boosts the performance of a vanilla sequence-to-sequence model on both tasks.

paragraphs: Generating a complex structured output, such as source code, can require getting many connected pieces right. This paper starts from the idea that adapting an existing example may be easier. Its framework retrieves a training example using the current input, then edits that example to produce the requested output.

The central contribution is how the system learns what to retrieve. It represents inputs in a space shaped by the prediction task, allowing retrieval to reflect the task rather than a manually designed similarity rule. The proposed training method is computationally efficient and avoids the expense of jointly training the retrieval component and the editor.

The framework is presented as applicable on top of any base model. The authors evaluate it with a standard sequence-to-sequence model on a new GitHub Python autocomplete task and the Hearthstone cards benchmark. They report substantial improvements on both, supporting retrieval followed by editing as a useful way to strengthen structured prediction.
summary.tldr: Learning to retrieve useful examples and then edit them substantially improves sequence-to-sequence prediction on two code-related tasks.

title: A Retrieve-and-Edit Framework for Predicting Structured Outputs

abstract: Due to the inherent model uncertainty, learning to infer Bayesian posterior from a few-shot dataset is an important step towards robust meta-learning. In this paper, we propose a novel Bayesian model-agnostic meta-learning method. The proposed method combines efficient gradient-based meta-learning with nonparametric variational inference in a principled probabilistic framework. Unlike previous methods, during fast adaptation, the method is capable of learning complex uncertainty structure beyond a simple Gaussian approximation, and during meta-update, a novel Bayesian mechanism prevents meta-level overfitting. Remaining a gradient-based method, it is also the first Bayesian model-agnostic meta-learning method applicable to various tasks including reinforcement learning. Experiment results show the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method in sinusoidal regression, image classification, active learning, and reinforcement learning.

Experiment results show the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method in sinusoidal regression, image classification, active learning, and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Learning a new task from only a few examples leaves considerable uncertainty about which model best explains the observations. This paper develops Bayesian model-agnostic meta-learning to represent that uncertainty during rapid adaptation. Its aim is to learn how to infer a distribution over plausible models from a small task dataset.

The method combines gradient-based meta-learning with nonparametric variational inference in a probabilistic framework. During adaptation, it can represent uncertainty more complex than a simple Gaussian approximation. During the meta-update, a separate Bayesian mechanism is designed to prevent overfitting at the level where information is shared across tasks. The approach therefore addresses both uncertainty within a new task and overfitting across the training tasks.

The method retains gradient-based learning and applies to several kinds of problems, including reinforcement learning. Experiments examine sinusoidal regression, image classification, active learning, and reinforcement learning, with results supporting its accuracy and robustness. The contribution is a way to combine fast task adaptation with richer uncertainty modeling across these different learning settings.
summary.tldr: Bayesian model-agnostic meta-learning combines fast gradient-based adaptation with richer uncertainty inference and a Bayesian mechanism against meta-level overfitting.

title: Bayesian Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning

abstract: Metric Elicitation is a principled framework for selecting the performance metric that best reflects implicit user preferences. However, available strategies have so far been limited to binary classification. In this paper, we propose novel strategies for eliciting multiclass classification performance metrics using only relative preference feedback. We also show that the strategies are robust to both finite sample and feedback noise.
originalAbstract: Metric Elicitation is a principled framework for selecting the performance metric that best reflects implicit user preferences. However, available strategies have so far been limited to binary classification. In this paper, we propose novel strategies for eliciting multiclass classification performance metrics using only relative preference feedback. We also show that the strategies are robust to both finite sample and feedback noise.

paragraphs: Selecting a classification metric amounts to deciding what kinds of performance a user values. Those preferences may be implicit, making it difficult to choose a metric directly. This paper studies metric elicitation: a principled process for finding a performance measure that reflects the user’s preferences.

The authors extend this framework from binary classification to classification with multiple classes. Their strategies use only relative preference feedback. In practical terms, this means learning from judgments about which alternative is preferred, rather than requiring the user to specify the desired metric outright. The contribution concerns how evaluation criteria are selected for multiclass problems.

The paper also shows robustness to finite-sample effects and noisy feedback. These address two distinct sources of uncertainty: limited data used to assess performance and imperfect preference information from the user. The stated result supports eliciting metrics without assuming unlimited data or perfectly reliable feedback. Its significance is to make preference-based metric selection applicable beyond two-class problems while accounting for uncertainty in the information it receives.
summary.tldr: The paper extends preference-based performance metric elicitation to multiclass classification with robustness to limited data and noisy feedback.

title: Multiclass Performance Metric Elicitation

abstract: We propose the first black-box approach to obtaining long-term memory guarantees for online learning in the sense of Bousquet and Warmuth, 2002, by reducing the problem to achieving typical switching regret. Specifically, for the classical expert problem with $K$ actions and $T$ rounds, using our general framework we develop various algorithms with a regret bound of order $\order(\sqrt{T(S\ln T + n \ln K)})$ compared to any sequence of experts with $S-1$ switches among $n \leq \min\{S, K\}$ distinct experts. In addition, by plugging specific adaptive algorithms into our framework we also achieve the best of both stochastic and adversarial environments simultaneously, which resolves an open problem of Warmuth and Koolen 2014. Furthermore, we extend our results to the sparse multi-armed bandit setting and show both negative and positive results for long-term memory guarantees. As a side result, our lower bound also implies that sparse losses do not help improve the worst-case regret for contextual bandit, a sharp contrast with the non-contextual case.

paragraphs: Online learning can require repeatedly returning to options that were useful earlier. This paper develops a general framework for long-term memory guarantees, comparing a learner with sequences that switch among experts while reusing a limited number of distinct experts. The approach reduces this problem to obtaining conventional switching-regret guarantees.

For K actions and T rounds, the framework yields regret of order sqrt(T(S ln T + n ln K)), against sequences with S minus one switches among n distinct experts. The bound separately tracks switching and the number of different experts used. With particular adaptive algorithms plugged into the framework, the authors also obtain guarantees suited to both stochastic and adversarial environments simultaneously.

The paper extends its investigation to sparse multi-armed bandits, establishing both positive and negative results for long-term memory. A related lower bound shows that sparse losses do not improve worst-case contextual-bandit regret. This distinguishes the contextual setting from the non-contextual one and identifies a boundary on the usefulness of sparsity.
summary.tldr: A general reduction gives online learners long-term memory guarantees that account for both expert switching and reuse.

title: Equipping Experts/Bandits with Long-term Memory

abstract: We study differentially private (DP) algorithms for stochastic convex optimization (SCO). In this problem the goal is to approximately minimize the population loss given i.i.d.~samples from a distribution over convex and Lipschitz loss functions. A long line of existing work on private convex optimization focuses on the empirical loss and derives asymptotically tight bounds on the excess empirical loss. However a significant gap exists in the known bounds for the population loss. We show that, up to logarithmic factors, the optimal excess population loss for DP algorithms is equal to the larger of the optimal non-private excess population loss, and the optimal excess empirical loss of DP algorithms. This implies that, contrary to intuition based on private ERM, private SCO has asymptotically the same rate of $1/\sqrt{n}$ as non-private SCO in the parameter regime most common in practice. The best previous result in this setting gives rate of $1/n^{1/4}$. Our approach builds on existing differentially private algorithms and relies on the analysis of algorithmic stability to ensure generalization.
