paragraphs: Private stochastic convex optimization aims to minimize population loss using independent, identically distributed samples while satisfying differential privacy. The paper assumes convex, Lipschitz loss functions. Much previous work tightly characterized excess loss on the observed sample, but bounds for the underlying population remained substantially less precise.

The authors show that, up to logarithmic factors, optimal private excess population loss equals the larger of two quantities: optimal non-private excess population loss and optimal private excess empirical loss. This relates the cost of learning from finite data to the cost of protecting privacy, giving a sharp characterization of their combined effect.

In the parameter regime the authors describe as most common in practice, private optimization consequently achieves the same asymptotic 1/sqrt(n) rate as non-private optimization. The previous best result in that setting was 1/n^(1/4). The approach builds on existing private algorithms and analyzes their stability to establish generalization. The matching rate is tied to the specified regime, while the broader maximum-of-two-quantities result describes the tradeoff more generally.
summary.tldr: Sharp population-loss bounds show private convex optimization can match the non-private 1/sqrt(n) rate in a practically common parameter regime.

title: Private Stochastic Convex Optimization with Optimal Rates

abstract: Deep generative models are able to suggest new organic molecules by generating strings, trees, and graphs representing their structure. While such models allow one to generate molecules with desirable properties, they give no guarantees that the molecules can actually be synthesized in practice. We propose a new molecule generation model, mirroring a more realistic real-world process, where (a) reactants are selected, and (b) combined to form more complex molecules. More specifically, our generative model proposes a bag of initial reactants (selected from a pool of commercially-available molecules) and uses a reaction model to predict how they react together to generate new molecules. We first show that the model can generate diverse, valid and unique molecules due to the useful inductive biases of modeling reactions. Furthermore, our model allows chemists to interrogate not only the properties of the generated molecules but also the feasibility of the synthesis routes. We conclude by using our model to solve retrosynthesis problems, predicting a set of reactants that can produce a target product.

paragraphs: Generating a molecular structure with attractive properties does not establish that chemists can make it. This paper addresses that gap by organizing molecule generation around a proposed chemical process. Instead of proposing only a finished structure, the model selects starting materials and predicts the molecule that their reaction would produce.

The starting materials come from a pool of commercially available molecules. The generative model proposes a collection of these reactants, and a reaction model predicts how they combine. This design introduces information about reactions into the generation process, giving chemists both a proposed product and starting materials whose suitability they can investigate.

The authors show that the approach generates diverse, valid, and unique molecules, attributing these properties to the useful structure imposed by modeling reactions. They also apply it to retrosynthesis: finding reactants predicted to produce a specified target. The contribution is a way to connect molecular proposals with assessable synthesis routes; the abstract does not establish that every predicted reaction succeeds in practice.
summary.tldr: A molecule generator selects commercially available reactants and predicts their products, making proposed synthesis routes available for inspection.

title: A Model to Search for Synthesizable Molecules

abstract: We introduce deep scale-spaces, a generalization of convolutional neural networks, exploiting the scale symmetry structure of conventional image recognition tasks. Put plainly, the class of an image is invariant to the scale at which it is viewed. We construct scale equivariant cross-correlations based on a principled extension of convolutions, grounded in the theory of scale-spaces and semigroups. As a very basic operation, these cross-correlations can be used in almost any modern deep learning architecture in a plug-and-play manner. We demonstrate our networks on the Patch Camelyon and Cityscapes datasets, to prove their utility and perform introspective studies to further understand their properties.
originalAbstract: We introduce deep scale-spaces, a generalization of convolutional neural networks, exploiting the scale symmetry structure of conventional image recognition tasks. Put plainly, the class of an image is invariant to the scale at which it is viewed. We construct scale equivariant cross-correlations based on a principled extension of convolutions, grounded in the theory of scale-spaces and semigroups. As a very basic operation, these cross-correlations can be used in almost any modern deep learning architecture in a plug-and-play manner. We demonstrate our networks on the Patch Camelyon and Cityscapes datasets, to prove their utility and perform introspective studies to further understand their properties.

paragraphs: In conventional image recognition, viewing an image at a different scale should preserve its class. This paper uses that symmetry to generalize convolutional neural networks. Its aim is to make scale changes part of the network's mathematical structure, so internal computations respond to changes in viewing scale in a controlled way.

The proposed building blocks are scale-equivariant cross-correlations, developed as an extension of convolution using scale-space and semigroup theory. Equivariance means that changing the input scale produces a corresponding structured change in the representation. This relates the behavior of internal features across scales to the broader goal of recognizing the same class at different sizes.

Because cross-correlation is a basic network operation, the authors describe these components as suitable for plug-and-play use in almost any modern deep learning architecture. They demonstrate the networks on Patch Camelyon and Cityscapes and conduct introspective studies of their properties. The contribution is both an architectural operation and a principled account of how scale symmetry can shape image processing.
summary.tldr: Deep scale-spaces extend convolution with scale-equivariant operations that can be incorporated into modern image-processing networks.

title: Deep Scale-spaces: Equivariance Over Scale

abstract: Ranking and selection tasks appear in different contexts with specific desiderata, such as the maximizaton of average relevance on the top of the list, the requirement of diverse rankings, or, relatedly, the focus on providing at least one relevant items to as many users as possible. This paper addresses the question of which of these tasks are asymptotically solved by sorting by decreasing order of expected utility, for some suitable notion of utility, or, equivalently, \emph{when is square loss regression consistent for ranking \emph{via} score-and-sort?}. We provide an answer to this question in the form of a structural characterization of ranking losses for which a suitable regression is consistent. This result has two fundamental corollaries. First, whenever there exists a consistent approach based on convex risk minimization, there also is a consistent approach based on regression. Second, when regression is not consistent, there are data distributions for which consistent surrogate approaches necessarily have non-trivial local minima, and optimal scoring function are necessarily discontinuous, even when the underlying data distribution is regular. In addition to providing a better understanding of surrogate approaches for ranking, these results illustrate the intrinsic difficulty of solving general ranking problems with the score-and-sort approach.

This paper addresses the question of which of these tasks are asymptotically solved by sorting by decreasing order of expected utility, for some suitable notion of utility, or, equivalently, \emph{when is square loss regression consistent for ranking \emph{via} score-and-sort?}. Second, when regression is not consistent, there are data distributions for which consistent surrogate approaches necessarily have non-trivial local minima, and optimal scoring function are necessarily discontinuous, even when the underlying data distribution is regular. In addition to providing a better understanding of surrogate approaches for ranking, these results illustrate the intrinsic difficulty of solving general ranking problems with the score-and-sort approach.

paragraphs: Ranking systems often assign each item a score and then sort the scores. Yet ranking objectives differ: some emphasize relevance near the top, while others prioritize diversity or serving more users with at least one relevant item. This paper asks which objectives can be solved asymptotically by estimating an appropriate expected utility through square-loss regression.

The authors give a structural characterization of ranking losses for which this regression-based approach is consistent. One consequence is that whenever a consistent method based on convex risk minimization exists, a consistent regression method also exists. This establishes how far a comparatively simple score-and-sort strategy can reach within that class of learning approaches.

The characterization also exposes difficulties outside that regime. When regression is inconsistent, some data distributions force consistent surrogate approaches to have nontrivial local minima and optimal scoring functions to be discontinuous, even for regular underlying distributions. These are existence results about difficult distributions. They explain why changing the training surrogate cannot always remove the intrinsic obstacles associated with solving ranking problems through scores.
summary.tldr: A structural characterization identifies when regression followed by sorting is consistent and reveals unavoidable difficulties for some other ranking problems.

title: On ranking via sorting by estimated expected utility

abstract: Facial expression and action units (AUs) represent two levels of descriptions of the facial behavior. Due to the underlying facial anatomy and the need to form a meaningful coherent expression, they are strongly correlated. This paper proposes to systematically capture their dependencies and incorporate them into a deep learning framework for joint facial expression recognition and action unit detection. Specifically, we first propose a constraint optimization method to encode the generic knowledge on expression-AUs probabilistic dependencies into a Bayesian Network (BN). The BN is then integrated into a deep learning framework as a weak supervision for an AU detection model. A data-driven facial expression recognition(FER) model is then constructed from data. Finally, the FER model and AU detection model are trained jointly to refine their learning. Evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed knowledge integration in improving the performance of both the FER model and the AU detection model. The proposed AU detection model is demonstrated to be able to achieve competitive performance without AU annotations. Furthermore, the proposed Bayesian Network capturing the generic knowledge is demonstrated to generalize well to different datasets.

paragraphs: Facial expressions and facial action units describe behavior at different levels, but they are related through anatomy and the combinations that form coherent expressions. This paper uses those dependencies to connect expression recognition with action-unit detection. The central idea is to make general knowledge about their relationship useful during neural-network training.

A constrained optimization method first encodes probabilistic expression–action-unit dependencies in a Bayesian network. That network supplies weak supervision for the action-unit detector. A separate facial expression model is learned from data, after which the two models are trained jointly to refine their learning. This gives the detector guidance from structured knowledge while also allowing the models to learn from observations.

Benchmark evaluations show improvements for both expression recognition and action-unit detection. The authors also report competitive action-unit detection without action-unit annotations, and good generalization of the knowledge-based Bayesian network across datasets. These findings suggest that explicitly modeling relationships between labels can reduce reliance on direct annotations while helping both related recognition tasks.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian network of expression–action-unit relationships guides joint neural learning, improving both tasks and enabling competitive action-unit detection without its annotations.

title: Knowledge Augmented Deep Neural Networks for Joint Facial Expression and Action Unit Recognition

abstract: Machine learning as a service has given raise to privacy concerns surrounding clients' data and providers' models and has catalyzed research in private inference (PI): methods to process inferences without disclosing inputs. Recently, researchers have adapted cryptographic techniques to show PI is possible, however all solutions increase inference latency beyond practical limits. This paper makes the observation that existing models are ill-suited for PI and proposes a novel NAS method, named CryptoNAS, for finding and tailoring models to the needs of PI. The key insight is that in PI operator latency cost are inverted: non-linear operations (e.g., ReLU) dominate latency, while linear layers become effectively free. We develop the idea of a ReLU budget as a proxy for inference latency and use CryptoNAS to build models that maximize accuracy within a given budget. CryptoNAS improves accuracy by 3.4% and latency by 2.4x over the state-of-the-art.

This paper makes the observation that existing models are ill-suited for PI and proposes a novel NAS method, named CryptoNAS, for finding and tailoring models to the needs of PI. The key insight is that in PI operator latency cost are inverted: non-linear operations (e.g., ReLU) dominate latency, while linear layers become effectively free. paragraphs: Private inference uses cryptographic techniques to process a client's input without disclosing it. The paper identifies inference latency as a major obstacle and argues that conventional neural network architectures are poorly matched to this setting. An architecture that is efficient under ordinary computation may allocate work badly when cryptographic processing changes which operations are expensive.

CryptoNAS centers architecture search on that changed cost structure. In the private inference setting described, nonlinear operations such as ReLU dominate latency, while linear layers are effectively free by comparison. The authors therefore use a ReLU budget as a proxy for latency and search for models that maximize accuracy while staying within that budget.

The reported results improve accuracy by 3.4% and latency by a factor of 2.4 over the state of the art. These findings support tailoring architecture search to the costs of private inference, rather than assuming ordinary efficiency measures transfer directly. The budget is a latency proxy: its role is to guide model design toward the operations that matter most in this computational setting.
summary.tldr: CryptoNAS improves private inference by searching for accurate networks under a budget on costly ReLU operations.

title: CryptoNAS: Private Inference on a ReLU Budget

abstract: While the self-attention mechanism has been widely used in a wide variety of tasks, it has the unfortunate property of a quadratic cost with respect to the input length, which makes it difficult to deal with long inputs. In this paper, we present a method for accelerating and structuring self-attentions: Sparse Adaptive Connection (SAC). In SAC, we regard the input sequence as a graph and attention operations are performed between linked nodes. In contrast with previous self-attention models with pre-defined structures (edges), the model learns to construct attention edges to improve task-specific performances. In this way, the model is able to select the most salient nodes and reduce the quadratic complexity regardless of the sequence length. Based on SAC, we show that previous variants of self-attention models are its special cases. Through extensive experiments on neural machine translation, language modeling, graph representation learning and image classification, we demonstrate SAC is competitive with state-of-the-art models while significantly reducing memory cost.

In SAC, we regard the input sequence as a graph and attention operations are performed between linked nodes. paragraphs: Standard self-attention has a computational cost that grows quadratically with input length, making long inputs difficult to handle. Sparse Adaptive Connection, or SAC, represents the input sequence as a graph. Attention takes place only between nodes connected by edges, making the connection pattern a central part of how the model processes information.

SAC learns these attention edges to improve task performance instead of relying on a predefined structure. This lets it select salient nodes and reduce the quadratic complexity associated with unrestricted attention. The authors also show that earlier self-attention variants can be expressed as special cases, positioning SAC as a broader framework for choosing attention structure.

Experiments cover neural machine translation, language modeling, graph representation learning, and image classification. SAC is competitive with state-of-the-art models while substantially reducing memory use in the reported evaluations. The results support learning sparse connections as a way to preserve useful task performance across several applications while reducing the resources consumed by attention.
summary.tldr: SAC learns sparse attention connections, reducing memory costs while remaining competitive across language, graph, and image tasks.

title: SAC: Accelerating and Structuring Self-Attention via Sparse Adaptive Connection

abstract: We present the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB), a diverse set of challenging and realistic benchmark datasets to facilitate scalable, robust, and reproducible graph machine learning (ML) research. OGB datasets are large-scale, encompass multiple important graph ML tasks, and cover a diverse range of domains, ranging from social and information networks to biological networks, molecular graphs, source code ASTs, and knowledge graphs. For each dataset, we provide a unified evaluation protocol using meaningful application-specific data splits and evaluation metrics. In addition to building the datasets, we also perform extensive benchmark experiments for each dataset. Our experiments suggest that OGB datasets present significant challenges of scalability to large-scale graphs and out-of-distribution generalization under realistic data splits, indicating fruitful opportunities for future research. Finally, OGB provides an automated end-to-end graph ML pipeline that simplifies and standardizes the process of graph data loading, experimental setup, and model evaluation. OGB will be regularly updated and welcomes inputs from the community. OGB datasets as well as data loaders, evaluation scripts, baseline code, and leaderboards are publicly available at https://ogb.stanford.edu .

It covers multiple tasks and domains, including social and information networks, biological networks, molecules, source-code structures, and knowledge graphs. The aim is to support research that is scalable, robust, and reproducible across varied graph problems.

Each dataset comes with a unified evaluation protocol, application-specific data splits, and suitable metrics. An automated pipeline standardizes data loading, experimental setup, and evaluation. The benchmark also supplies baseline code and leaderboards, making the evaluation process a substantial part of the contribution alongside the datasets themselves.

The authors conduct extensive benchmark experiments and find significant challenges in scaling to large graphs and generalizing beyond the training distribution under realistic splits. Those results identify opportunities for future methods to improve. OGB therefore offers both shared experimental infrastructure and evidence that the included problems remain demanding, especially when evaluation reflects the kinds of distribution differences that arise in the intended applications.
summary.tldr: Open Graph Benchmark supplies large, varied graph datasets and standardized evaluations that expose challenges in scalability and out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Open Graph Benchmark: Datasets for Machine Learning on Graphs

abstract: We propose firefly neural architecture descent, a general framework for progressively and dynamically growing neural networks to jointly optimize the networks' parameters and architectures. Our method works in a steepest descent fashion, which iteratively finds the best network within a functional neighborhood of the original network that includes a diverse set of candidate network structures. By using Taylor approximation, the optimal network structure in the neighborhood can be found with a greedy selection procedure. We show that firefly descent can flexibly grow networks both wider and deeper, and can be applied to learn accurate but resource-efficient neural architectures that avoid catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. Empirically, firefly descent achieves promising results on both neural architecture search and continual learning. In particular, on a challenging continual image classification task, it learns networks that are smaller in size but have higher average accuracy than those learned by the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Neural-network training usually involves choosing a structure as well as learning its parameters. Firefly neural architecture descent brings those decisions together by progressively growing the network during optimization. The framework can increase both width and depth, allowing its structure to evolve as learning proceeds instead of treating architecture as a separate, fixed choice.

The method follows a steepest-descent idea over a neighborhood of possible network functions. That neighborhood includes diverse candidate structures, so an optimization step can change the architecture as well as its numerical parameters. A Taylor approximation makes the local structural search amenable to a greedy selection procedure, providing a practical route through the candidate changes.

The authors apply the framework to architecture search and continual learning, where retaining earlier knowledge matters while learning new tasks. They report promising results in both settings and show that the approach can learn accurate, resource-efficient architectures that avoid catastrophic forgetting. On a challenging continual image-classification task, the resulting networks are smaller and have higher average accuracy than those learned by the state-of-the-art methods considered.
summary.tldr: Firefly descent jointly optimizes network weights and growing architectures, with promising results in architecture search and continual learning.

title: Firefly Neural Architecture Descent: a General Approach for Growing Neural Networks

abstract: This paper studies offline Imitation Learning (IL) where an agent learns to imitate an expert demonstrator without additional online environment interactions. Instead, the learner is presented with a static offline dataset of state-action-next state triples from a potentially less proficient behavior policy. We introduce Model-based IL from Offline data (MILO): an algorithmic framework that utilizes the static dataset to solve the offline IL problem efficiently both in theory and in practice. In theory, even if the behavior policy is highly sub-optimal compared to the expert, we show that as long as the data from the behavior policy provides sufficient coverage on the expert state-action traces (and with no necessity for a global coverage over the entire state-action space), MILO can provably combat the covariate shift issue in IL. Complementing our theory results, we also demonstrate that a practical implementation of our approach mitigates covariate shift on benchmark MuJoCo continuous control tasks. We demonstrate that with behavior policies whose performances are less than half of that of the expert, MILO still successfully imitates with an extremely low number of expert state-action pairs while traditional offline IL methods such as behavior cloning (BC) fail completely. Source code is provided at https://github.com/jdchang1/milo.

paragraphs: Offline imitation learning asks an agent to learn expert behavior without collecting additional interactions from the environment. This paper studies how a fixed dataset of transitions from a potentially much weaker behavior policy can help. It introduces MILO, a model-based framework that uses those recorded state-action-next-state examples to support imitation.

The theoretical result depends on a targeted coverage condition: the offline data must sufficiently cover the expert's state-action traces. It need not cover the entire state-action space. Under that condition, MILO can provably combat covariate shift even when the policy that collected the data performs substantially worse than the expert.

Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks support the approach. With behavior policies performing at less than half the expert's level, MILO successfully imitates using very few expert state-action pairs, while behavior cloning fails in the reported comparison. The result distinguishes data quality from behavioral proficiency: weaker policies can still supply useful offline experience when their data cover the parts of the problem needed for imitation.
summary.tldr: MILO can mitigate offline imitation-learning covariate shift using weak-policy data, provided it sufficiently covers the expert's state-action traces.

title: Mitigating Covariate Shift in Imitation Learning via Offline Data With Partial Coverage

abstract: Fairness has emerged as an important consideration in algorithmic decision making. Unfairness occurs when an agent with higher merit obtains a worse outcome than an agent with lower merit. Our central point is that a primary cause of unfairness is uncertainty. A principal or algorithm making decisions never has access to the agents' true merit, and instead uses proxy features that only imperfectly predict merit (e.g., GPA, star ratings, recommendation letters). None of these ever fully capture an agent's merit; yet existing approaches have mostly been defining fairness notions directly based on observed features and outcomes.Our primary point is that it is more principled to acknowledge and model the uncertainty explicitly. The role of observed features is to give rise to a posterior distribution of the agents' merits. We use this viewpoint to define a notion of approximate fairness in ranking. We call an algorithm $\phi$-fair (for $\phi \in [0,1]$) if it has the following property for all agents $x$ and all $k$: if agent $x$ is among the top $k$ agents with respect to merit with probability at least $\rho$ (according to the posterior merit distribution), then the algorithm places the agent among the top $k$ agents in its ranking with probability at least $\phi \rho$.We show how to compute rankings that optimally trade off approximate fairness against utility to the principal. In addition to the theoretical characterization, we present an empirical analysis of the potential impact of the approach in simulation studies. For real-world validation, we applied the approach in the context of a paper recommendation system that we built and fielded at the KDD 2020 conference.

paragraphs: Rankings often rely on imperfect indicators of merit, such as grades or ratings. This paper argues that fairness should explicitly account for the resulting uncertainty. Observed features are used to form a posterior distribution over merit, so fairness depends on plausible underlying merits rather than treating proxy measurements as exact.

The proposed definition links an agent’s chance of deserving a high position to its chance of receiving one. If the posterior assigns probability at least ρ to an agent belonging in the top k, a φ-fair algorithm must place that agent in the top k with probability at least φρ. This requirement applies to every agent and every cutoff k, with φ controlling the strength of the guarantee.

The authors show how to compute rankings that optimally balance this approximate fairness against utility to the decision-maker. They also study potential effects in simulations and apply the approach to a paper recommendation system fielded at KDD 2020. The framework makes uncertainty an explicit part of allocating ranking opportunities, with guarantees defined relative to the posterior merit distribution.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic ranking-fairness definition ties placement opportunities to uncertain merit and supports optimal trade-offs with decision-maker utility.

title: Fairness in Ranking under Uncertainty

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, i.e., an imperceptible perturbation to the input can mislead DNNs trained on clean images into making erroneous predictions. To tackle this, adversarial training is currently the most effective defense method, by augmenting the training set with adversarial samples generated on the fly. \textbf{Interestingly, we discover for the first time that there exist subnetworks with inborn robustness, matching or surpassing the robust accuracy of the adversarially trained networks with comparable model sizes, within randomly initialized networks without any model training}, indicating that adversarial training on model weights is not indispensable towards adversarial robustness. We name such subnetworks Robust Scratch Tickets (RSTs), which are also by nature efficient. Distinct from the popular lottery ticket hypothesis, neither the original dense networks nor the identified RSTs need to be trained. To validate and understand this fascinating finding, we further conduct extensive experiments to study the existence and properties of RSTs under different models, datasets, sparsity patterns, and attacks, drawing insights regarding the relationship between DNNs’ robustness and their initialization/overparameterization. Furthermore, we identify the poor adversarial transferability between RSTs of different sparsity ratios drawn from the same randomly initialized dense network, and propose a Random RST Switch (R2S) technique, which randomly switches between different RSTs, as a novel defense method built on top of RSTs. We believe our findings about RSTs have opened up a new perspective to study model robustness and extend the lottery ticket hypothesis.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether resistance to adversarial image perturbations must come from training network weights. The authors report finding subnetworks inside randomly initialized networks whose robust accuracy matches or exceeds that of adversarially trained networks of comparable size. They call these selected subnetworks Robust Scratch Tickets, or RSTs.

Neither the original dense network nor the identified subnetwork requires weight training in this approach. The distinction is between finding a suitable subnetwork and adjusting its weights: the result concerns robustness already available within the random initialization. The authors investigate this phenomenon across models, datasets, sparsity patterns, and attacks, using the experiments to examine how initialization and overparameterization relate to robustness.

They also find that attacks transfer poorly between RSTs with different sparsity ratios drawn from the same dense network. This motivates Random RST Switch, a defense that randomly alternates among such subnetworks. The findings indicate that adversarial training of weights is not indispensable for obtaining robust models in the studied settings, and extend the question of useful random subnetworks to adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: Selected subnetworks within randomly initialized networks exhibit strong adversarial robustness without training their weights.

title: Drawing Robust Scratch Tickets: Subnetworks with Inborn Robustness Are Found within Randomly Initialized Networks

abstract: Collaborating with humans requires rapidly adapting to their individual strengths, weaknesses, and preferences. Unfortunately, most standard multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques, such as self-play (SP) or population play (PP), produce agents that overfit to their training partners and do not generalize well to humans. Alternatively, researchers can collect human data, train a human model using behavioral cloning, and then use that model to train "human-aware" agents ("behavioral cloning play", or BCP). While such an approach can improve the generalization of agents to new human co-players, it involves the onerous and expensive step of collecting large amounts of human data first. Here, we study the problem of how to train agents that collaborate well with human partners without using human data. We argue that the crux of the problem is to produce a diverse set of training partners. Drawing inspiration from successful multi-agent approaches in competitive domains, we find that a surprisingly simple approach is highly effective. We train our agent partner as the best response to a population of self-play agents and their past checkpoints taken throughout training, a method we call Fictitious Co-Play (FCP). Our experiments focus on a two-player collaborative cooking simulator that has recently been proposed as a challenge problem for coordination with humans. We find that FCP agents score significantly higher than SP, PP, and BCP when paired with novel agent and human partners. Furthermore, humans also report a strong subjective preference to partnering with FCP agents over all baselines.

paragraphs: An agent that cooperates successfully with its training partners may still struggle with a human whose habits and abilities differ. Training against a model of human behavior can help, but building that model first requires collecting human demonstrations. This paper investigates whether useful human collaboration can instead emerge from training entirely with artificial partners.

The proposed method, Fictitious Co-Play, trains an agent to respond effectively to a population of self-play agents. Crucially, that population includes saved versions from different stages of those agents’ training. These past checkpoints broaden the range of partners encountered during learning. The approach puts diversity of training partners at the center of preparation for unfamiliar collaborators.

Experiments use a two-player collaborative cooking simulator. In that setting, Fictitious Co-Play scores significantly higher with unfamiliar artificial and human partners than self-play, population play, and training against behaviorally cloned human models. Human participants also report a strong preference for the resulting partners. These findings support partner diversity as an effective route to human collaboration in the studied environment.
summary.tldr: Training against diverse self-play agents and their past checkpoints produces effective human collaborators without human training data in a cooking simulator.

title: Collaborating with Humans without Human Data

abstract: We study the problem of extracting correspondences between a pair of point clouds for registration. For correspondence retrieval, existing works benefit from matching sparse keypoints detected from dense points but usually struggle to guarantee their repeatability. To address this issue, we present CoFiNet - Coarse-to-Fine Network which extracts hierarchical correspondences from coarse to fine without keypoint detection. On a coarse scale and guided by a weighting scheme, our model firstly learns to match down-sampled nodes whose vicinity points share more overlap, which significantly shrinks the search space of a consecutive stage. On a finer scale, node proposals are consecutively expanded to patches that consist of groups of points together with associated descriptors. Point correspondences are then refined from the overlap areas of corresponding patches, by a density-adaptive matching module capable to deal with varying point density. Extensive evaluation of CoFiNet on both indoor and outdoor standard benchmarks shows our superiority over existing methods. Especially on 3DLoMatch where point clouds share less overlap, CoFiNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by at least 5% on Registration Recall, with at most two-third of their parameters.

paragraphs: Aligning two point clouds requires identifying points that correspond across the two observations. Methods that first detect sparse keypoints can struggle when those detections are not repeatable. CoFiNet addresses this problem by constructing correspondences through a coarse-to-fine process that does not require keypoint detection.

At the coarse stage, the network matches downsampled nodes using a weighting scheme that favors neighborhoods with greater overlap. These matches narrow the search for detailed correspondences. The proposed nodes are then expanded into patches containing points and their descriptors. A density-adaptive matching module refines correspondences within overlapping patch regions, accommodating differences in point density.

Evaluations on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show advantages over existing approaches. On the low-overlap 3DLoMatch benchmark, the authors report at least a 5% improvement in Registration Recall over state-of-the-art methods while using at most two-thirds as many parameters. The findings support the value of first locating promising shared regions and then resolving their detailed matches, particularly when only a limited portion of the two point clouds overlaps.
summary.tldr: CoFiNet finds point-cloud correspondences through coarse-to-fine matching, improving registration especially when the clouds have little overlap.

title: CoFiNet: Reliable Coarse-to-fine Correspondences for Robust PointCloud Registration

abstract: The representation learning on textual graph is to generate low-dimensional embeddings for the nodes based on the individual textual features and the neighbourhood information. Recent breakthroughs on pretrained language models and graph neural networks push forward the development of corresponding techniques. The existing works mainly rely on the cascaded model architecture: the textual features of nodes are independently encoded by language models at first; the textual embeddings are aggregated by graph neural networks afterwards. However, the above architecture is limited due to the independent modeling of textual features. In this work, we propose GraphFormers, where layerwise GNN components are nested alongside the transformer blocks of language models. With the proposed architecture, the text encoding and the graph aggregation are fused into an iterative workflow, making each node's semantic accurately comprehended from the global perspective. In addition, a progressive learning strategy is introduced, where the model is successively trained on manipulated data and original data to reinforce its capability of integrating information on graph. Extensive evaluations are conducted on three large-scale benchmark datasets, where GraphFormers outperform the SOTA baselines with comparable running efficiency. The source code is released at https://github.com/microsoft/GraphFormers .

paragraphs: A textual graph contains nodes with text as well as connections to other nodes. Learning a useful node representation requires combining the node's own language with its neighborhood. Existing approaches commonly encode each node's text independently, then pass the resulting vectors to a graph neural network. This separates text interpretation from graph context.

GraphFormers places graph neural network components alongside the Transformer blocks inside the language model. Text processing and graph aggregation therefore interact repeatedly as the representation develops. The intended benefit is that a node's meaning can be understood with information from the wider graph, rather than being fixed before neighborhood information enters the computation.

The authors also introduce progressive training, first using manipulated data and then the original data to strengthen graph-information integration. Evaluations on three large benchmark datasets report better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered, with comparable running efficiency. These results support interleaving language and graph computation as a useful way to represent connected text without sacrificing the reported level of execution efficiency.
summary.tldr: GraphFormers interleaves graph aggregation with Transformer text encoding to improve representations of nodes in textual graphs.

title: GraphFormers: GNN-nested Transformers for Representation Learning on Textual Graph

abstract: Graph neural architecture search (GraphNAS) has recently aroused considerable attention in both academia and industry. However, two key challenges seriously hinder the further research of GraphNAS. First, since there is no consensus for the experimental setting, the empirical results in different research papers are often not comparable and even not reproducible, leading to unfair comparisons. Secondly, GraphNAS often needs extensive computations, which makes it highly inefficient and inaccessible to researchers without access to large-scale computation. To solve these challenges, we propose NAS-Bench-Graph, a tailored benchmark that supports unified, reproducible, and efficient evaluations for GraphNAS. Specifically, we construct a unified, expressive yet compact search space, covering 26,206 unique graph neural network (GNN) architectures and propose a principled evaluation protocol. To avoid unnecessary repetitive training, we have trained and evaluated all of these architectures on nine representative graph datasets, recording detailed metrics including train, validation, and test performance in each epoch, the latency, the number of parameters, etc. Based on our proposed benchmark, the performance of GNN architectures can be directly obtained by a look-up table without any further computation, which enables fair, fully reproducible, and efficient comparisons. To demonstrate its usage, we make in-depth analyses of our proposed NAS-Bench-Graph, revealing several interesting findings for GraphNAS. We also showcase how the benchmark can be easily compatible with GraphNAS open libraries such as AutoGL and NNI. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first benchmark for graph neural architecture search.

paragraphs: Searching for graph neural network architectures can require substantial computation, and inconsistent experimental settings make results difficult to compare or reproduce. NAS-Bench-Graph addresses both problems by defining a shared search space and evaluation protocol. Its search space contains 26,206 distinct graph neural network architectures.

The authors train and evaluate every architecture on nine graph datasets. They record training, validation, and test performance at each epoch, together with information such as latency and parameter count. Researchers can then obtain the recorded performance through table lookup rather than repeatedly training the same candidate architectures.

This changes the cost of evaluating search methods within the benchmark: the expensive architecture evaluations have already been performed under a common protocol. The paper also analyzes the benchmark and demonstrates compatibility with graph architecture-search libraries including AutoGL and NNI. Its contribution is a reusable basis for efficient and reproducible comparisons within the supplied architecture space and datasets, making those experiments more accessible to researchers with limited computation.
summary.tldr: NAS-Bench-Graph precomputes results for 26,206 graph architectures on nine datasets to make architecture-search comparisons cheaper and reproducible.

title: NAS-Bench-Graph: Benchmarking Graph Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We study the problem of allocating $T$ sequentially arriving items among $n$ homogenous agents under the constraint that each agent must receive a prespecified fraction of all items, with the objective of maximizing the agents' total valuation of items allocated to them. The agents' valuations for the item in each round are assumed to be i.i.d. but their distribution is apriori unknown to the central planner.vTherefore, the central planner needs to implicitly learn these distributions from the observed values in order to pick a good allocation policy. However, an added challenge here is that the agents are strategic with incentives to misreport their valuations in order to receive better allocations. This sets our work apart both from the online auction mechanism design settings which typically assume known valuation distributions and/or involve payments, and from the online learning settings that do not consider strategic agents. To that end, our main contribution is an online learning based allocation mechanism that is approximately Bayesian incentive compatible, and when all agents are truthful, guarantees a sublinear regret for individual agents' utility compared to that under the optimal offline allocation policy.

The agents' valuations for the item in each round are assumed to be i.i.d. but their distribution is apriori unknown to the central planner.vTherefore, the central planner needs to implicitly learn these distributions from the observed values in order to pick a good allocation policy. However, an added challenge here is that the agents are strategic with incentives to misreport their valuations in order to receive better allocations. This sets our work apart both from the online auction mechanism design settings which typically assume known valuation distributions and/or involve payments, and from the online learning settings that do not consider strategic agents. To that end, our main contribution is an online learning based allocation mechanism that is approximately Bayesian incentive compatible, and when all agents are truthful, guarantees a sublinear regret for individual agents' utility compared to that under the optimal offline allocation policy.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocating items as they arrive, with each agent required to receive a prespecified fraction of all items. The planner wants to maximize the agents' total value from their allocations. Valuations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed, but their distribution is initially unknown, so the planner must learn while making decisions.

Learning is complicated by strategic reporting. Agents may misstate how much they value an item if doing so improves their allocation. The problem therefore combines uncertainty about preferences with incentives to manipulate the observations used for learning. The proposed mechanism uses online learning while explicitly accounting for these strategic incentives.

The authors establish approximate Bayesian incentive compatibility, a qualified incentive guarantee rather than an assertion that manipulation is impossible. When all agents report truthfully, they also guarantee sublinear regret for each agent's utility relative to the optimal offline allocation policy. Sublinear regret means that this cumulative utility gap grows more slowly than the number of arriving items, making the per-item gap diminish as the sequence grows.
summary.tldr: An online allocation mechanism learns unknown valuations while providing approximate incentive compatibility and sublinear individual regret under truthful reporting.

title: Online Allocation and Learning in the Presence of Strategic Agents

abstract: Synthetic data generation has become a key ingredient for training machine learning procedures, addressing tasks such as data augmentation, analysing privacy-sensitive data, or visualising representative samples. Assessing the quality of such synthetic data generators hence has to be addressed. As (deep) generative models for synthetic data often do not admit explicit probability distributions, classical statistical procedures for assessing model goodness-of-fit may not be applicable. In this paper, we propose a principled procedure to assess the quality of a synthetic data generator. The procedure is a Kernelised Stein Discrepancy-type test which is based on a non-parametric Stein operator for the synthetic data generator of interest. This operator is estimated from samples which are obtained from the synthetic data generator and hence can be applied even when the model is only implicit. In contrast to classical testing, the sample size from the synthetic data generator can be as large as desired, while the size of the observed data that the generator aims to emulate is fixed. Experimental results on synthetic distributions and trained generative models on synthetic and real datasets illustrate that the method shows improved power performance compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: A synthetic data generator can produce convincing examples without providing an explicit formula for their probabilities. This creates a problem for statistical checks that depend on knowing that formula. The paper develops a goodness-of-fit procedure for assessing whether an implicit generator matches the observed data it is intended to reproduce.

The method builds a test related to Kernelised Stein Discrepancy. Its central component is a nonparametric Stein operator estimated using samples drawn from the generator. In practical terms, the assessment machinery is learned from generated examples, allowing the procedure to work without an explicit probability distribution. The approach also distinguishes two sources of evidence: the observed dataset has a fixed size, while additional synthetic samples can be requested from the model.

Experiments cover synthetic distributions and trained generators using both synthetic and real datasets. The reported improvement is in statistical power: the test is better able to identify mismatches in those comparisons. This supports its usefulness as a generator assessment method, rather than establishing that any particular generator produces adequate data.
summary.tldr: A sample-based Stein test assesses implicit data generators and shows improved power to detect distributional mismatches in experiments.

title: A Kernelised Stein Statistic for Assessing Implicit Generative Models

abstract: In probably approximately correct (PAC) reinforcement learning (RL), an agent is required to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with probability $1-\delta$. While minimax optimal algorithms exist for this problem, its instance-dependent complexity remains elusive in episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs). In this paper, we propose the first nearly matching (up to a horizon squared factor and logarithmic terms) upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of PAC RL in deterministic episodic MDPs with finite state and action spaces. In particular, our bounds feature a new notion of sub-optimality gap for state-action pairs that we call the deterministic return gap. While our instance-dependent lower bound is written as a linear program, our algorithms are very simple and do not require solving such an optimization problem during learning. Their design and analyses employ novel ideas, including graph-theoretical concepts (minimum flows) and a new maximum-coverage exploration strategy.

paragraphs: Probably approximately correct reinforcement learning asks an agent to identify a nearly optimal policy with a specified high probability. Although worst-case optimal algorithms exist, the number of samples required for a particular environment is less understood. This paper studies that question for deterministic episodic Markov decision processes with finite state and action spaces.

The authors establish upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that nearly match, leaving a squared-horizon factor and logarithmic terms. Both bounds use a new measure called the deterministic return gap, which describes suboptimality for state-action pairs. This gives the analysis a way to reflect the difficulty of an individual problem instance rather than only worst-case difficulty.

The lower bound is expressed as a linear program, but the proposed learning algorithms do not need to solve that program. Their design and analysis use minimum-flow concepts from graph theory and a new maximum-coverage exploration strategy. The result combines detailed instance-dependent guarantees with algorithms described as simple, within the paper's deterministic, finite, episodic setting.
summary.tldr: New instance-dependent bounds and simple exploration algorithms nearly characterize PAC learning complexity in finite deterministic episodic MDPs.

title: Near Instance-Optimal PAC Reinforcement Learning for Deterministic MDPs

abstract: The No Unmeasured Confounding Assumption is widely used to identify causal effects in observational studies. Recent work on proximal inference has provided alternative identification results that succeed even in the presence of unobserved confounders, provided that one has measured a sufficiently rich set of proxy variables, satisfying specific structural conditions. However, proximal inference requires solving an ill-posed integral equation. Previous approaches have used a variety of machine learning techniques to estimate a solution to this integral equation, commonly referred to as the bridge function. However, prior work has often been limited by relying on pre-specified kernel functions, which are not data adaptive and struggle to scale to large datasets. In this work, we introduce a flexible and scalable method based on a deep neural network to estimate causal effects in the presence of unmeasured confounding using proximal inference. Our method achieves state of the art performance on two well-established proximal inference benchmarks. Finally, we provide theoretical consistency guarantees for our method.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects from observational data often assumes that all confounding variables have been measured. Proximal inference offers an alternative when some confounders remain hidden, provided sufficiently rich proxy measurements satisfy particular structural conditions. This paper develops a neural-network approach to estimation within that framework, retaining the importance of those proxy requirements.

The computational challenge is estimating a bridge function by solving an ill-posed integral equation. Earlier methods often rely on kernel functions selected in advance. The abstract identifies two drawbacks of that approach: those kernels do not adapt to the data, and the resulting methods can struggle with large datasets. The proposed deep-learning method aims to make bridge estimation more flexible and scalable.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on two established proximal-inference benchmarks and provide theoretical consistency guarantees. The contribution combines an estimation method with empirical and theoretical support. Its significance is making a proxy-based route to causal estimation more practical when unmeasured confounding is present and the required identification conditions hold.
summary.tldr: A neural approach makes proximal causal inference more flexible and scalable while retaining proxy-based assumptions and consistency guarantees.

title: Deep Learning Methods for Proximal Inference via Maximum Moment Restriction

abstract: Stochastic approximation (SA) with multiple coupled sequences has found broad applications in machine learning such as bilevel learning and reinforcement learning (RL). In this paper, we study the finite-time convergence of nonlinear SA with multiple coupled sequences. Different from existing multi-timescale analysis, we seek scenarios where a fine-grained analysis can provide a tight performance guarantee for single-timescale multi-sequence SA (STSA). At the heart of our analysis is the smoothness property of the fixed points in multi-sequence SA that holds in many applications. When all sequences have strongly monotone increments, we establish the iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ to achieve $\epsilon$-accuracy, which improves the existing $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ complexity for two coupled sequences. When the main sequence does not have a strongly monotone increment, we establish the iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$. We showcase the power of our result by applying it to stochastic bilevel and compositional optimization problems, as well as RL problems, all of which recover the best known or lead to improvements over their existing guarantees.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms update several quantities that depend on one another while using noisy information. This paper studies how quickly such coupled stochastic approximation procedures converge when their updates operate on a single timescale. The aim is to identify settings where carefully analyzing these interactions yields stronger guarantees without relying on separate update timescales.

The analysis centers on smoothness of the fixed points associated with the coupled sequences. Informally, this concerns how regularly their equilibrium values change as related quantities change. Under this property and strongly monotone increments for every sequence, the authors establish an iteration requirement of order one over the target accuracy. This improves an existing dependence of order accuracy to the power minus one-and-a-half for two coupled sequences.

When the main sequence lacks a strongly monotone increment, the stated iteration requirement becomes order one over accuracy squared. The distinction makes the assumptions consequential: the faster guarantee does not apply indiscriminately. Applications to stochastic bilevel optimization, compositional optimization, and reinforcement learning recover the best known guarantees or improve existing ones, demonstrating the usefulness of a shared analysis across several learning problems.
summary.tldr: A single-timescale analysis gives sharper conditional convergence guarantees for stochastic algorithms with multiple interacting update sequences.

title: A Single-timescale Analysis for Stochastic Approximation with Multiple Coupled Sequences

abstract: In medical image analysis, we often need to build an image recognition system for a target scenario with the access to small labeled data and abundant unlabeled data, as well as multiple related models pretrained on different source scenarios. This presents the combined challenges of multi-source-free domain adaptation and semi-supervised learning simultaneously. However, both problems are typically studied independently in the literature, and how to effectively combine existing methods is non-trivial in design. In this work, we introduce a novel MetaTeacher framework with three key components: (1) A learnable coordinating scheme for adaptive domain adaptation of individual source models, (2) A mutual feedback mechanism between the target model and source models for more coherent learning, and (3) A semi-supervised bilevel optimization algorithm for consistently organizing the adaption of source models and the learning of target model. It aims to leverage the knowledge of source models adaptively whilst maximize their complementary benefits collectively to counter the challenge of limited supervision. Extensive experiments on five chest x-ray image datasets show that our method outperforms clearly all the state-of-the-art alternatives. The code is available at https://github.com/wongzbb/metateacher.

paragraphs: Medical-image adaptation may involve a small labeled target dataset, many unlabeled target examples, and several models trained on related source domains. This combines semisupervised learning with adaptation that does not revisit source data. MetaTeacher addresses the difficulty of making those ingredients work together.

The framework learns how to coordinate adaptation of individual source models, passes feedback between source and target models, and uses semisupervised bilevel optimization to organize their updates. The aim is to exploit complementary source knowledge without assuming every pretrained model is equally useful for the target setting.

Experiments across five chest X-ray datasets outperform the compared state-of-the-art alternatives. The abstract does not report numerical classification gains or clinical deployment outcomes. The contribution is a coordinated learning framework for this particular combination of limited supervision and multiple available source models, supported by image-classification evaluations rather than evidence of general diagnostic superiority.
summary.tldr: MetaTeacher coordinates multiple pretrained source models to learn from limited target-domain labels.

title: MetaTeacher: Coordinating Multi-Model Domain Adaptation for Medical Image Classification

abstract: A conceptually appealing approach for learning Extensive-Form Games (EFGs) is to convert them to Normal-Form Games (NFGs). This approach enables us to directly translate state-of-the-art techniques and analyses in NFGs to learning EFGs, but typically suffers from computational intractability due to the exponential blow-up of the game size introduced by the conversion. In this paper, we address this problem in natural and important setups for the \emph{$\Phi$-Hedge} algorithm---A generic algorithm capable of learning a large class of equilibria for NFGs. We show that $\Phi$-Hedge can be directly used to learn Nash Equilibria (zero-sum settings), Normal-Form Coarse Correlated Equilibria (NFCCE), and Extensive-Form Correlated Equilibria (EFCE) in EFGs. We prove that, in those settings, the \emph{$\Phi$-Hedge} algorithms are equivalent to standard Online Mirror Descent (OMD) algorithms for EFGs with suitable dilated regularizers, and run in polynomial time. This new connection further allows us to design and analyze a new class of OMD algorithms based on modifying its log-partition function. In particular, we design an improved algorithm with balancing techniques that achieves a sharp $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{XAT})$ EFCE-regret under bandit-feedback in an EFG with $X$ information sets, $A$ actions, and $T$ episodes. To our best knowledge, this is the first such rate and matches the information-theoretic lower bound.

paragraphs: Sequential games can be converted into normal-form games, making established learning methods available. The obstacle is computational: this conversion can expand the game's representation exponentially. The paper investigates when the benefits of a normal-form algorithm called Phi-Hedge can be retained without paying that exponential cost.

The authors establish a connection between Phi-Hedge and online mirror descent operating on extensive-form games with suitable dilated regularizers. In the settings they analyze, the algorithms are equivalent and run in polynomial time. These settings cover learning Nash equilibria in zero-sum games, normal-form coarse correlated equilibria, and extensive-form correlated equilibria.

The connection also provides a route to new algorithms by modifying the log-partition function. Using balancing techniques, the authors obtain an extensive-form-correlated-equilibrium regret bound of approximately √(XAT), with logarithmic factors suppressed, under bandit feedback. Here X counts information sets, A counts actions, and T counts episodes. They identify this as the first such rate to their knowledge and show that it matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to the suppressed factors.
summary.tldr: An equivalence with online mirror descent makes Phi-Hedge efficient in several sequential-game settings and yields a near-optimal bandit-feedback regret bound.

title: Efficient Phi-Regret Minimization in Extensive-Form Games via Online Mirror Descent

abstract: We propose and analyse a novel statistical procedure, coined AgraSSt, to assess the quality of graph generators which may not be available in explicit forms. In particular, AgraSSt can be used to determine whether a learned graph generating process is capable of generating graphs which resemble a given input graph. Inspired by Stein operators for random graphs, the key idea of AgraSSt is the construction of a kernel discrepancy based on an operator obtained from the graph generator. AgraSSt can provide interpretable criticisms for a graph generator training procedure and help identify reliable sample batches for downstream tasks. We give theoretical guarantees for a broad class of random graph models. Moreover, we provide empirical results on both synthetic input graphs with known graph generation procedures, and real-world input graphs that the state-of-the-art (deep) generative models for graphs are trained on.

paragraphs: A graph generator can produce examples without making its underlying probability model available in an explicit form. This makes assessing its output a distinct statistical problem. AgraSSt addresses that problem by asking whether a learned generation process can produce graphs resembling a given input graph, rather than requiring an explicit formula for the full generator.

The method constructs a kernel discrepancy using an operator obtained from the generator. Its design draws on Stein operators for random graphs, turning properties of the generating process into a statistical comparison. This provides a way to evaluate a generator through the relationship between its implied graph behavior and the graph being used as a reference.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for a broad class of random graph models and empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs. Synthetic examples have known generation procedures, while the real-world examples are used to train advanced graph generators. AgraSSt can also provide interpretable criticism of training and help identify reliable sample batches, making assessment potentially useful for improving generators and selecting outputs for later tasks.
summary.tldr: AgraSSt uses a generator-derived statistical discrepancy to assess graph generators and provide interpretable feedback without requiring an explicit probability model.

title: AgraSSt: Approximate Graph Stein Statistics for Interpretable Assessment of Implicit Graph Generators

abstract: Large-scale language models often learn behaviors that are misaligned with user expectations. Generated text may contain offensive or toxic language, contain significant repetition, or be of a different sentiment than desired by the user. We consider the task of unlearning these misalignments by fine-tuning the language model on signals of what not to do. We introduce Quantized Reward Konditioning (Quark), an algorithm for optimizing a reward function that quantifies an (un)wanted property, while not straying too far from the original model. Quark alternates between (i) collecting samples with the current language model, (ii) sorting them into quantiles based on reward, with each quantile identified by a reward token prepended to the language model’s input, and (iii) using a standard language modeling loss on samples from each quantile conditioned on its reward token, while remaining nearby the original language model via a KL-divergence penalty. By conditioning on a high-reward token at generation time, the model generates text that exhibits less of the unwanted property. For unlearning toxicity, negative sentiment, and repetition, our experiments show that Quark outperforms both strong baselines and state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods like PPO, while relying only on standard language modeling primitives.

paragraphs: Language models can produce unwanted properties such as toxicity, repetition, or an undesired sentiment. Quark addresses these behaviors by fine-tuning with a reward function that scores the property of interest. The objective is to reduce unwanted behavior while keeping the resulting model close to the original language model.

Training repeats a three-part cycle. The current model generates text, the samples are divided into reward quantiles, and each group receives a corresponding reward token. The model then trains on those samples using a standard language-modelling loss conditioned on the tokens. A KL-divergence penalty discourages excessive departure from the original model during this process.

At generation time, a high-reward token steers the model toward text with less of the unwanted property. Experiments on toxicity, negative sentiment, and repetition report improvements over strong baselines and reinforcement-learning methods including PPO. The contribution is a reward-driven procedure built from standard language-modelling operations, with demonstrated behavioral reductions rather than a guarantee that unwanted outputs become impossible.
summary.tldr: Quark uses reward-group tokens and ordinary language-model training to reduce unwanted text properties while limiting deviation from the original model.

title: QUARK: Controllable Text Generation with Reinforced Unlearning

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) encapsulates multiple learned tasks in a single model and often lets those tasks learn better jointly. Multi-tasking models have become successful and often essential for many sophisticated systems such as autonomous driving and indoor robots. However, when deploying MTL onto those real-world systems that are often resource-constrained or latency-sensitive, two prominent challenges arise: (i) during training, simultaneously optimizing all tasks is often difficult due to gradient conflicts across tasks, and the challenge is amplified when a growing number of tasks have to be squeezed into one compact model; (ii) at inference, current MTL regimes have to activate nearly the entire model even to just execute a single task. Yet most real systems demand only one or two tasks at each moment, while flexibly switching between tasks per need: therefore such “all tasks activated” inference is also highly inefficient and non-scalable in practice. In this paper, we present a model-accelerator co-design framework to enable efficient on-device MTL, that tackles both training and inference bottlenecks. Our framework, dubbed M³ViT, customizes mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers into a vision transformer (ViT) backbone for MTL, and sparsely activates task-specific experts during training, which effectively disentangles the parameter spaces to avoid different tasks’ training conflicts. Then at inference with any task of interest, the same design allows for activating only the task-corresponding sparse “expert” pathway, instead of the full model. Our new model design is further enhanced by hardware-level innovations, in particular, a novel computation reordering scheme tailored for memory-constrained MTL that achieves zero-overhead switching between tasks and can scale to any number of experts. Extensive experiments on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2 datasets at both software and hardware levels are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed design. When executing the practical scenario of single-task inference, M³ViT achieves higher accuracies than encoder-focused MTL methods, while significantly reducing 88% inference FLOPs. When implemented on a hardware platform of one Xilinx ZCU104 FPGA, our co-design framework reduces the memory requirement by 2.40×, while achieving energy efficiency (as the product of latency and power) up to 9.23× times higher than a comparable FPGA baseline.

title: M³ViT: Mixture-of-Experts Vision Transformer for Efficient Multi-task Learning with Model-Accelerator Co-design

abstract: This paper studies the problem of model training under Federated Learning when clients exhibit cluster structure. We contextualize this problem in mixed regression, where each client has limited local data generated from one of $k$ unknown regression models. We design an algorithm that achieves global convergence from any initialization, and works even when local data volume is highly unbalanced -- there could exist clients that contain $O(1)$ data points only. Our algorithm first runs moment descent on a few anchor clients (each with $\tilde{\Omega}(k)$ data points) to obtain coarse model estimates. Then each client alternately estimates its cluster labels and refines the model estimates based on FedAvg or FedProx. title: Global Convergence of Federated Learning for Mixed Regression

abstract: Large language models have been widely adopted but require significant GPU memory for inference. We develop a procedure for Int8 matrix multiplication for feed-forward and attention projection layers in transformers, which cut the memory needed for inference by half while retaining full precision performance. With our method, a 175B parameter 16/32-bit checkpoint can be loaded, converted to Int8, and used immediately without performance degradation. This is made possible by understanding and working around properties of highly systematic emergent features in transformer language models that dominate attention and transformer predictive performance. To cope with these features, we develop a two-part quantization procedure, {\bf LLM.int8()}. We first use vector-wise quantization with separate normalization constants for each inner product in the matrix multiplication, to quantize most of the features. However, for the emergent outliers, we also include a new mixed-precision decomposition scheme, which isolates the outlier feature dimensions into a 16-bit matrix multiplication while still more than 99.9\% of values are multiplied in 8-bit. Using LLM.int8(), we show empirically it is possible to perform inference in LLMs with up to 175B parameters without any performance degradation. This result makes such models much more accessible, for example making it possible to use OPT-175B/BLOOM on a single server with consumer GPUs. We open source our software.

title: GPT3.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale

abstract: Exploration is one of the main challenges in Reinforcement Learning (RL), especially in environments with sparse rewards. Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) is a promising approach to solving this problem by leveraging expert demonstrations. However, expert demonstrations of high quality are usually costly or even impossible to collect in real-world applications. In this work, we propose a novel RL algorithm called HYbrid Policy Optimization (HYPO), which uses a small number of imperfect demonstrations to accelerate an agent's online learning process. The key idea is to train an offline guider policy using imitation learning in order to instruct an online agent policy to explore efficiently. Through mutual update of the guider policy and the agent policy, the agent can leverage suboptimal demonstrations for efficient exploration while avoiding the conservative policy caused by imperfect demonstrations. Empirical results show that HYPO significantly outperforms several baselines in various challenging tasks, such as MuJoCo with sparse rewards, Google Research Football, and the AirSim drone simulation.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning, an agent may struggle to discover useful behavior when rewards are sparse. Demonstrations can guide exploration, but high-quality examples may be expensive or unavailable. HYPO addresses this situation by using a small number of imperfect demonstrations to accelerate learning through subsequent interaction with the environment.

The method first uses imitation learning to train an offline guider policy. That guider helps an online agent policy explore more efficiently. The two policies then undergo mutual updates, allowing the agent to benefit from suboptimal examples while avoiding the conservative behavior that can result from remaining tied to those demonstrations.

The key role of the demonstrations is therefore to support exploration within an ongoing learning process. The authors report that HYPO significantly outperforms several baselines on challenging tasks involving sparse-reward MuJoCo, Google Research Football, and AirSim drone simulation. These empirical results support the usefulness of the guider-agent arrangement across the evaluated settings. The paper presents imperfect demonstrations as a practical starting point for learning, with policy updates helping the agent move beyond their limitations.
summary.tldr: HYPO uses mutually updated guider and agent policies to turn a small set of imperfect demonstrations into more effective online exploration.

title: Hybrid Policy Optimization from Imperfect Demonstrations

abstract: Despite the rapid advance of 3D-aware image synthesis, existing studies usually adopt a mixture of techniques and tricks, leaving it unclear how each part contributes to the final performance in terms of generality. Following the most popular and effective paradigm in this field, which incorporates a neural radiance field (NeRF) into the generator of a generative adversarial network (GAN), we builda well-structured codebase through modularizing the generation process. Such a design allows researchers to develop and replace each module independently, and hence offers an opportunity to fairly compare various approaches and recognize their contributions from the module perspective. The reproduction of a range of cutting-edge algorithms demonstrates the availability of our modularized codebase. We also perform a variety of in-depth analyses, such as the comparison across different types of point feature, the necessity of the tailing upsampler in the generator, the reliance on the camera pose prior, etc., which deepen our understanding of existing methods and point out some further directions of the research work. Code and models will be made publicly available to facilitate the development and evaluation of this field.
