paragraphs: Research on 3D-aware image generation often combines several architectural choices and training techniques. When a complete system works well, that mixture makes it difficult to determine which parts deserve credit. This paper addresses the problem by organizing the generation process into independently replaceable modules within a shared codebase.

The codebase follows an established approach that places a neural radiance field inside a generative adversarial network’s generator. Its modular structure lets researchers develop individual components and compare alternatives within a common implementation. Reproducing a range of leading algorithms demonstrates that the framework can accommodate existing methods, making it useful for examining component contributions across systems.

The authors also analyze different point-feature representations, the role of the generator’s final upsampler, and dependence on assumptions about camera poses. These investigations aim to clarify how existing systems work and identify research directions. The abstract does not state a preferred choice for each component; its central contribution is a practical basis for more controlled comparisons and deeper analysis.
summary.tldr: A modular codebase makes 3D-aware image generators easier to reproduce, compare, and analyze component by component.

title: Benchmarking and Analyzing 3D-aware Image Synthesis with a Modularized Codebase

abstract: Robust loss functions are essential for training deep neural networks in the presence of noisy labels. Some robust loss functions use Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as its necessary component. For example, the recently proposed Active Passive Loss (APL) uses MAE as its passive loss function. However, MAE treats every sample equally, slows down the convergence and can make training difficult. In this work, we propose a new class of theoretically robust passive loss functions different from MAE, namely *Normalized Negative Loss Functions* (NNLFs), which focus more on memorized clean samples. By replacing the MAE in APL with our proposed NNLFs, we improve APL and propose a new framework called *Active Negative Loss* (ANL). Experimental results on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrate that the new set of loss functions created by our ANL framework can outperform state-of-the-art methods. The code is available athttps://github.com/Virusdoll/Active-Negative-Loss.

paragraphs: Training with incorrect labels creates a problem for the loss function: it needs to guide learning without encouraging the network to absorb every labeling mistake. Some robust approaches use Mean Absolute Error, or MAE, as a component. The paper identifies a drawback of this choice: treating samples equally can slow convergence and make optimization difficult.

The authors introduce Normalized Negative Loss Functions, a class of passive losses with theoretical robustness properties. These losses put greater emphasis on clean samples that the model has already memorized. They then replace the MAE component in the existing Active Passive Loss framework with these new losses, producing a framework called Active Negative Loss.

Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets show that losses constructed through this framework can outperform state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is therefore both a new family of robust losses and a way to incorporate them into an established approach. The findings support reconsidering how a robust loss distributes attention across training examples, rather than treating equal weighting as the default.
summary.tldr: Active Negative Loss replaces MAE with robust losses that emphasize memorized clean samples and can improve learning with noisy labels.

title: Active Negative Loss Functions for Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: The growth of Graph Convolution Network (GCN) model sizes has revolutionized numerous applications, surpassing human performance in areas such as personal healthcare and financial systems. The deployment of GCNs in the cloud raises privacy concerns due to potential adversarial attacks on client data. To address security concerns, Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) using Homomorphic Encryption (HE) secures sensitive client data. However, it introduces substantial computational overhead in practical applications. To tackle those challenges, we present LinGCN, a framework designed to reduce multiplication depth and optimize the performance of HE based GCN inference. LinGCN is structured around three key elements: (1) A differentiable structural linearization algorithm, complemented by a parameterized discrete indicator function, co-trained with model weights to meet the optimization goal. This strategy promotes fine-grained node-level non-linear location selection, resulting in a model with minimized multiplication depth. (2) A compact node-wise polynomial replacement policy with a second-order trainable activation function, steered towards superior convergence by a two-level distillation approach from an all-ReLU based teacher model. (3) an enhanced HE solution that enables finer-grained operator fusion for node-wise activation functions, further reducing multiplication level consumption in HE-based inference. Our experiments on the NTU-XVIEW skeleton joint dataset reveal that LinGCN excels in latency, accuracy, and scalability for homomorphically encrypted inference, outperforming solutions such as CryptoGCN. Remarkably, LinGCN achieves a 14.2× latency speedup relative to CryptoGCN, while preserving an inference accuracy of ~75\% and notably reducing multiplication depth. Additionally, LinGCN proves scalable for larger models, delivering a substantial 85.78\% accuracy with 6371s latency, a 10.47\% accuracy improvement over CryptoGCN.

LinGCN targets multiplication depth, a central source of overhead in this setting. It coordinates changes to the network and the encrypted execution procedure so that privacy-preserving inference requires fewer multiplication levels.

The framework learns where nonlinear operations should remain at individual nodes, jointly training those structural choices with model weights. It replaces selected activations with trainable second-order polynomials and uses two-level distillation from an all-ReLU teacher to improve convergence. These results demonstrate different accuracy-latency configurations and support the value of designing the network structure together with its encrypted execution.
summary.tldr: LinGCN jointly redesigns graph-network nonlinearities and encrypted execution to reduce multiplication depth and improve homomorphic inference performance.

title: LinGCN: Structural Linearized Graph Convolutional Network for Homomorphically Encrypted Inference

abstract: Graph property prediction tasks are important and numerous. While each task offers a small size of labeled examples, unlabeled graphs have been collected from various sources and at a large scale. A conventional approach is training a model with the unlabeled graphs on self-supervised tasks and then fine-tuning the model on the prediction tasks. However, the self-supervised task knowledge could not be aligned or sometimes conflicted with what the predictions needed. In this paper, we propose to extract the knowledge underlying the large set of unlabeled graphs as a specific set of useful data points to augment each property prediction model. We use a diffusion model to fully utilize the unlabeled graphs and design two new objectives to guide the model's denoising process with each task's labeled data to generate task-specific graph examples and their labels. Experiments demonstrate that our data-centric approach performs significantly better than fifteen existing various methods on fifteen tasks. The performance improvement brought by unlabeled data is visible as the generated labeled examples unlike the self-supervised learning.

The contribution makes the use of unlabeled information concrete: it appears as generated labeled examples that augment the predictor’s training set. This provides a different route for transferring knowledge from a broad graph collection, with task relevance built into generation rather than left solely to later fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model turns unlabeled graph collections into task-specific labeled examples that improve graph property prediction.

title: Data-Centric Learning from Unlabeled Graphs with Diffusion Model

abstract: Massive data is often considered essential for deep learning applications, but it also incurs significant computational and infrastructural costs. Therefore, dataset pruning (DP) has emerged as an effective way to improve data efficiency by identifying and removing redundant training samples without sacrificing performance. In this work, we aim to address the problem of DP for transfer learning, i.e., how to prune a source dataset for improved pretraining efficiency and lossless finetuning accuracy on downstream target tasks. To our best knowledge, the problem of DP for transfer learning remains open, as previous studies have primarily addressed DP and transfer learning as separate problems. By contrast, we establish a unified viewpoint to integrate DP with transfer learning and find that existing DP methods are not suitable for the transfer learning paradigm. We then propose two new DP methods, label mapping and feature mapping, for supervised and self-supervised pretraining settings respectively, by revisiting the DP problem through the lens of source-target domain mapping. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on numerous transfer learning tasks. We show that source data classes can be pruned by up to $40\%\sim 80\%$ without sacrificing the downstream performance, resulting in a significant $2\sim 5\times$ speed-up during the pretraining stage. Besides, our proposal exhibits broad applicability and can improve other computationally intensive transfer learning techniques, such as adversarial pretraining.

paragraphs: Dataset pruning removes training data to reduce computation while preserving useful performance. This paper studies pruning specifically for transfer learning, where a model first learns from a source dataset and then is fine-tuned on downstream target tasks. The question is which source data can be removed without harming those later tasks.

The authors find that existing pruning methods are unsuitable for this transfer setting and approach selection through the relationship between source and target domains. They propose label mapping for supervised pretraining and feature mapping for self-supervised pretraining. These methods make downstream relevance part of the decision about which source data to retain.

Across numerous transfer-learning tasks, the experiments show source-class pruning of up to 40–80% without sacrificing downstream performance, alongside pretraining speedups of two to five times. These are reported experimental outcomes rather than guarantees for every source–target combination. The approach also applies to costly transfer techniques such as adversarial pretraining, showing how target-aware data selection can reduce effort across more than one pretraining setup.
summary.tldr: Source–target mapping guides dataset pruning that preserves downstream accuracy while delivering reported pretraining speedups of two to five times.

title: Selectivity Drives Productivity: Efficient Dataset Pruning for Enhanced Transfer Learning

abstract: We explore the problem of imitation learning (IL) in the context of mean-field games (MFGs), where the goal is to imitate the behavior of a population of agents following a Nash equilibrium policy according to some unknown payoff function. IL in MFGs presents new challenges compared to single-agent IL, particularly when both the reward function and the transition kernel depend on the population distribution. In this paper, departing from the existing literature on IL for MFGs, we introduce a new solution concept called the Nash imitation gap. Then we show that when only the reward depends on the population distribution, IL in MFGs can be reduced to single-agent IL with similar guarantees. However, when the dynamics is population-dependent, we provide a novel upper-bound that suggests IL is harder in this setting. To address this issue, we propose a new adversarial formulation where the reinforcement learning problem is replaced by a mean-field control (MFC) problem, suggesting progress in IL within MFGs may have to build upon MFC.

paragraphs: Imitation learning usually asks how to reproduce observed behavior without knowing the reward that produced it. This paper studies that question for populations of agents in mean-field games. The observed population follows a Nash equilibrium policy under an unknown payoff, and both rewards and state transitions may depend on the population's distribution.

The authors introduce the Nash imitation gap as a new solution concept for evaluating imitation in this setting. They then distinguish two cases. When population dependence appears only in rewards, the problem can be reduced to single-agent imitation learning with similar guarantees. When transitions also depend on the population, a new upper bound suggests that imitation is harder.

To address the population-dependent dynamics case, the paper proposes an adversarial formulation that replaces its reinforcement-learning problem with a mean-field control problem. This changes the optimization formulation to account for population effects in the dynamics. The results suggest a role for mean-field control in further progress, without establishing that every approach to imitation in these games must take that form.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces the Nash imitation gap and shows how population-dependent dynamics complicate imitation learning in mean-field games.

title: On Imitation in Mean-field Games

abstract: Self-consistent Field (SCF) equation is a type of nonlinear eigenvalue problem in which the matrix to be eigen-decomposed is a function of its own eigenvectors. It is of great significance in computational science for its connection to the Schrödinger equation. Traditional fixed-point iteration methods for solving such equations suffer from non-convergence issues. In this work, we present a novel perspective on such SCF equations as a principal component analysis (PCA) for non-stationary time series, in which a distribution and its own top principal components are mutually updated over time, and the equilibrium state of the model corresponds to the solution of the SCF equations. By the new perspective, online PCA techniques are able to engage in so as to enhance the convergence of the model towards the equilibrium state, acting as a new set of tools for converging the SCF equations. With several numerical adaptations, we then develop a new algorithm for converging the SCF equation, and demonstrated its high convergence capacity with experiments on both synthesized and real electronic structure scenarios.

paragraphs: A self-consistent field equation is an eigenvalue problem in which the matrix depends on its own eigenvectors. Solving it requires finding a mutually consistent matrix and set of vectors. Such equations matter in computational science through their connection to the Schrödinger equation, but traditional fixed-point iterations can fail to converge.

The paper reinterprets this circular dependence as principal component analysis on a changing time series. A distribution and its leading principal components update one another over time, with equilibrium corresponding to a solution of the original equation. This perspective makes online PCA techniques available as tools for guiding the coupled updates toward consistency.

Using this formulation and several numerical adaptations, the authors develop a new SCF solution algorithm. Experiments on synthetic problems and real electronic-structure scenarios demonstrate strong convergence capability. The contribution is both conceptual and algorithmic: it connects a nonlinear scientific-computing problem to an online learning formulation and uses that connection to improve convergence in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Recasting self-consistent field equations as evolving PCA enables an algorithm with strong convergence results on synthetic and electronic-structure problems.

title: Online PCA in Converging Self-consistent Field Equations

abstract: Dynamic graph neural networks (DGNNs) are increasingly pervasive in exploiting spatio-temporal patterns on dynamic graphs. However, existing works fail to generalize under distribution shifts, which are common in real-world scenarios. As the generation of dynamic graphs is heavily influenced by latent environments, investigating their impacts on the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is critical. However, it remains unexplored with the following two major challenges: **(1)** How to properly model and infer the complex environments on dynamic graphs with distribution shifts? **(2)** How to discover invariant patterns given inferred spatio-temporal environments? To solve these challenges, we propose a novel **E**nvironment-**A**ware dynamic **G**raph **LE**arning (**EAGLE**) framework for OOD generalization by modeling complex coupled environments and exploiting spatio-temporal invariant patterns. Specifically, we first design the environment-aware EA-DGNN to model environments by multi-channel environments disentangling. Then, we propose an environment instantiation mechanism for environment diversification with inferred distributions. Finally, we discriminate spatio-temporal invariant patterns for out-of-distribution prediction by the invariant pattern recognition mechanism and perform fine-grained causal interventions node-wisely with a mixture of instantiated environment samples. Experiments on real-world and synthetic dynamic graph datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method against state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study OOD generalization on dynamic graphs from the environment learning perspective.

However, existing works fail to generalize under distribution shifts, which are common in real-world scenarios. As the generation of dynamic graphs is heavily influenced by latent environments, investigating their impacts on the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is critical. However, it remains unexplored with the following two major challenges: **(1)** How to properly model and infer the complex environments on dynamic graphs with distribution shifts? **(2)** How to discover invariant patterns given inferred spatio-temporal environments? To solve these challenges, we propose a novel **E**nvironment-**A**ware dynamic **G**raph **LE**arning (**EAGLE**) framework for OOD generalization by modeling complex coupled environments and exploiting spatio-temporal invariant patterns. Specifically, we first design the environment-aware EA-DGNN to model environments by multi-channel environments disentangling. Then, we propose an environment instantiation mechanism for environment diversification with inferred distributions. Finally, we discriminate spatio-temporal invariant patterns for out-of-distribution prediction by the invariant pattern recognition mechanism and perform fine-grained causal interventions node-wisely with a mixture of instantiated environment samples. Experiments on real-world and synthetic dynamic graph datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method against state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study OOD generalization on dynamic graphs from the environment learning perspective.

paragraphs: Dynamic graphs contain relationships that evolve over time, and their patterns can change when the surrounding environment changes. A model trained in one setting may consequently struggle in another. This paper treats hidden environments as an explicit part of learning how to generalize across such distribution shifts.

The EAGLE framework first uses an environment-aware dynamic graph network to separate environmental influences through multiple channels. It then creates diverse environment instances from inferred distributions. An invariant-pattern recognition mechanism seeks spatial and temporal patterns that remain useful across these environments, while node-level causal interventions use mixtures of the instantiated environment samples.

The approach links environment inference with the search for stable predictive structure. Its purpose is to help prediction rely on patterns that survive changes in the conditions generating the graph. Experiments on real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts. These results support the proposed environment-learning perspective for the evaluated out-of-distribution settings.
summary.tldr: EAGLE models hidden environments in dynamic graphs to learn spatial and temporal patterns that transfer better under distribution shifts.

title: Environment-Aware Dynamic Graph Learning for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: We study the problem of exploration in Reinforcement Learning and present a novel model-free solution. We adopt an information-theoretical viewpoint and start from the instance-specific lower bound of the number of samples that have to be collected to identify a nearly-optimal policy. Deriving this lower bound along with the optimal exploration strategy entails solving an intricate optimization problem and requires a model of the system. In turn, most existing sample optimal exploration algorithms rely on estimating the model. We derive an approximation of the instance-specific lower bound that only involves quantities that can be inferred using model-free approaches. Leveraging this approximation, we devise an ensemble-based model-free exploration strategy applicable to both tabular and continuous Markov decision processes. Numerical results demonstrate that our strategy is able to identify efficient policies faster than state-of-the-art exploration approaches.

This paper starts from an information-theoretic question: how many samples does a particular problem require to identify a nearly optimal policy? Such instance-specific lower bounds can inform exploration, but deriving them and the corresponding optimal strategy requires a system model and a difficult optimization.

The authors derive an approximation to this lower bound that depends only on quantities obtainable through model-free methods. This creates a connection between a theoretically motivated sample requirement and exploration that does not rely on estimating the system model. They use the approximation to construct an exploration strategy based on an ensemble.

The resulting strategy applies to both tabular and continuous Markov decision processes. Numerical experiments show that it identifies efficient policies faster than state-of-the-art exploration approaches in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a model-free route to exploration guided by an approximation of instance-specific information requirements, with empirical evidence that this guidance accelerates policy discovery.
summary.tldr: An ensemble-based exploration strategy uses a model-free approximation of information-theoretic sample requirements to accelerate empirical policy discovery.

title: Model-Free Active Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent research on online Gradient Balancing (GraB) has revealed that there exist permutation-based example orderings for SGD that are guaranteed to outperform random reshuffling (RR). Whereas RR arbitrarily permutes training examples, GraB leverages stale gradients from prior epochs to order examples -- achieving a provably faster convergence rate than RR. However, GraB is limited by design: while it demonstrates an impressive ability to scale-up training on centralized data, it does not naturally extend to modern distributed ML workloads. We therefore propose Coordinated Distributed GraB (CD-GraB), which uses insights from prior work on kernel thinning to translate the benefits of provably faster permutation-based example ordering to distributed settings. With negligible overhead, CD-GraB exhibits a linear speedup in convergence rate over centralized GraB and outperforms distributed RR on a variety of benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: The order in which training examples are processed can affect how quickly stochastic gradient descent converges. Random reshuffling chooses a new arbitrary order, whereas Gradient Balancing, or GraB, uses gradients retained from earlier epochs to choose an order. Prior results establish that this informed ordering can achieve a faster convergence rate than random reshuffling.

GraB was designed for centralized data and does not naturally carry over to distributed training. The paper introduces Coordinated Distributed GraB, or CD-GraB, to bring the same ordering advantage to that setting. Its design draws on ideas from kernel thinning, using them to coordinate example orders across distributed computation.

The authors report negligible overhead and a linear speedup in convergence rate relative to centralized GraB. CD-GraB also outperforms distributed random reshuffling across several benchmark tasks. These findings connect a theoretical benefit of carefully chosen example orderings with a practical distributed training method, showing that the ordering advantage can extend beyond a single centralized training process.
summary.tldr: CD-GraB coordinates training-example orders across distributed computation to extend GraB's convergence benefits with negligible reported overhead.

title: Coordinating Distributed Example Orders for Provably Accelerated Training

abstract: A widely discussed hypothesis regarding the cause of visual models' lack of robustness is that they can exploit human-imperceptible high-frequency components (HFC) in images, which in turn leads to model vulnerabilities, such as the adversarial examples. However, (1) inconsistent findings regarding the validation of this hypothesis reflect in a limited understanding of HFC, and (2) solutions inspired by the hypothesis tend to involve a robustness-accuracy trade-off and leaning towards suppressing the model's learning on HFC. In this paper, inspired by the long-tailed characteristic observed in frequency spectrum, we first formally define the HFC from long-tailed perspective and then revisit the relationship between HFC and model robustness. In the frequency long-tailed scenario, experimental results on common datasets and various network structures consistently indicate that models in standard training exhibit high sensitivity to HFC. We investigate the reason of the sensitivity, which reflects in model's under-fitting behavior on HFC. Furthermore, the cause of the model's under-fitting behavior is attributed to the limited information content in HFC. Based on these findings, we propose a Balance Spectrum Sampling (BaSS) strategy, which effectively counteracts the long-tailed effect and enhances the model's learning on HFC. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a substantially better robustness-accuracy trade-off when combined with existing defense methods, while also indicating the potential of encouraging HFC learning in improving model performance.

paragraphs: A common explanation for visual-model vulnerability is that models exploit high-frequency image information that people cannot perceive. Approaches motivated by this view often suppress learning from those components. This paper revisits the explanation by defining high-frequency components through the long-tailed distribution observed in image frequency spectra.

Across the tested datasets and network structures, standard training produces strong sensitivity to these components. The authors connect that sensitivity to underfitting, which they attribute to the limited information contained in the high-frequency portion. This interpretation motivates improving how models learn from that information, instead of treating its presence only as a source of vulnerability.

The proposed Balance Spectrum Sampling strategy counteracts the long-tailed frequency distribution and strengthens learning on high-frequency components. When combined with existing defenses, it achieves a substantially better robustness-accuracy trade-off in the reported experiments. The findings indicate that encouraging such learning has potential to improve model performance. They support a more nuanced account of high-frequency information, where insufficient learning can contribute to sensitivity in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Balance Spectrum Sampling improves the reported robustness-accuracy trade-off by helping visual models learn underrepresented high-frequency information.

title: Revisiting Visual Model Robustness: A Frequency Long-Tailed Distribution View

abstract: In theoretical Machine Learning, the teacher-student paradigm is often employed as an effective metaphor for real-life tuition. A student network is trained on data generated by a fixed teacher network until it matches the instructor’s ability to cope with the assigned task. The above scheme proves particularly relevant when the student network is overparameterized (namely, when larger layer sizes are employed) as compared to the underlying teacher network. Under these operating conditions, it is tempting to speculate that the student ability to handle the given task could be eventually stored in a sub-portion of the whole network. This latter should be to some extent reminiscent of the frozen teacher structure, according to suitable metrics, while being approximately invariant across different architectures of the student candidate network. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art conventional learning techniques could not help in identifying the existence of such an invariant subnetwork, due to the inherent degree of non-convexity that characterizes the examined problem. In this work, we take a decisive leap forward by proposing a radically different optimization scheme which builds on a spectral representation of the linear transfer of information between layers. The gradient is hence calculated with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors with negligible increase in terms of computational and complexity load, as compared to standard training algorithms. Working in this framework, we could isolate a stable student substructure, that mirrors the true complexity of the teacher in terms of computing neurons, path distribution and topological attributes. When pruning unimportant nodes of the trained student, as follows a ranking that reflects the optimized eigenvalues, no degradation in the recorded performance is seen above a threshold that corresponds to the effective teacher size. The observed behavior can be pictured as a genuine second-order phase transition that bears universality traits.

paragraphs: In a teacher–student experiment, a student network learns from data generated by a fixed teacher. When the student is larger, a natural question is whether its learned ability resides in a smaller substructure resembling the teacher. This paper investigates that question using a different way to optimize information transfer between network layers.

The method represents those linear transfers spectrally and computes gradients with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The authors report negligible additional computational and complexity costs compared with standard training. In this framework, they isolate a stable student substructure that reflects the teacher's complexity in its number of computing neurons, distribution of paths, and topology.

The optimized eigenvalues also supply a ranking for removing unimportant nodes. In the reported observations, pruning causes no performance degradation while the remaining size stays above a threshold corresponding to the teacher's effective size. The authors describe the observed transition using a second-order phase-transition interpretation with universality traits. The findings connect the training representation to the discovery and removal of excess network structure.
summary.tldr: Spectral training reveals a stable teacher-like substructure inside larger student networks and enables pruning without observed performance loss above a size threshold.

title: How a Student becomes a Teacher: learning and forgetting through Spectral methods

abstract: Remarkable progress has been made in 3D reconstruction from single-view RGB-D inputs. MCC is the current state-of-the-art method in this field, which achieves unprecedented success by combining vision Transformers with large-scale training. However, we identified two key limitations of MCC: 1) The Transformer decoder is inefficient in handling large number of query points; 2) The 3D representation struggles to recover high-fidelity details. In this paper, we propose a new approach called NU-MCC that addresses these limitations. NU-MCC includes two key innovations: a Neighborhood decoder and a Repulsive Unsigned Distance Function (Repulsive UDF). First, our Neighborhood decoder introduces center points as an efficient proxy of input visual features, allowing each query point to only attend to a small neighborhood. This design not only results in much faster inference speed but also enables the exploitation of finer-scale visual features for improved recovery of 3D textures. Second, our Repulsive UDF is a novel alternative to the occupancy field used in MCC, significantly improving the quality of 3D object reconstruction. Compared to standard UDFs that suffer from holes in results, our proposed Repulsive UDF can achieve more complete surface reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that NU-MCC is able to learn a strong 3D representation, significantly advancing the state of the art in single-view 3D reconstruction. Particularly, it outperforms MCC by 9.7% in terms of the F1-score on the CO3D-v2 dataset with more than 5x faster running speed.

paragraphs: NU-MCC reconstructs three-dimensional objects from a single RGB-D input, which combines color and depth. It addresses two weaknesses identified in MCC: expensive decoding when many spatial query points are used and difficulty recovering fine geometric details. The proposed changes target both computation and the representation of the reconstructed surface.

A neighborhood decoder introduces center points that summarize input visual features. Each query attends only to a small nearby group, reducing decoding work and enabling the use of finer-scale visual features. The second change replaces MCC's occupancy representation with a repulsive unsigned distance function. This representation improves reconstruction quality and produces more complete surfaces than standard unsigned distance functions, which can leave holes.

The experiments report improved single-view reconstruction quality alongside faster execution. On CO3D-v2, NU-MCC outperforms MCC by 9.7% in F1-score and runs more than five times faster. The stated result shows that the two changes can improve surface recovery while also addressing the computational burden of querying a detailed three-dimensional representation.
summary.tldr: NU-MCC combines local decoding with a repulsive distance representation to improve single-view 3D reconstruction quality and speed.

title: NU-MCC: Multiview Compressive Coding with Neighborhood Decoder and Repulsive UDF

abstract: Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) provides a robust pathway for acquiring embeddings without expert labelling, a capability that carries profound implications for molecular graphs due to the staggering number of potential molecules and the high cost of obtaining labels. However, GSSL methods are designed not for optimisation within a specific domain but rather for transferability across a variety of downstream tasks. This broad applicability complicates their evaluation. Addressing this challenge, we present "Molecular Graph Representation Evaluation" (MOLGRAPHEVAL), generating detailed profiles of molecular graph embeddings with interpretable and diversified attributes. MOLGRAPHEVAL offers a suite of probing tasks grouped into three categories: (i) generic graph, (ii) molecular substructure, and (iii) embedding space properties. By leveraging MOLGRAPHEVAL to benchmark existing GSSL methods against both current downstream datasets and our suite of tasks, we uncover significant inconsistencies between inferences drawn solely from existing datasets and those derived from more nuanced probing. These findings suggest that current evaluation methodologies fail to capture the entirety of the landscape.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce representations of molecular graphs without expensive expert labels. Evaluating these representations is difficult because they are meant to support many later tasks. A result on a particular prediction dataset may reveal something useful without fully explaining which properties of molecules the representation captures.

The paper introduces MOLGRAPHEVAL to build more interpretable profiles of these learned representations. Its probing tasks examine three kinds of properties: general graph structure, molecular substructures, and the organization of the embedding space itself. These complementary views make it possible to examine the representation beyond its performance on existing downstream datasets.

When the authors benchmark existing graph self-supervised methods, conclusions from conventional datasets differ substantially from those drawn through the probes. The finding suggests that current evaluation practices provide an incomplete picture. MOLGRAPHEVAL's value is therefore diagnostic: it helps distinguish different strengths and weaknesses that could otherwise be hidden behind a small set of downstream results.
summary.tldr: MOLGRAPHEVAL reveals molecular representation properties that conventional downstream evaluations can miss.

title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graph Embeddings

abstract: Traditional cameras produce desirable vision results but struggle with motion blur in high-speed scenes due to long exposure windows. Existing frame-based deblurring algorithms face challenges in extracting useful motion cues from severely blurred images. Recently, an emerging bio-inspired vision sensor known as the spike camera has achieved an extremely high frame rate while preserving rich spatial details, owing to its novel sampling mechanism. However, typical binary spike streams are relatively low-resolution, degraded image signals devoid of color information, making them unfriendly to human vision. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that integrates the two modalities from two branches, leveraging spike streams as auxiliary visual cues for guiding deblurring in high-speed motion scenes. We propose the first spike-based motion deblurring model with bidirectional information complementarity. We introduce a content-aware motion magnitude attention module that utilizes learnable mask to extract relevant information from blurry images effectively, and we incorporate a transposed cross-attention fusion module to efficiently combine features from both spike data and blurry RGB images.Furthermore, we build two extensive synthesized datasets for training and validation purposes, encompassing high-temporal-resolution spikes, blurry images, and corresponding sharp images. The experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively recovers clear RGB images from highly blurry scenes and outperforms state-of-the-art deblurring algorithms in multiple settings.

paragraphs: Fast motion can blur a conventional camera image so severely that recovering motion cues from the frame becomes difficult. Spike cameras provide much finer temporal information, but their binary streams lack color and typically have low resolution and degraded image signals. This paper combines the complementary information available from these two sensor modalities.

The proposed model has branches for blurry RGB images and spike data, with information flowing between them. A content-aware motion attention module uses a learned mask to select relevant image information. A transposed cross-attention module then fuses features from the two inputs, allowing spike streams to guide reconstruction of a sharp color image.

The authors also create two synthetic datasets containing high-temporal-resolution spike streams, blurry frames, and corresponding sharp images for training and validation. Experiments show recovery of clear RGB images from highly blurred scenes and improvements over state-of-the-art deblurring methods in multiple tested settings. The approach matters because it combines temporal detail from spikes with the color and visual content of ordinary images.
summary.tldr: A two-branch model combines spike-camera motion cues with blurry RGB images to improve deblurring in high-speed scenes.

title: Enhancing Motion Deblurring in High-Speed Scenes with Spike Streams

abstract: Vision-language models, such as CLIP, have shown impressive generalization capacities when using appropriate text descriptions. While optimizing prompts on downstream labeled data has proven effective in improving performance, these methods entail labor costs for annotations and are limited by their quality. Additionally, since CLIP is pre-trained on highly imbalanced Web-scale data, it suffers from inherent label bias that leads to suboptimal performance. To tackle the above challenges, we propose a label-**F**ree p**ro**mpt distribution **l**earning and b**i**as **c**orrection framework, dubbed as **Frolic**, which boosts zero-shot performance without the need for labeled data. Specifically, our Frolic learns distributions over prompt prototypes to capture diverse visual representations and adaptively fuses these with the original CLIP through confidence matching.This fused model is further enhanced by correcting label bias via a label-free logit adjustment. Notably, our method is not only training-free but also circumvents the necessity for hyper-parameter tuning. Extensive experimental results across 16 datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, particularly outperforming the state-of-the-art by an average of $2.6\%$ on 10 datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16 and achieving an average margin of $1.5\%$ on ImageNet and its five distribution shifts with CLIP ViT-B/16. Codes are available in [https://github.com/zhuhsingyuu/Frolic](https://github.com/zhuhsingyuu/Frolic).

paragraphs: Vision-language models such as CLIP depend on the text descriptions used to recognize image categories. Optimizing these prompts with labeled examples can help, but requires annotation work. The paper also identifies label bias inherited from imbalanced pretraining data as a separate source of reduced performance. Frolic addresses both issues without requiring labeled downstream data.

The framework learns distributions over prompt prototypes to capture diverse visual representations. It combines these with the original CLIP model through confidence matching, then applies a label-free adjustment to the output logits to correct label bias. The approach is described as training-free and avoids hyperparameter tuning, so the proposed adaptation does not rely on a conventional labeled prompt-training procedure.

Experiments span 16 datasets. With CLIP ViT-B/16, Frolic reports an average improvement of 2.6% over the state of the art on ten datasets and an average margin of 1.5% on ImageNet and five distribution shifts. These results support combining prompt diversity with bias correction as a practical way to improve the evaluated zero-shot predictions.
summary.tldr: Frolic improves zero-shot CLIP predictions through prompt distributions, confidence-based fusion, and label-bias correction without labeled data or training.

title: Enhancing Zero-Shot Vision Models by Label-Free Prompt Distribution Learning and Bias Correcting

abstract: Driving world models have gained increasing attention due to their ability to model complex physical dynamics. However, their superb modeling capability is yet to be fully unleashed due to the limited video diversity in current driving datasets. We introduce DrivingDojo, the first dataset tailor-made for training interactive world models with complex driving dynamics. Our dataset features video clips with a complete set of driving maneuvers, diverse multi-agent interplay, and rich open-world driving knowledge, laying a stepping stone for future world model development. We further define an action instruction following (AIF) benchmark for world models and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed dataset for generating action-controlled future predictions.

paragraphs: Driving world models predict how a driving scene develops, including its physical dynamics. Their ability to learn this behavior depends on the situations represented in training videos. The paper argues that limited diversity in existing driving datasets restricts the potential of these models, particularly when predictions must respond to driving actions.

DrivingDojo is a dataset designed specifically for training interactive driving world models. Its video clips cover a full set of driving maneuvers, varied interactions among multiple road participants, and broad driving knowledge from open-world situations. These ingredients target the complexity of driving as an interactive process, where future events involve more than the movement of one vehicle.

The authors also introduce an action instruction following benchmark for world models. This makes responsiveness to action instructions an explicit evaluation target alongside future prediction. Their results demonstrate the proposed dataset's advantage for generating futures controlled by actions. The contribution therefore connects richer training examples with an evaluation focused on whether a world model follows the intended driving behavior.
summary.tldr: DrivingDojo provides diverse driving videos and an action-following benchmark for training interactive driving world models.

title: DrivingDojo Dataset: Advancing Interactive and Knowledge-Enriched Driving World Model

abstract: Fine-tuning is a crucial process for adapting large language models (LLMs) to diverse applications. In certain scenarios, such as multi-tenant serving, deploying multiple LLMs becomes necessary to meet complex demands. Recent studies suggest decomposing a fine-tuned LLM into a base model and corresponding delta weights, which are then compressed using low-rank or low-bit approaches to reduce costs. In this work, we observe that existing low-rank and low-bit compression methods can significantly harm the model performance for task-specific fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., WizardMath for math problems). Motivated by the long-tail distribution of singular values in the delta weights, we propose a delta quantization approach using mixed-precision. This method employs higher-bit representation for singular vectors corresponding to larger singular values. We evaluate our approach on various fine-tuned LLMs, including math LLMs, code LLMs, chat LLMs, and even VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach performs comparably to full fine-tuned LLMs, surpassing both low-rank and low-bit baselines by a considerable margin. Additionally, we show that our method is compatible with various backbone LLMs, such as Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, highlighting its generalizability.
originalAbstract: Fine-tuning is a crucial process for adapting large language models (LLMs) to diverse applications. In certain scenarios, such as multi-tenant serving, deploying multiple LLMs becomes necessary to meet complex demands. Recent studies suggest decomposing a fine-tuned LLM into a base model and corresponding delta weights, which are then compressed using low-rank or low-bit approaches to reduce costs. In this work, we observe that existing low-rank and low-bit compression methods can significantly harm the model performance for task-specific fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., WizardMath for math problems). Motivated by the long-tail distribution of singular values in the delta weights, we propose a delta quantization approach using mixed-precision. This method employs higher-bit representation for singular vectors corresponding to larger singular values. We evaluate our approach on various fine-tuned LLMs, including math LLMs, code LLMs, chat LLMs, and even VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach performs comparably to full fine-tuned LLMs, surpassing both low-rank and low-bit baselines by a considerable margin. Additionally, we show that our method is compatible with various backbone LLMs, such as Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, highlighting its generalizability.

paragraphs: Serving several fine-tuned language models can require storing many versions of a shared base model. One strategy stores the base once and compresses each model’s delta weights, which describe its changes from that base. The authors observe that existing low-rank and low-bit compression methods can substantially damage the performance of specialized models, including models tuned for mathematics.

Delta-CoMe uses mixed precision to compress these differences without additional training. Its design follows the observed long-tailed distribution of singular values in delta weights. Singular vectors associated with larger singular values receive higher-bit representations, allocating precision unevenly according to this structure rather than treating all components alike.

The authors report performance comparable to the full fine-tuned models and considerably better than the tested low-rank and low-bit alternatives. Compatibility with Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral further supports the approach’s applicability across backbones. The findings show that how precision is distributed within a delta can matter greatly for preserving specialized capabilities.
summary.tldr: Delta-CoMe compresses fine-tuning changes with mixed precision, preserving specialized model performance better than tested low-rank and low-bit alternatives.

title: Delta-CoMe: Training-Free Delta-Compression with Mixed-Precision for Large Language Models

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have achieved remarkable success in text-to-image generation, but they also pose safety risks, such as the potential generation of harmful content and copyright violations. The techniques of machine unlearning, also known as concept erasing, have been developed to address these risks. However, these techniques remain vulnerable to adversarial prompt attacks, which can prompt DMs post-unlearning to regenerate undesired images containing concepts (such as nudity) meant to be erased. This work aims to enhance the robustness of concept erasing by integrating the principle of adversarial training (AT) into machine unlearning, resulting in the robust unlearning framework referred to as AdvUnlearn. However, achieving this effectively and efficiently is highly nontrivial. First, we find that a straightforward implementation of AT compromises DMs’ image generation quality post-unlearning. To address this, we develop a utility-retaining regularization on an additional retain set, optimizing the trade-off between concept erasure robustness and model utility in AdvUnlearn. Moreover, we identify the text encoder as a more suitable module for robustification compared to UNet, ensuring unlearning effectiveness. And the acquired text encoder can serve as a plug-and-play robust unlearner for various DM types. Empirically, we perform extensive experiments to demonstrate the robustness advantage of AdvUnlearn across various DM unlearning scenarios, including the erasure of nudity, objects, and style concepts. In addition to robustness, AdvUnlearn also achieves a balanced tradeoff with model utility. To our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically explore robust DM unlearning through AT, setting it apart from existing methods that overlook robustness in concept erasing. Codes are available at https://github.com/OPTML-Group/AdvUnlearn.Warning: This paper contains model outputs that may be offensive in nature.

paragraphs: Concept erasure aims to stop a text-to-image diffusion model from generating particular content. However, adversarial prompts can sometimes recover concepts after they have supposedly been removed. This paper introduces AdvUnlearn, which incorporates adversarial training into unlearning so that erasure is more resistant to prompts designed to defeat it.

The authors find that applying adversarial training directly can damage image quality. They address this with a regularization term based on an additional retain set, balancing resistance to concept recovery against preservation of useful generation behavior. They also identify the text encoder as a more suitable component to strengthen than the UNet, and report that the resulting encoder can function as a plug-and-play robust unlearner across different diffusion model types.

Experiments cover removal of nudity, objects, and styles. The reported results show a robustness advantage while maintaining a balanced trade-off with model utility. The work therefore treats successful unlearning as more than suppressing a concept under ordinary prompting: it also examines whether that suppression survives deliberate attempts to reverse it.
summary.tldr: AdvUnlearn uses adversarial training and utility-preserving regularization to make diffusion-model concept erasure more resistant to adversarial prompts.

title: Defensive Unlearning with Adversarial Training for Robust Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models

abstract: There are increasing cases where the class labels of test samples are unavailable, creating a significant need and challenge in measuring the discrepancy between training and test distributions. This distribution discrepancy complicates the assessment of whether the hypothesis selected by an algorithm on training samples remains applicable to test samples. We present a novel approach called Importance Divergence (I-Div) to address the challenge of test label unavailability, enabling distribution discrepancy evaluation using only training samples. I-Div transfers the sampling patterns from the test distribution to the training distribution by estimating density and likelihood ratios. Specifically, the density ratio, informed by the selected hypothesis, is obtained by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the actual and estimated input distributions. Simultaneously, the likelihood ratio is adjusted according to the density ratio by reducing the generalization error of the distribution discrepancy as transformed through the two ratios. Experimentally, I-Div accurately quantifies the distribution discrepancy, as evidenced by a wide range of complex data scenarios and tasks.

paragraphs: When test labels are unavailable, it is difficult to judge whether a predictor learned from training data remains suitable for the test distribution. Importance Divergence, or I-Div, addresses this by transferring test-distribution sampling patterns onto training data. This lets the discrepancy evaluation operate on training samples while incorporating information about how test inputs are distributed.

The method estimates two linked quantities: a density ratio and a likelihood ratio. The density-ratio estimate depends on the selected hypothesis and is learned by minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between actual and estimated input distributions. The likelihood ratio is adjusted in relation to that density ratio by reducing the generalization error of the discrepancy transformed through both ratios.

This construction makes distribution comparison sensitive to the hypothesis being assessed and avoids requiring test class labels. Across a broad range of complex data scenarios and tasks, the authors report that I-Div accurately quantifies distribution discrepancy. The stated contribution is a way to evaluate the mismatch through sampling transfer, helping address the uncertainty surrounding the applicability of a training-selected predictor.
summary.tldr: I-Div estimates train–test distribution discrepancy without test labels by transferring test sampling patterns onto training data through learned ratios.

title: Revealing Distribution Discrepancy by Sampling Transfer in Unlabeled Data

abstract: Recent development in Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has propelled their application in scientific discovery, but the validation and exploration of these discoveries require subsequent empirical experimentation. The concept of self-driving laboratories promises to automate and thus boost the experimental process following AI-driven discoveries. However, the transition of experimental protocols, originally crafted for human comprehension, into formats interpretable by machines presents significant challenges, which, within the context of specific expert domain, encompass the necessity for structured as opposed to natural language, the imperative for explicit rather than tacit knowledge, and the preservation of causality and consistency throughout protocol steps. Presently, the task of protocol translation predominantly requires the manual and labor-intensive involvement of domain experts and information technology specialists, rendering the process time-intensive. To address these issues, we propose a framework that automates the protocol translation process through a three-stage workflow, which incrementally constructs Protocol Dependence Graphs (PDGs) that approach structured on the syntax level, completed on the semantics level, and linked on the execution level. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations have demonstrated its performance at par with that of human experts, underscoring its potential to significantly expedite and democratize the process of scientific discovery by elevating the automation capabilities within self-driving laboratories.

paragraphs: Laboratory protocols written for people often rely on tacit knowledge and informal sequencing. Automated laboratories need explicit operations whose dependencies remain consistent. This paper targets the translation step that otherwise requires labor-intensive collaboration between domain experts and software specialists.

The proposed workflow incrementally builds Protocol Dependence Graphs in three stages. It first structures syntax, then completes semantic information, and finally links execution-level relationships, aiming to preserve causality and consistency across the protocol’s steps.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations find performance comparable to human experts. The abstract does not identify the scientific domains, evaluation metrics, or the extent of physical execution testing. The supported contribution is automated protocol translation with expert-level evaluated quality, rather than evidence that every translated procedure can be executed autonomously without further validation in a self-driving laboratory.
summary.tldr: A three-stage translation workflow converts human laboratory protocols into structured dependence graphs.

title: Expert-level protocol translation for self-driving labs

abstract: In multi-output regression, we identify a previously neglected challenge that arises from the inability of training distribution to cover all combinations of input features, leading to combinatorial distribution shift (CDS). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to formally define and address this problem. We tackle it through a novel tensor decomposition perspective, proposing the Functional t-Singular Value Decomposition (Ft-SVD) theorem which extends the classical tensor SVD to infinite and continuous feature domains, providing a natural tool for representing and analyzing multi-output functions. Within the Ft-SVD framework, we formulate the multi-output regression problem under CDS as a low-rank tensor estimation problem under the missing not at random (MNAR) setting, and introduce a series of assumptions about the true functions, training and testing distributions, and spectral properties of the ground-truth embeddings, making the problem more tractable.To address the challenges posed by CDS in multi-output regression, we develop a tailored Double-Stage Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM-DS) algorithm that leverages the spectral properties of the embeddings and uses specific hypothesis classes in each frequency component to better capture the varying spectral decay patterns. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses that establish performance guarantees for the ERM-DS algorithm. This work lays a preliminary theoretical foundation for multi-output regression under CDS.

paragraphs: A training dataset may include individual input features without covering every combination that appears at test time. This paper formalizes the resulting challenge for predicting multiple outputs as combinatorial distribution shift. Its focus is on understanding how learning can succeed when the missing coverage concerns combinations of features.

The authors introduce Functional t-Singular Value Decomposition, extending classical tensor decomposition to continuous and infinite feature domains. This gives them a representation for multi-output functions and recasts learning under combinatorial shift as low-rank tensor estimation with data missing not at random. The analysis imposes assumptions on the true functions, training and test distributions, and spectral properties of the underlying embeddings.

Within that framework, the proposed Double-Stage Empirical Risk Minimization algorithm uses different hypothesis classes for different frequency components to accommodate varying spectral decay. The authors establish performance guarantees through theoretical analysis. The contribution is a preliminary foundation for this distribution-shift problem, with its guarantees grounded in the stated structural and distributional assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a tensor-based theory and learning algorithm for multi-output prediction when training data omit relevant feature combinations.

title: Generalized Tensor Decomposition for Understanding Multi-Output Regression under Combinatorial Shifts

abstract: A recent study has shown that large-scale visual datasets are very biased: they can be easily classified by modern neural networks. However, the concrete forms of bias among these datasets remain unclear. In this study, we propose a framework to identify the unique visual attributes distinguishing these datasets. Our approach applies various transformations to extract semantic, structural, boundary, color, and frequency information from datasets, and assess how much each type of information reflects their bias. We further decompose their semantic bias with object-level analysis, and leverage natural language methods to generate detailed, open-ended descriptions of each dataset's characteristics. Our work aims to help researchers understand the bias in existing large-scale pre-training datasets, and build more diverse and representative ones in the future. Our project page and code are available at boyazeng.github.io/understand_bias.

paragraphs: Large visual datasets can carry recognizable signatures: neural networks can identify which dataset an image comes from. That observation indicates systematic differences, but does not explain their visual form. This paper develops a framework for identifying the attributes that distinguish datasets and make those differences easier to interpret.

The method applies transformations that expose different types of information, including semantic content, structure, boundaries, color, and frequency. It then assesses how much each information type reflects dataset bias. An additional object-level analysis breaks down semantic differences, while natural-language methods generate detailed, open-ended descriptions of the characteristics associated with each dataset.

The contribution turns dataset distinguishability into a more concrete investigation of what differs between collections. Rather than stopping at a classifier’s ability to recognize a source, the framework seeks explanations in visual attributes and object content. The intended use is to help researchers understand existing pretraining datasets and guide the construction of more diverse and representative ones; the abstract does not claim that this construction goal has already been achieved.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes visual attributes, objects, and natural-language descriptions to explain the biases distinguishing large image datasets.

title: Understanding Bias in Large-Scale Visual Datasets

abstract: Recent works have shown the remarkable superiority of transformer models in reinforcement learning (RL), where the decision-making problem is formulated as sequential generation. Transformer-based agents could emerge with self-improvement in online environments by providing task contexts, such as multiple trajectories, called in-context RL. However, due to the quadratic computation complexity of attention in transformers, current in-context RL methods suffer from huge computational costs as the task horizon increases. In contrast, the Mamba model is renowned for its efficient ability to process long-term dependencies, which provides an opportunity for in-context RL to solve tasks that require long-term memory. To this end, we first implement Decision Mamba (DM) by replacing the backbone of Decision Transformer (DT). Then, we propose a Decision Mamba-Hybrid (DM-H) with the merits of transformers and Mamba in high-quality prediction and long-term memory. Specifically, DM-H first generates high-value sub-goals from long-term memory through the Mamba model. Then, we use sub-goals to prompt the transformer, establishing high-quality predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that DM-H achieves state-of-the-art in long and short-term tasks, such as D4RL, Grid World, and Tmaze benchmarks. Regarding efficiency, the online testing of DM-H in the long-term task is 28$\times$ times faster than the transformer-based baselines.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning agents make decisions by treating experience and actions as sequences. Transformers can use task context, including multiple trajectories, to improve behavior during online interaction. However, attention becomes computationally expensive as that context grows. This paper explores Mamba as a way to support decisions that depend on long histories.

In the reported long-term task, online testing is 28 times faster than transformer-based baselines. summary.tldr: Decision Mamba-Hybrid uses Mamba-generated sub-goals to guide a transformer, improving tested decision tasks while accelerating long-term online evaluation.

title: Decision Mamba: Reinforcement Learning via Hybrid Selective Sequence Modeling

abstract: Shape assembly is a ubiquitous task in daily life, integral for constructing complex 3D structures like IKEA furniture. While significant progress has been made in developing autonomous agents for shape assembly, existing datasets have not yet tackled the 4D grounding of assembly instructions in videos, essential for a holistic understanding of assembly in 3D space over time. We introduce IKEA Video Manuals, a dataset that features 3D models of furniture parts, instructional manuals, assembly videos from the Internet, and most importantly, annotations of dense spatio-temporal alignments between these data modalities. To demonstrate the utility of IKEA Video Manuals, we present five applications essential for shape assembly: assembly plan generation, part-conditioned segmentation, part-conditioned pose estimation, video object segmentation, and furniture assembly based on instructional video manuals. For each application, we provide evaluation metrics and baseline methods. Through experiments on our annotated data, we highlight many challenges in grounding assembly instructions in videos to improve shape assembly, including handling occlusions, varying viewpoints, and extended assembly sequences.

paragraphs: Understanding furniture assembly requires connecting instructions with parts and actions as they unfold in three-dimensional space over time. The paper introduces IKEA Video Manuals to support this form of 4D grounding. Its goal is to make the relationships between assembly instructions, physical parts, and recorded demonstrations available for systematic study.

The dataset combines 3D furniture-part models, instruction manuals, and Internet assembly videos. Its central addition is dense spatial and temporal alignment annotations across these sources. Those annotations connect the different ways an assembly process is represented, providing a basis for studying how an agent can relate a manual to what occurs in a video.

The authors demonstrate five applications: assembly planning, part-conditioned segmentation, part-conditioned pose estimation, video object segmentation, and furniture assembly using instructional videos. They provide baseline methods and evaluation metrics for each. Experiments highlight difficulties caused by occlusion, changing viewpoints, and long assembly sequences. The contribution is therefore both an aligned dataset and a set of evaluation tasks that expose concrete challenges in understanding assembly across space and time.
summary.tldr: IKEA Video Manuals aligns furniture parts, manuals, and assembly videos across space and time to support five assembly-related evaluation tasks.

title: IKEA Manuals at Work: 4D Grounding of Assembly Instructions on Internet Videos

abstract: Serialization-based methods, which serialize the 3D voxels and group them into multiple sequences before inputting to Transformers, have demonstrated their effectiveness in 3D object detection. However, serializing 3D voxels into 1D sequences will inevitably sacrifice the voxel spatial proximity. Such an issue is hard to be addressed by enlarging the group size with existing serialization-based methods due to the quadratic complexity of Transformers with feature sizes. Inspired by the recent advances of state space models (SSMs), we present a Voxel SSM, termed as Voxel Mamba, which employs a group-free strategy to serialize the whole space of voxels into a single sequence. The linear complexity of SSMs encourages our group-free design, alleviating the loss of spatial proximity of voxels. To further enhance the spatial proximity, we propose a Dual-scale SSM Block to establish a hierarchical structure, enabling a larger receptive field in the 1D serialization curve, as well as more complete local regions in 3D space. Moreover, we implicitly apply window partition under the group-free framework by positional encoding, which further enhances spatial proximity by encoding voxel positional information. Our experiments on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes dataset show that Voxel Mamba not only achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods, but also demonstrates significant advantages in computational efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/gwenzhang/Voxel-Mamba.

paragraphs: Point-cloud detectors can turn 3D voxels into one-dimensional sequences, but this rearrangement disrupts spatial proximity. Transformer-based methods often divide those sequences into groups, and their quadratic complexity makes enlarging groups costly. Voxel Mamba uses a state-space model with linear complexity to process the whole voxel space as one sequence.

The group-free design aims to alleviate the loss of neighborhood information. A Dual-scale State Space Model Block adds a hierarchy that expands the receptive field along the sequence while capturing more complete local regions in 3D. Positional encoding also introduces implicit window partitioning within the group-free framework, further incorporating voxel location information.

Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes report higher detection accuracy than state-of-the-art methods along with substantial computational-efficiency advantages. The design matters because sequence efficiency and spatial structure are addressed together: whole-space processing removes grouping constraints, while the hierarchy and positional information help preserve relationships that serialization would otherwise weaken.
summary.tldr: Voxel Mamba processes all voxels in one linear-complexity sequence and adds spatial structure to improve 3D detection accuracy and efficiency.

title: Voxel Mamba: Group-Free State Space Models for Point Cloud based 3D Object Detection

abstract: The exploration-exploitation dilemma has been a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) with complex model classes. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, Monotonic Q-Learning with Upper Confidence Bound (MQL-UCB) for RL with general function approximation. Our key algorithmic design includes (1) a general deterministic policy-switching strategy that achieves low switching cost, (2) a monotonic value function structure with carefully controlled function class complexity, and (3) a variance-weighted regression scheme that exploits historical trajectories with high data efficiency. MQL-UCB achieves minimax optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{HK})$ when $K$ is sufficiently large and near-optimal policy switching cost of $\tilde{O}(dH)$, with $d$ being the eluder dimension of the function class, $H$ being the planning horizon, and $K$ being the number of episodes. Our work sheds light on designing provably sample-efficient and deployment-efficient Q-learning with nonlinear function approximation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must balance trying unfamiliar actions with using actions that already appear rewarding. With complex function approximators, learning efficiently also raises a deployment question: how often must the agent replace its current policy? This paper introduces MQL-UCB, a Q-learning algorithm designed to address both the amount of experience needed and the number of policy changes.

The algorithm combines three ideas. A deterministic switching strategy controls policy updates. A monotonic value-function structure keeps the complexity of the functions under control. Variance-weighted regression then uses historical trajectories efficiently, incorporating information about their variability into learning. These components connect exploration, value estimation, and deployment frequency within one algorithm.

For sufficiently many episodes, the authors prove minimax-optimal regret scaling as d times the square root of HK, up to logarithmic factors. Here d measures function-class complexity, H is the planning horizon, and K counts episodes. Policy switching scales near-optimally as dH, again up to logarithmic factors. The result supports efficient learning and infrequent deployment changes together under the stated large-episode condition.
summary.tldr: MQL-UCB combines efficient exploration with infrequent policy changes and achieves optimal regret for sufficiently many episodes.

title: A Nearly Optimal and Low-Switching Algorithm for Reinforcement Learning with General Function Approximation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit complementary strengths in various tasks, motivating the research of LLM ensembling.However, existing work focuses on training an extra reward model or fusion model to select or combine all candidate answers, posing a great challenge to the generalization on unseen data distributions.Besides, prior methods use textual responses as communication media, ignoring the valuable information in the internal representations.In this work, we propose a training-free ensemble framework \textsc{DeePEn}, fusing the informative probability distributions yielded by different LLMs at each decoding step.Unfortunately, the vocabulary discrepancy between heterogeneous LLMs directly makes averaging the distributions unfeasible due to the token misalignment.To address this challenge, \textsc{DeePEn} maps the probability distribution of each model from its own probability space to a universal \textit{relative space} based on the relative representation theory, and performs aggregation.Next, we devise a search-based inverse transformation to transform the aggregated result back to the probability space of one of the ensembling LLMs (main model), in order to determine the next token.We conduct extensive experiments on ensembles of different number of LLMs, ensembles of LLMs with different architectures, and ensembles between the LLM and the specialist model.Experimental results show that (i) \textsc{DeePEn} achieves consistent improvements across six benchmarks covering subject examination, reasoning, and knowledge, (ii) a well-performing specialist model can benefit from a less effective LLM through distribution fusion, and (iii) \textsc{DeePEn} has complementary strengths with other ensemble methods such as voting.

paragraphs: DeePEn combines language models during generation by fusing their next-token probability distributions at each decoding step. It requires no additional training. This allows the ensemble to use information about alternative tokens throughout generation, beyond the information available in completed textual answers.

Different models may use different vocabularies, so corresponding positions in their probability vectors need not refer to the same token. Direct averaging would therefore mix incompatible quantities. DeePEn maps each distribution into a shared relative representation, aggregates there, and uses a search-based inverse transformation to return the result to the main model's vocabulary. That model can then select the next token.

Experiments cover different ensemble sizes, model architectures, and combinations of general language models with specialists. The method consistently improves results across six benchmarks involving subject examinations, reasoning, and knowledge. A specialist can also benefit from fusion with a less effective general model. Its complementary strengths with voting suggest that collaboration during decoding can contribute information beyond that captured by combining final answers.
summary.tldr: DeePEn combines heterogeneous language models' token probabilities through a shared representation, improving benchmark performance without additional training.

title: Ensemble Learning for Heterogeneous Large Language Models with Deep Parallel Collaboration

abstract: We present variational inference with sequential sample-average approximations (VISA), a method for approximate inference in computationally intensive models, such as those based on numerical simulations. VISA extends importance-weighted forward-KL variational inference by employing a sequence of sample-average approximations, which are considered valid inside a trust region. This makes it possible to reuse model evaluations across multiple gradient steps, thereby reducing computational cost. We perform experiments on high-dimensional Gaussians, Lotka-Volterra dynamics, and a Pickover attractor, which demonstrate that VISA can achieve comparable approximation accuracy to standard importance-weighted forward-KL variational inference with computational savings of a factor two or more for conservatively chosen learning rates.
