paragraphs: Approximate inference can become expensive when evaluating the underlying model requires substantial numerical computation. VISA addresses this cost within importance-weighted forward-KL variational inference. Its focus is on reducing repeated model evaluations while maintaining the accuracy of the approximate distribution, particularly for models built around numerical simulations.

The method constructs a sequence of sample-average approximations. Each approximation is treated as valid within a trust region, allowing the same model evaluations to support multiple gradient steps. This creates a controlled setting for reusing expensive computational work as the variational approximation is updated, rather than requiring fresh evaluations for every step.

Experiments cover high-dimensional Gaussian distributions, Lotka–Volterra dynamics, and a Pickover attractor. With conservatively chosen learning rates, VISA achieves approximation accuracy comparable to standard importance-weighted forward-KL variational inference while reducing computational cost by a factor of two or more. The learning-rate qualification matters to the reported result. The contribution is a practical mechanism for reusing evaluations within a trusted range while preserving approximation quality in the tested models.
summary.tldr: VISA reuses expensive model evaluations within trust regions, reporting comparable inference accuracy at half the cost or less with conservative learning rates.

title: VISA: Variational Inference with Sequential Sample-Average Approximations

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically aligned to a single, universal policy, obscuring the rich plurality of human moral perspectives that drive creative practice. We present a study of prompt-level moral steering in large language models with ten-principle constitutions. Seven constitutions matched in length (Intersectional Feminist, Ecological Justice, Ubuntu, Indigenous Sovereignty, Universal Human Rights, Neutral, and a Random Adjective placebo) are paired with a 100-question benchmark spanning Everyday Advice, Policy Scenarios, Normative Dilemmas, and Rewrite Tasks. We generated 2800 completions across four models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-4 Scout-17B, Qwen-3-235B) and evaluate them with four complementary metrics: toxicity, semantic alignment with the canon of each constitution, lexical marker ratio, and an LLM-as-a-Judge composite of authenticity, helpfulness, and safety. Prompted moral frames yield consistent improvements in alignment and judged quality without increasing toxicity; placebo prompts do not. Effects replicate across models and are strongest on morally charged tasks. The open-source toolkit lets researchers or artists author new frames in minutes, supporting participatory, culturally adaptive AI. Our results show that pluralistic prompting is a practical lever for value-conditional behavior and a fertile instrument for creative AI exploration. The code and results obtained in this study is available at: https://github.com/ArjunBalaji79/encoding values neurips

paragraphs: This study tests whether prompts can steer language models toward different moral perspectives. The authors create seven equally long constitutions, each containing ten principles. These include perspectives such as ecological justice and Ubuntu, alongside neutral and random-adjective conditions that help distinguish meaningful moral framing from merely adding prompt text.

Four models generate 2,800 responses to a benchmark covering everyday advice, policy scenarios, normative dilemmas, and rewriting. Evaluation considers toxicity, semantic agreement with each constitution’s reference ideas, characteristic vocabulary, and a model-based judgment combining authenticity, helpfulness, and safety. This examines several aspects of response behavior rather than relying on one alignment score.

Meaningful moral frames consistently improve measured alignment and judged quality without increasing measured toxicity; the placebo prompts do not. Effects appear across the tested models and are strongest on morally charged tasks. The accompanying open-source toolkit supports authoring additional frames. The findings establish prompting as a practical means of producing value-conditional behavior in the studied settings, with potential uses in participatory and creative AI.
summary.tldr: Ten-principle moral prompts steer tested language models toward different value frameworks while improving judged quality without increasing measured toxicity.

title: Encoding Values: Injecting Morality into Machines via Prompt-Conditioned Moral Frames

abstract: Recent advances in Audio-Language Models (ALMs) have significantly improved multimodal understanding capabilities. However, the introduction of the audio modality also brings new and unique vulnerability vectors. Previous studies have proposed jailbreak attacks that specifically target ALMs, revealing that defenses directly transferred from traditional audio adversarial attacks or text-based Large Language Model (LLM) jailbreaks are largely ineffective against these ALM-specific threats. To address this issue, we propose ALMGuard, the first defense framework tailored to ALMs. Based on the assumption that safety-aligned shortcuts naturally exist in ALMs, we design a method to identify universal Shortcut Activation Perturbations (SAPs) that serve as triggers that activate the safety shortcuts to safeguard ALMs at inference time. To better sift out effective triggers while preserving the model’s utility on benign tasks, we further propose Mel-Gradient Sparse Mask (M-GSM), which restricts perturbations to Mel-frequency bins that are sensitive to jailbreaks but insensitive to speech understanding. Both theoretical analyses and empirical results demonstrate the robustness of our method against both seen and unseen attacks. Overall, \MethodName reduces the average success rate of advanced ALM-specific jailbreak attacks to 4.6\% across four models, while maintaining comparable utility on benign benchmarks, establishing it as the new state of the art. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/WeifeiJin/ALMGuard.

paragraphs: Audio-language models face jailbreak attempts that exploit the audio modality itself. ALMGuard addresses this mismatch with a defense designed specifically for models that jointly process audio and language.

Its central assumption is that these models already contain shortcuts associated with safety-aligned behavior. The method searches for reusable audio perturbations that trigger those shortcuts during inference. To preserve ordinary speech understanding, a Mel-Gradient Sparse Mask confines changes to frequency bins that are sensitive to jailbreaks but comparatively insensitive to speech understanding. This makes the choice of where to perturb part of the defense.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and experiments supporting robustness against both previously seen and unseen attacks. Across four models, they report an average attack success rate of 4.6% for advanced audio-language jailbreaks while retaining comparable performance on benign benchmarks. The findings support activating existing safety behavior through carefully targeted input changes, conditional on the framework's shortcut assumption.
summary.tldr: ALMGuard uses targeted audio perturbations to activate assumed safety shortcuts while preserving performance on benign tasks.

title: ALMGuard: Safety Shortcuts and Where to Find Them as Guardrails for Audio–Language Models

abstract: Faces and humans are crucial elements in social interaction and are widely included in everyday photos and videos. Therefore, a deep understanding of faces and humans will enable multi-modal assistants to achieve improved response quality and broadened application scope. Currently, the multi-modal assistant community lacks a comprehensive and scientific evaluation of face and human understanding abilities. In this paper, we first propose a hierarchical ability taxonomy that includes three levels of abilities. Then, based on this taxonomy, we collect images and annotations from publicly available datasets in the face and human community and build a semi-automatic data pipeline to produce problems for the new benchmark. Finally, the obtained Face-Human-Bench includes a development set and a test set, each with 1800 problems, supporting both English and Chinese. We conduct evaluations over 25 mainstream multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with our Face-Human-Bench, focusing on the correlation between abilities, the impact of the relative position of targets on performance, and the impact of Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting on performance. We also explore which abilities of MLLMs need to be supplemented by specialist models. The dataset and evaluation code have been made publicly available at https://face-human-bench.github.io.

paragraphs: Faces and people appear throughout everyday images, making their interpretation an important capability for multimodal assistants. Face-Human-Bench addresses the lack of a comprehensive evaluation focused on this area. The paper begins with a three-level hierarchy of abilities, giving the benchmark an explicit structure for organizing what models are asked to understand.

The authors draw images and annotations from publicly available face and human datasets. A semi-automatic pipeline turns those materials into benchmark problems. The resulting development and test sets each contain 1,800 problems, with support for both English and Chinese. This provides a common evaluation resource across models and the two supported languages.

It also investigates which abilities could benefit from specialist models. The abstract describes these evaluation questions without reporting a particular ranking or directional outcome. The contribution is a structured benchmark and analysis of distinct dimensions of face and human understanding.
summary.tldr: Face-Human-Bench organizes and evaluates multimodal assistants' face and human understanding through a bilingual, structured benchmark.

title: Face-Human-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Face and Human Understanding for Multi-modal Assistants

abstract: Although significant progress has been made in audio-driven talking head generation, text-driven methods remain underexplored. In this work, we present OmniTalker, a unified framework that jointly generates synchronized talking audio-video content from input text while emulating the target identity's speaking and facial movement styles, including speech characteristics, head motion, and facial dynamics. Our framework adopts a dual-branch diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture, with one branch dedicated to audio generation and the other to video synthesis. At the shallow layers, cross-modal fusion modules are introduced to integrate information between the two modalities. In deeper layers, each modality is processed independently, with the generated audio decoded by a vocoder and the video rendered using a GAN-based high-quality visual renderer. Leveraging DiT’s in-context learning capability through a masked-infilling strategy, our model can simultaneously capture both audio and visual styles without requiring explicit style extraction modules. Thanks to the efficiency of the DiT backbone and the optimized visual renderer, OmniTalker achieves real-time inference at 25 FPS. To the best of our knowledge, OmniTalker is the first one-shot framework capable of jointly modeling speech and facial styles in real time. Extensive experiments demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in terms of generation quality, particularly in preserving style consistency and ensuring precise audio-video synchronization, all while maintaining efficient inference.

abstract: The rapid proliferation of domain-specialized machine learning models presents a challenge: while individual models excel in specific domains, their performance varies significantly across diverse applications. This makes selecting the optimal model when faced with an unknown mixture of tasks, especially with limited or no data to estimate the mixture, a difficult problem. We address this challenge by formulating it as a multiple-source domain adaptation (MSA) problem. We introduce a novel, scalable algorithm that effectively routes each input to the best-suited model from a pool of available models. Our approach provides a strong performance guarantee: remarkably, for any mixture domain, the accuracy achieved by the best source model is maintained. This guarantee is established through a theoretical bound on the regret for new domains, expressed as a convex combination of the best regrets in the source domains, plus a concentration term that diminishes as the amount of source data increases. While our primary contributions are theoretical and algorithmic, we also present empirical results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: A collection of specialist models creates a selection problem: which model should handle each new input when incoming tasks mix several domains? Estimating that mixture can be difficult with little or no target data. This paper formulates the problem as adaptation from multiple source domains and introduces a scalable routing algorithm.

The router directs each input toward a suitable model from the available pool. Its theoretical analysis bounds regret on a new mixture domain using a convex combination of the best source-domain regrets, plus a concentration term. That extra term decreases as more source data become available, explicitly linking the guarantee to the amount of evidence from known domains.

Within this formulation, the authors state that routing maintains the accuracy of the best source model for any mixture domain. Empirical results also support the method's effectiveness. The contribution provides both an algorithm and a theoretical account of how specialist models can be combined when the proportions of their source domains in future workloads are unknown.
summary.tldr: The paper develops model routing for unknown domain mixtures with a regret guarantee tied to source-domain performance and available source data.

title: Principled Model Routing for Unknown Mixtures of Source Domains

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process entire input contexts indiscriminately, which is inefficient when the information required to answer a query is localized within the context. We present dynamic context cutoff, a novel method enabling LLMs to self-terminate processing upon acquiring sufficient task-relevant information. Through analysis of model internals, we discover that specific attention heads inherently encode "sufficiency signals" -- detectable through lightweight classifiers -- that predict when critical information has been processed. This reveals a new efficiency paradigm: models' internal understanding naturally dictates processing needs rather than external compression heuristics. Comprehensive experiments across six QA datasets (up to 40K tokens) with three model families (LLaMA/Qwen/Mistral, 1B-70B) demonstrate 3.4% accuracy improvement while achieving 1.33x token reduction on average. Furthermore, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to other context efficiency methods at equivalent token reduction rates. Additionally, we observe an emergent scaling phenomenon: while smaller models require probing for sufficiency detection, larger models exhibit intrinsic self-assessment capabilities through prompting.

paragraphs: Dynamic context cutoff aims to stop a language model from processing more input once it has enough information to answer a question. This matters when the relevant evidence occupies only part of a long context. Processing every remaining token can then consume computation without supplying information the task still needs.

The authors identify signals in particular attention heads that predict whether critical information has already been processed. Lightweight classifiers detect these signals and use them to decide when to stop. The stopping decision therefore draws on the model's internal processing of the question and context, rather than relying solely on externally chosen compression rules.

Experiments cover six question-answering datasets, contexts up to 40,000 tokens, and three model families ranging from one to seventy billion parameters. The reported averages combine a 1.33-fold token reduction with a 3.4% accuracy improvement, and the method outperforms other efficiency methods at equivalent reduction rates. The authors also observe a scale-dependent difference: smaller models require probing, while larger models show sufficiency self-assessment through prompting.
summary.tldr: Internal attention signals help language models stop reading once they have sufficient evidence, reducing context processing while improving reported question-answering accuracy.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Efficient Context Processing via Latent Sufficiency Signals

abstract: Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) aims to retrieve precise temporal segments in a video conditioned on natural language queries. Unlike conventional neural frameworks that rely heavily on computationally expensive dense matrix multiplications, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)—previously underexplored in this domain—offer a unique opportunity to tackle VTG tasks through bio-plausible spike-based communication and an event-driven accumulation-based computational paradigm. We introduce SpikingVTG, a multi-modal spiking detection transformer, designed to harness the computational simplicity and sparsity of SNNs for VTG tasks. Leveraging the temporal dynamics of SNNs, our model introduces a Saliency Feedback Gating (SFG) mechanism that assigns dynamic saliency scores to video clips and applies multiplicative gating to highlight relevant clips while suppressing less informative ones. SFG enhances performance and reduces computational overhead by minimizing neural activity. We analyze the layer-wise convergence dynamics of SFG-enabled model and apply implicit differentiation at equilibrium to enable efficient, BPTT-free training. To improve generalization and maximize performance, we enable knowledge transfer by optimizing a Cos-L2 representation matching loss that aligns the layer-wise representation and attention maps of a non-spiking teacher with those of our student SpikingVTG. Additionally, we present Normalization-Free (NF)-SpikingVTG, which eliminates non-local operations like softmax and layer normalization, and an extremely quantized 1-bit (NF)-SpikingVTG variant for potential deployment on edge devices. Our models achieve competitive results on QVHighlights, Charades-STA, TACoS, and YouTube Highlights, establishing a strong baseline for multi-modal spiking VTG solutions.

title: SpikingVTG: A Spiking Detection Transformer for Video Temporal Grounding

abstract: Conventional score-based diffusion models (DMs) may struggle with anisotropic Gaussian diffusion processes due to the required inversion of covariance matrices in the denoising score matching training objective \cite{vincent_connection_2011}. We propose Whitened Score (WS) diffusion models, a novel framework based on stochastic differential equations that learns the Whitened Score function instead of the standard score. This approach circumvents covariance inversion, extending score-based DMs by enabling stable training of DMs on arbitrary Gaussian forward noising processes. WS DMs establish equivalence with flow matching for arbitrary Gaussian noise, allow for tailored spectral inductive biases, and provide strong Bayesian priors for imaging inverse problems with structured noise. We experiment with a variety of computational imaging tasks using the CIFAR, CelebA ($64\times64$), and CelebA-HQ ($256\times256$) datasets and demonstrate that WS diffusion priors trained on anisotropic Gaussian noising processes consistently outperform conventional diffusion priors based on isotropic Gaussian noise.

The difficulty arises from covariance-matrix inversion in the denoising training objective. This paper introduces Whitened Score diffusion to accommodate such structured noise without that inversion.

The framework uses stochastic differential equations and learns a whitened score function instead of the standard score. This enables stable training with arbitrary Gaussian forward noising processes. The authors also establish an equivalence with flow matching for arbitrary Gaussian noise and allow tailored spectral inductive biases. These properties make the noise structure a configurable part of the prior used for imaging reconstruction.

Experiments cover computational imaging tasks using CIFAR, CelebA at 64 by 64 pixels, and CelebA-HQ at 256 by 256 pixels. Priors trained with anisotropic Gaussian noising consistently outperform conventional isotropic-noise diffusion priors in these evaluations. The results support matching the diffusion framework to structured noise, while the mathematical reformulation removes a training obstacle to doing so.
summary.tldr: Whitened Score diffusion avoids covariance inversion and learns structured-noise image priors that outperform isotropic diffusion priors in the reported experiments.

title: Whitened Score Diffusion: A Structured Prior for Imaging Inverse Problems

abstract: Online portfolio selection seeks to determine a sequence of allocations to maximize capital growth. Classical universal strategies asymptotically match the best constant-rebalanced portfolio but ignore potential forecasts, whereas heuristic methods often collapse when belief fails. We formalize this tension in a learning-augmented setting in which an investor observes (possibly erroneous) predictions prior to each decision moment, and we introduce the Rebalanced Arithmetic Mean portfolio with predictions (RAM). Under arbitrary return sequences, we prove that RAM captures at least a constant fraction of the hindsight-optimal wealth when forecasts are perfect while still exceeding the geometric mean of the sequence even when the predictions are adversarial. Comprehensive experiments on large-scale equity data strengthen our theory, spanning both synthetic prediction streams and production-grade machine-learning models. RAM advantages over universal-portfolio variants equipped with side information across various regimes. These results demonstrate that modest predictive power can be reliably converted into tangible gains without sacrificing worst-case guarantees.

This paper formalizes a setting in which predictions arrive before each allocation and may contain arbitrary errors.

The guarantees concern the stated wealth comparisons and do not assert profits in every market.
summary.tldr: RAM incorporates investment forecasts while providing separate wealth guarantees for perfect and adversarial predictions.

title: Online Portfolio Selection with ML Predictions

abstract: We study the high-dimensional asymptotics of empirical risk minimization (ERM) in over-parametrized two-layer neural networks with quadratic activations trained on synthetic data. We derive sharp asymptotics for both training and test errors by mapping the $\ell_2$-regularized learning problem to a convex matrix sensing task with nuclear norm penalization. This reveals that capacity control in such networks emerges from a low-rank structure in the learned feature maps. Our results characterize the global minima of the loss and yield precise generalization thresholds, showing how the width of the target function governs learnability. This analysis bridges and extends ideas from spin-glass methods, matrix factorization, and convex optimization and emphasizes the deep link between low-rank matrix sensing and learning in quadratic neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how overparameterized two-layer networks with quadratic activations learn from synthetic data in high dimensions. It seeks precise descriptions of training and test error, rather than only broad qualitative statements about generalization. The setting includes L2 regularization, which penalizes model weights during empirical risk minimization.

The key step translates the neural-network learning problem into a convex matrix sensing problem with nuclear norm penalization. That translation reveals a low-rank structure in the learned feature maps as the source of capacity control. Their broader conceptual value is to connect neural learning with low-rank matrix recovery, showing how an apparently large model can have its effective capacity governed by a more structured representation.
summary.tldr: A convex matrix-sensing reformulation yields precise high-dimensional error and learnability results for regularized, overparameterized quadratic networks.

title: The Nuclear Route: Sharp Asymptotics of ERM in Overparameterized Quadratic Networks

abstract: The Unaligned Multi-view Clustering (UMC) aims to learn a discriminative cluster structure from unaligned multi-view data, where the features of samples are not completely aligned across multiple views. Most existing methods usually prioritize employing various alignment strategies to align sample representations across views and then conduct cross-view fusion on aligned representations for subsequent clustering. However, ***due to the heterogeneity of representations across different views, these alignment strategies often fail to achieve ideal view-alignment results, inevitably leading to unreliable alignment-based fusion.*** To address this issue, we propose an alignment-free consistency fusion framework named AF-UMC, which bypasses the traditional view-alignment operation and directly extracts consistent representations from each view to perform global cross-view consistency fusion. Specifically, we first construct a cross-view consistent basis space by a cross-view reconstruction loss and a designed Structural Clarity Regularization (SCR), where autoencoders extract consistent representations from each view through projecting view-specific data to the constructed basis space. Afterwards, these extracted representations are globally pulled together for further cross-view fusion according to a designed Instance Global Contrastive Fusion (IGCF). Compared with previous methods, AF-UMC directly extracts consistent representations from each view for global fusion instead of alignment for fusion, which significantly mitigates the degraded fusion performance caused by undesired view-alignment results while greatly reducing algorithm complexity and enhancing its efficiency. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our AF-UMC exhibits superior performance against other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Clustering across multiple views becomes difficult when samples are not fully matched between those views. Existing approaches often try to align their representations before combining them. The paper argues that differences between views can make that alignment unreliable, causing mistakes in the alignment stage to weaken the later clustering.

AF-UMC builds a shared basis space and extracts representations that are consistent across views directly. It constructs this space using a cross-view reconstruction objective together with Structural Clarity Regularization. Autoencoders then project each view's data into that space. A further component, Instance Global Contrastive Fusion, brings the extracted representations together for global fusion.

This design removes the separate view-alignment operation from the fusion process. The authors report that doing so reduces the degradation associated with poor alignment, lowers algorithm complexity, and improves efficiency. Experiments across several datasets also show better clustering performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a way to combine heterogeneous views through a common representation space without first depending on successful sample alignment.
summary.tldr: AF-UMC improves unaligned multi-view clustering by extracting shared representations directly and combining them without a separate alignment stage.

title: AF-UMC: An Alignment-Free Fusion Framework for Unaligned Multi-View Clustering

abstract: Heterogeneous temporal graphs (HTGs) are ubiquitous data structures in the real world. Recently, to enhance representation learning on HTGs, numerous attention-based neural networks have been proposed. Despite these successes, existing methods rely on a decoupled temporal and spatial learning paradigm, which weakens interactions of spatio-temporal information and leads to a high model complexity. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel learning paradigm for HTGs called Simple and Efficient Heterogeneous Temporal Graph Neural Network (SE-HTGNN). Specifically, we innovatively integrate temporal modeling into spatial learning via a novel dynamic attention mechanism, which substantially reduces model complexity while enhancing discriminative representation learning on HTGs. Additionally, to comprehensively and adaptively understand HTGs, we leverage large language models to prompt SE-HTGNN, enabling the model to capture the implicit properties of node types as prior knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SE-HTGNN achieves up to 10× speed-up over the state-of-the-art and latest baseline while maintaining the best forecasting accuracy.

paragraphs: SE-HTGNN learns from graphs that contain different types of entities and change over time. The paper identifies a weakness in approaches that model temporal and spatial information separately: this separation can weaken their interaction while increasing model complexity. Its proposed architecture combines these aspects more directly during representation learning.

A dynamic attention mechanism incorporates temporal modeling into spatial learning. Time information therefore participates in learning graph relationships within the same mechanism. The method also uses large language models to provide prompts that supply prior knowledge about implicit properties of node types. This adds semantic information about the heterogeneous entities alongside the graph's structural and temporal information.

Experiments report speedups of up to tenfold over the compared leading and recent baselines while retaining the best forecasting accuracy in the evaluation. The findings support integrating temporal information into graph attention as a way to reduce complexity without sacrificing predictive quality in these settings. They also demonstrate the proposed combination of graph learning and language-model-derived node-type knowledge.
summary.tldr: SE-HTGNN integrates temporal and spatial graph learning, reporting up to tenfold speedups alongside the best evaluated forecasting accuracy.

title: Simple and Efficient Heterogeneous Temporal Graph Neural Network

abstract: Modern autonomous vehicle perception systems often struggle with occlusions and limited perception range. Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of cooperative perception in extending the perception range and overcoming occlusions, thereby enhancing the safety of autonomous driving. In recent years, a series of cooperative perception datasets have emerged; however, these datasets primarily focus on cameras and LiDAR, neglecting 4D Radar—a sensor used in single-vehicle autonomous driving to provide robust perception in adverse weather conditions. In this paper, to bridge the gap created by the absence of 4D Radar datasets in cooperative perception, we present V2X-Radar, the first large-scale, real-world multi-modal dataset featuring 4D Radar. V2X-Radar dataset is collected using a connected vehicle platform and an intelligent roadside unit equipped with 4D Radar, LiDAR, and multi-view cameras. The collected data encompasses sunny and rainy weather conditions, spanning daytime, dusk, and nighttime, as well as various typical challenging scenarios. The dataset consists of 20K LiDAR frames, 40K camera images, and 20K 4D Radar data, including 350K annotated boxes across five categories. To support various research domains, we have established V2X-Radar-C for cooperative perception, V2X-Radar-I for roadside perception, and V2X-Radar-V for single-vehicle perception. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive benchmarks across these three sub-datasets.

This paper introduces V2X-Radar to fill a dataset gap: existing cooperative-perception resources largely emphasize cameras and LiDAR, despite the use of 4D radar for robust single-vehicle perception in adverse weather.

Collection covers sunny and rainy weather, daytime, dusk, nighttime, and challenging scenarios. The dataset contains 20,000 LiDAR frames, 40,000 camera images, 20,000 radar data items, and 350,000 annotated boxes across five categories.

Three sub-datasets support cooperative, roadside, and single-vehicle perception, with benchmarks for each. This organization enables study of radar-containing multimodal perception across distinct sensing configurations. The main contribution is a large-scale real-world resource that makes 4D radar available for cooperative-perception research alongside established camera and LiDAR modalities.
summary.tldr: V2X-Radar provides real-world radar, LiDAR, and camera data with benchmarks for cooperative, roadside, and single-vehicle perception.

title: V2X-Radar: A Multi-modal Dataset with 4D Radar for Cooperative Perception

abstract: The right batch size is important when training language models at scale: a large batch size is necessary for fast training, but a batch size that is *too large* will harm token efficiency. To navigate this tradeoff, McCandlish et al. (2018) suggest that a *critical batch size* (CBS), below which training will not substantially degrade loss, can be estimated based on the gradient noise scale during training. While their method has been adopted in practice, e.g., when training GPT-3, strong assumptions are required to justify gradient noise as a proxy for the CBS, which makes it unclear whether their approach should be trusted in practice, limiting its applicability. In this paper, we introduce a simple, empirical approach to *directly* measure the CBS and show how the CBS evolves over training. Applying our approach to the OLMo models, we find that CBS is near 0 at initialization, increases rapidly at first, and then plateaus as training progresses. Furthermore, we find that this trend holds across different model sizes (1B and 7B), suggesting CBS from small training runs can inform larger-scale training runs. Our findings about how the CBS changes over training motivate *batch size warmup* as a natural way to reliably train language models at large batch size: start the batch size small and increase it as the CBS grows. To validate this claim, we use batch size warmup to train OLMo 1B to slightly better loss than the original training run with 43% fewer gradient steps. This shows how our framework can be applied to reliably train language models at larger batch sizes, increasing data parallelism without compromising performance.

Existing estimates use gradient noise as a proxy, a connection whose justification requires strong assumptions.

summary.tldr: Direct measurements of critical batch size motivate gradually increasing batches, yielding slightly better OLMo 1B loss with 43% fewer gradient steps.

title: Critical Batch Size Revisited: A Simple Empirical Approach to Large-Batch Language Model Training

abstract: Mixed-integer programming (MIP) provides a powerful framework for optimization problems, with Branch-and-Cut (B&C) being the predominant algorithm in state-of-the-art solvers. The efficiency of B&C critically depends on heuristic policies for making sequential decisions, including node selection, cut selection, and branching variable selection. While traditional solvers often employ heuristics with manually tuned parameters, recent approaches increasingly leverage machine learning, especially neural networks, to learn these policies directly from data. A key challenge is to understand the theoretical underpinnings of these learned policies, particularly their generalization performance from finite data. This paper establishes rigorous sample complexity bounds for learning B&C policies where the scoring functions guiding each decision step (node, cut, branch) have a certain piecewise polynomial structure. This structure generalizes the linear models that form the most commonly deployed policies in practice and investigated recently in a foundational series of theoretical works by Balcan et al. Such piecewise polynomial policies also cover the neural network architectures (e.g., using ReLU activations) that have been the focal point of contemporary practical studies. Consequently, our theoretical framework closely reflects the models utilized by practitioners investigating machine learning within B&C, offering a unifying perspective relevant to both established theory and modern empirical research in this area. Furthermore, our theory applies to quite general sequential decision making problems beyond B&C.

paragraphs: Branch-and-Cut solves mixed-integer optimization problems through a sequence of decisions, including which node to explore, which cuts to select, and which variable to branch on. These choices strongly affect efficiency. As researchers replace manually tuned heuristics with learned policies, a central question is how much training data is needed for those policies to generalize.

This paper establishes sample complexity bounds for policies whose decision scores have a specified piecewise polynomial structure. The restriction is useful because it covers more than linear scoring rules: it also includes neural network architectures such as those using ReLU activations. The analysis therefore encompasses models studied in both established theoretical work and contemporary practical research.

The result supplies a common mathematical framework for reasoning about learning these sequential policies from finite datasets. Its guarantees depend on the stated structural class of scoring functions. The authors also extend the scope beyond Branch-and-Cut to fairly general sequential decision problems, making the contribution relevant to learning decision procedures as well as optimization heuristics.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the training data needed for Branch-and-Cut policies with piecewise polynomial scores, including relevant neural network policies.

title: Generalization Guarantees for Learning Score-Based Branch-and-Cut Policies in Integer Programming

abstract: Deep networks have shown remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet getting a global concept-level understanding of how they function remains a key challenge. Many post-hoc concept-based approaches have been introduced to understand their workings, yet they are not always faithful to the model. Further, they make restrictive assumptions on the concepts a model learns, such as class-specificity, small spatial extent, or alignment to human expectations. In this work, we put emphasis on the faithfulness of such concept-based explanations and propose a new model with model-inherent mechanistic concept-explanations. Our concepts are shared across classes and, from any layer, their contribution to the logit and their input-visualization can be faithfully traced. We also leverage foundation models to propose a new concept-consistency metric, C$^2$-Score, that can be used to evaluate concept-based methods. We show that, compared to prior work, our concepts are quantitatively more consistent and users find our concepts to be more interpretable, all while retaining competitive ImageNet performance.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations try to describe a neural network's decisions using recognizable patterns. However, explanations added after training do not always faithfully reflect the model's actual computations. Existing approaches can also impose restrictive expectations, such as assuming concepts belong to individual classes, occupy small image regions, or match concepts humans already anticipate.

FaCT introduces a model whose concept explanations are built into its mechanism. Concepts can be shared across classes, and their contributions to a class score can be traced from any layer. The model also supports tracing those concepts back to visualizations of the input. This connects what a concept looks like with how it contributes to a decision.

The authors additionally introduce C²-Score, a concept-consistency measure that uses foundation models to evaluate concept-based methods. Compared with prior work, they report more consistent concepts quantitatively and concepts that users judge more interpretable, while preserving competitive ImageNet performance. These findings address distinct requirements: an explanation should follow the model's computation, present coherent concepts, and remain understandable to people without giving up useful predictive performance.
summary.tldr: FaCT builds traceable concept explanations into a neural network while retaining competitive image-classification performance.

title: FaCT: Faithful Concept Traces for Explaining Neural Network Decisions

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable a new form of digital experimentation where treatments combine human and model-generated content in increasingly sophisticated ways. The main methodological challenge in this setting is representing these high-dimensional treatments without losing their semantic meaning or rendering analysis intractable. Here we address this problem by focusing on learning low-dimensional representations that capture the underlying structure of such treatments. These representations enable downstream applications such as guiding generative models to produce meaningful treatment variants and facilitating adaptive assignment in online experiments. We propose double kernel representation learning, which models the causal effect through the inner product of kernel-based representations of treatments and user covariates. We develop an alternating-minimization algorithm that learns these representations efficiently from data and provide convergence guarantees under a low-rank factor model. As an application of this framework, we introduce an adaptive design strategy for online experimentation and demonstrate the method's effectiveness through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: AI-generated content expands the range of treatments available in digital experiments, but makes those treatments difficult to represent analytically. A treatment can contain rich semantic information that is lost by an overly simple encoding. This paper learns compact representations intended to retain useful structure while making causal analysis manageable.

The proposed double kernel representation learning method represents both treatments and user covariates. It models the causal effect through an inner product between these kernel-based representations. An alternating-minimization algorithm learns them from data, and the authors establish convergence guarantees under a low-rank factor model. That model is the stated condition supporting the convergence result.

The representations can support generating meaningful treatment variants and choosing treatment assignments adaptively during online experiments. The paper develops an adaptive experimental design strategy as a concrete application and demonstrates effectiveness through numerical experiments. Its contribution links semantic treatment structure with causal effect modeling, giving the learned representations a role in both analyzing experiments and guiding subsequent experimentation.
summary.tldr: Double kernel representation learning compresses rich treatments and user characteristics into representations that support causal effect modeling and adaptive experimentation.

title: Leveraging semantic similarity for experimentation with AI-generated treatments

abstract: Generating full-body human gestures encompassing face, body, hands, and global movements from audio is crucial yet challenging for virtual avatar creation. Existing systems tokenize gestures frame-wise, predicting tokens of each frame from the input audio. However, expressive human gestures consist of varied patterns with different frame lengths, and different body parts exhibit motion patterns of varying durations. Existing systems fail to capture motion patterns across body parts and temporal scales due to the fixed frame-count setting of their gesture tokens. Inspired by the success of the feature pyramid technique in the multi-scale visual information extraction, we propose a novel framework named PyraMotion and an adaptive multi-scale feature capturing model called Attentive Pyramidal VQ-VAE (APVQ-VAE). Objective and subjective experiments demonstrate that the PyraMotion outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of generating natural and expressive full-body human gestures. Extensive ablation experiments highlight that the self-adaptiveness integration through attention maps contributes to performance.

These components do not all move on the same timescale, and expressive gestures can span different numbers of frames. The paper argues that gesture tokens with fixed frame counts fail to capture these varied patterns across body parts and time.

PyraMotion addresses this with an Attentive Pyramidal VQ-VAE, a model designed to capture motion features adaptively at multiple scales. Its pyramid structure draws inspiration from multiscale visual feature extraction. Attention maps support adaptive integration, allowing information from different temporal scales to contribute to the resulting motion representation.

Objective measurements and subjective evaluations show that PyraMotion produces more natural and expressive full-body gestures than the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. Ablation experiments further identify adaptive integration through attention maps as a contributor to performance. The results support representing gesture patterns at multiple durations when generating coordinated movements from audio, instead of forcing all relevant motion information into one fixed temporal scale.
summary.tldr: PyraMotion adaptively combines motion features across temporal scales to generate more natural and expressive full-body gestures from audio.

title: PyraMotion: Attentional Pyramid-Structured Motion Integration for Co-Speech 3D Gesture Synthesis

abstract: We propose a framework to convert $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-approximate Differential Privacy (DP) mechanisms into $(\varepsilon', 0)$-pure DP mechanisms under certain conditions, a process we call ``purification.'' This algorithmic technique leverages randomized post-processing with calibrated noise to eliminate the $\delta$ parameter while achieving near-optimal privacy-utility tradeoff for pure DP. It enables a new design strategy for pure DP algorithms: first run an approximate DP algorithm with certain conditions, and then purify. This approach allows one to leverage techniques such as strong composition and propose-test-release that require $\delta>0$ in designing pure-DP methods with $\delta=0$. We apply this framework in various settings, including Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization (DP-ERM), stability-based release, and query release tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work with a statistically and computationally efficient reduction from approximate DP to pure DP. Finally, we illustrate the use of this reduction for proving lower bounds under approximate DP constraints with explicit dependence in $\delta$, avoiding the sophisticated fingerprinting code construction.

paragraphs: This paper introduces purification: converting an approximately differentially private mechanism into a purely differentially private one under certain conditions. Approximate privacy uses epsilon and delta parameters, while the purified mechanism has delta equal to zero and potentially a different epsilon. The conversion uses randomized post-processing with calibrated noise to obtain a near-optimal privacy-utility trade-off for pure privacy.

The framework suggests designing a suitable approximate-private algorithm first, then purifying its output. This makes it possible to build pure-private methods using techniques such as strong composition and propose-test-release that require a positive delta during their usual design. The conditional nature of the reduction matters: the abstract does not claim that every approximate-private mechanism can be converted this way.

Applications include private empirical risk minimization, stability-based release, and query release. The authors describe the reduction as the first statistically and computationally efficient one of its kind, to their knowledge. They also use it to derive approximate-privacy lower bounds with explicit delta dependence, avoiding sophisticated fingerprinting-code constructions.
summary.tldr: Under certain conditions, randomized post-processing converts approximate differential privacy into pure privacy with a near-optimal privacy-utility trade-off.

title: Purifying Approximate Differential Privacy with Randomized Post-processing

abstract: Synthetic data refers to artificial samples generated by models. While it has been validated to significantly enhance the performance of large language models (LLMs) during training and has been widely adopted in LLM development, potential security risks it may introduce remain uninvestigated. This paper systematically evaluates the resilience of synthetic-data-integrated training paradigm for LLMs against mainstream poisoning and backdoor attacks. We reveal that such a paradigm exhibits strong resistance to existing attacks, primarily thanks to the different distribution patterns between poisoning data and queries used to generate synthetic samples. To enhance the effectiveness of these attacks and further investigate the security risks introduced by synthetic data, we introduce a novel and universal attack framework, namely, Virus Infection Attack (VIA), which enables the propagation of current attacks through synthetic data even under purely clean queries. Inspired by the principles of virus design in cybersecurity, VIA conceals the poisoning payload within a protective “shell” and strategically searches for optimal hijacking points in benign samples to maximize the likelihood of generating malicious content. Extensive experiments on both data poisoning and backdoor attacks show that VIA significantly increases the presence of poisoning content in synthetic data and correspondingly raises the attack success rate (ASR) on downstream models to levels comparable to those observed in the poisoned upstream models.

They attribute this resistance primarily to differences between the distribution of poisoned data and the clean queries used to generate synthetic examples.

Downstream models consequently reach attack success rates comparable to those of the poisoned upstream models. The findings show that resistance to conventional attacks does not establish resistance to attacks specifically adapted to synthetic-data transfer, exposing a security concern in model-to-model training pipelines.
summary.tldr: VIA shows that poisoning and backdoors can propagate through synthetic training data even when the generation queries are clean.

title: Virus Infection Attack on LLMs: Your Poisoning Can Spread "VIA" Synthetic Data

abstract: We propose a principled method for autoencoding with random forests. Our strategy builds on foundational results from nonparametric statistics and spectral graph theory to learn a low-dimensional embedding of the model that optimally represents relationships in the data. We provide exact and approximate solutions to the decoding problem via constrained optimization, split relabeling, and nearest neighbors regression. These methods effectively invert the compression pipeline, establishing a map from the embedding space back to the input space using splits learned by the ensemble's constituent trees. The resulting decoders are universally consistent under common regularity assumptions. The procedure works with supervised or unsupervised models, providing a window into conditional or joint distributions. We demonstrate various applications of this autoencoder, including powerful new tools for visualization, compression, clustering, and denoising. Experiments illustrate the ease and utility of our method in a wide range of settings, including tabular, image, and genomic data.

paragraphs: This paper turns random forests into an autoencoding system: one part compresses information into a lower dimensional representation, and another maps that representation back to the input space. The authors use results from nonparametric statistics and spectral graph theory to construct an embedding that optimally represents relationships in the data according to their formulation.

A central contribution is making the compressed representation reversible through a decoder. The paper develops exact and approximate decoding methods using constrained optimization, split relabeling, and nearest neighbors regression. These methods draw on the splits already learned by the forest’s individual trees, establishing a reconstruction procedure tied to the ensemble’s existing structure.

The decoders have universal consistency guarantees under common regularity assumptions, so the theoretical claim is conditional on those assumptions. The approach works with both supervised and unsupervised forests, supporting examination of conditional or joint distributions. Experiments across tabular, image, and genomic data illustrate uses in visualization, compression, clustering, and denoising, showing how a forest’s representation can support tasks beyond its original predictions.
summary.tldr: Random forests can support low-dimensional encoding and reconstruction, with conditional consistency guarantees and applications from visualization to denoising.

title: Autoencoding Random Forests

abstract: Understanding functional representations within higher visual cortex is a fundamental question in computational neuroscience. While artificial neural networks pretrained on large-scale datasets exhibit striking representational alignment with human neural responses, learning image-computable models of visual cortex relies on individual-level, large-scale fMRI datasets. The necessity for expensive, time-intensive, and often impractical data acquisition limits the generalizability of encoders to new subjects and stimuli. **BraInCoRL** uses in-context learning to predict voxelwise neural responses from few-shot examples *without any additional finetuning* for novel subjects and stimuli. We leverage a transformer architecture that can flexibly condition on a variable number of in-context image stimuli, learning an inductive bias over multiple subjects. During training, we explicitly optimize the model for in-context learning. By jointly conditioning on image features and voxel activations, our model learns to directly generate better performing voxelwise models of higher visual cortex. We demonstrate that BraInCoRL consistently outperforms existing voxelwise encoder designs in a low-data regime when evaluated on entirely novel images, while also exhibiting strong test-time scaling behavior. The model also generalizes to an entirely new visual fMRI dataset, which uses different subjects and fMRI data acquisition parameters. Further, BraInCoRL facilitates better interpretability of neural signals in higher visual cortex by attending to semantically relevant stimuli. Finally, we show that our framework enables interpretable mappings from natural language queries to voxel selectivity.

paragraphs: Predicting how a person’s higher visual cortex responds to images often requires extensive individual fMRI measurements. BraInCoRL addresses this data burden through in-context learning. Given a small set of examples pairing image information with neural responses, it predicts voxel-level responses for new subjects and stimuli without additional fine-tuning.

The transformer is explicitly trained to learn from such contextual examples across multiple subjects. It jointly conditions on image features and voxel activations and accepts a variable number of example stimuli. This design lets the model use new observations as context when producing predictions, drawing on patterns learned across people during training.

In low-data evaluations on entirely new images, BraInCoRL consistently outperforms existing voxelwise encoder designs and shows strong test-time scaling. It also transfers to a separate visual fMRI dataset with different subjects and acquisition parameters. Beyond prediction, attention to semantically relevant stimuli supports interpretation of neural signals, and the framework connects natural-language queries with voxel selectivity. These results link adaptation from limited observations with more interpretable response modeling.
summary.tldr: BraInCoRL predicts visual-cortex responses from a few contextual examples, adapting to new subjects and stimuli without fine-tuning.

title: Meta-Learning an In-Context Transformer Model of Human Higher Visual Cortex

abstract: Image-to-video generation has made remarkable progress with the advancements in diffusion models, yet generating videos with realistic motion remains highly challenging. This difficulty arises from the complexity of accurately modeling motion, which involves capturing physical constraints, object interactions, and domain-specific dynamics that are not easily generalized across diverse scenarios. To address this, we propose MotionRAG, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances motion realism by adapting motion priors from relevant reference videos through Context-Aware Motion Adaptation (CAMA). The key technical innovations include: (i) a retrieval-based pipeline extracting high-level motion features using video encoder and specialized resamplers to distill semantic motion representations; (ii) an in-context learning approach for motion adaptation implemented through a causal transformer architecture; (iii) an attention-based motion injection adapter that seamlessly integrates transferred motion features into pretrained video diffusion models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves significant improvements across multiple domains and various base models, all with negligible computational overhead during inference. Furthermore, our modular design enables zero-shot generalization to new domains by simply updating the retrieval database without retraining any components. This research enhances the core capability of video generation systems by enabling the effective retrieval and transfer of motion priors, facilitating the synthesis of realistic motion dynamics.

paragraphs: Generating a video from an image requires plausible motion as well as convincing appearance. Motion depends on physical constraints, interactions, and domain-specific behavior that can be hard to generalize. MotionRAG addresses this challenge by retrieving relevant reference videos and adapting their motion information to guide generation.

A video encoder and specialized resamplers extract high-level motion representations from the references. Context-Aware Motion Adaptation then uses a causal transformer to adapt these representations through in-context learning. An attention-based adapter injects the transferred motion features into a pretrained video diffusion model, connecting retrieved motion information to the generation process.

Experiments report significant improvements across multiple domains and different base models, with negligible additional inference computation. The modular design also enables zero-shot transfer to new domains by updating the retrieval database without retraining components. This makes the database an adaptable source of motion priors. The contribution is a pipeline for retrieving, adapting, and transferring motion, showing how reference videos can strengthen an existing generator’s ability to produce realistic dynamics.
summary.tldr: MotionRAG adapts motion from retrieved reference videos to improve image-to-video generation, with new-domain transfer enabled by database updates.

title: MotionRAG: Motion Retrieval-Augmented Image-to-Video Generation

abstract: In applications such as audio denoising, music transcription, music remixing, and audio-based forensics, it is desirable to decompose a single-channel recording into its respective sources. One of the current most effective class of methods to do so is based on non-negative matrix factorization and related latent variable models. Such techniques, however, typically perform poorly when no isolated training data is given and do not allow user feedback to correct for poor results. To overcome these issues, we allow a user to interactively constrain a latent variable model by painting on a time-frequency display of sound to guide the learning process. The annotations are used within the framework of posterior regularization to impose linear grouping constraints that would otherwise be difficult to achieve via standard priors. For the constraints considered, an efficient expectation-maximization algorithm is derived with closed-form multiplicative updates, drawing connections to non-negative matrix factorization methods, and allowing for high-quality interactive-rate separation without explicit training data.

paragraphs: Separating a single audio recording into its component sources is useful for denoising, transcription, remixing, and audio analysis. Models based on non-negative matrix factorization can perform this separation, but the abstract identifies two practical problems: weak results without isolated training examples and limited ability for users to correct an unsatisfactory decomposition.

The proposed system lets a user paint annotations on a display showing how sound varies across time and frequency. Those annotations guide a latent variable model through posterior regularization. Specifically, they impose linear grouping constraints on the model’s inferred explanation of the recording, expressing relationships that would be difficult to impose through standard prior distributions.

For the constraints studied, the authors derive an efficient expectation-maximization algorithm with closed-form multiplicative updates. This connects the method to existing matrix-factorization techniques while supporting interactive computation. The stated result is high-quality separation at interactive rates without explicit training data. Human feedback becomes part of the learning process, allowing the decomposition to respond directly to annotations on the sound itself.
summary.tldr: User annotations on a time-frequency display guide efficient sound-source separation without explicit training data.

title: An Efficient Posterior Regularized Latent Variable Model for Interactive Sound Source Separation

abstract: Sparse estimation methods based on l1 relaxation, such as the Lasso and the Dantzig selector, require the knowledge of the variance of the noise in order to properly tune the regularization parameter. This constitutes a major obstacle in applying these methods in several frameworks, such as time series, random fields, inverse problems, for which noise is rarely homoscedastic and the noise level is hard to know in advance. In this paper, we propose a new approach to the joint estimation of the conditional mean and the conditional variance in a high-dimensional (auto-) regression setting. An attractive feature of the proposed estimator is that it is efficiently computable even for very large scale problems by solving a second-order cone program (SOCP). We present theoretical analysis and numerical results assessing the performance of the proposed procedure.

We present theoretical analysis and numerical results assessing the performance of the proposed procedure.

paragraphs: Sparse regression methods such as the Lasso and Dantzig selector need noise-variance information to tune their regularization appropriately. This becomes difficult when noise levels are unknown or vary with the observations. The paper targets this issue in high-dimensional regression and autoregression, where assuming a single known noise level can be an obstacle to using sparse estimation.

The proposed approach estimates the conditional mean and conditional variance together. These describe, respectively, the expected response and the amount of noise around that response under the observed conditions. Joint estimation addresses the need to learn the predictive relationship while also accounting for changing uncertainty, within the group-sparsity setting identified by the paper.

A central computational feature is that the estimator can be obtained by solving a second-order cone program, a convex optimization formulation. The authors state that this makes it efficiently computable even for very large problems. They provide theoretical analysis and numerical assessments of performance. The contribution is therefore a tractable joint estimation method for settings where noise information cannot readily be supplied in advance.
summary.tldr: A convex estimator jointly learns conditional means and changing noise variances in high-dimensional regression.

title: Learning Heteroscedastic Models by Convex Programming under Group Sparsity

abstract: In several applications of automatic diagnosis and active learning a central problem is the evaluation of a discrete function by adaptively querying the values of its variables until the values read uniquely determine the value of the function. In general reading the value of a variable is done at the expense of some cost (computational or possibly a fee to pay the corresponding experiment). The goal is to design a strategy for evaluating the function incurring little cost (in the worst case or in expectation according to a prior distribution on the possible variables’ assignments). We provide an algorithm that builds a strategy (decision tree) with both expected cost and worst cost which are at most an O(\log n) factor away from, respectively, the minimum possible expected cost and the minimum possible worst cost. Our algorithm provides the best possible approximation simultaneously with respect to both criteria. In fact, there is no algorithm that can guarantee o(\log n) approximation, under the assumption that \cal P ≠\cal NP.

paragraphs: Diagnosis and active learning can require a sequence of costly tests before an answer becomes certain. The paper models this as evaluating a discrete function by querying variables until the observed values uniquely determine its output. A decision tree specifies which variable to query next based on the answers already received.

There are two distinct cost objectives: keeping average expenditure low under a prior distribution and protecting against an expensive worst case. The proposed algorithm constructs one tree whose expected cost and worst-case cost are each within an O(log n) factor of their respective minimum possible values. The comparisons are to the best strategy for each objective, even though the algorithm must satisfy both guarantees simultaneously.

The paper also establishes that this approximation order cannot be improved to o(log n), assuming P differs from NP. The contribution therefore combines a constructive strategy with a matching computational barrier at the stated approximation scale. It provides simultaneous control of routine testing cost and worst-case expense within that guarantee.
summary.tldr: A decision-tree algorithm simultaneously approximates optimal expected and worst-case testing costs within the best possible logarithmic factor under P ≠ NP.

title: Diagnosis determination: decision trees optimizing simultaneously worst and expected testing cost

abstract: We study the design of interactive clustering algorithms for data sets satisfying natural stability assumptions. Our algorithms start with any initial clustering and only make local changes in each step; both are desirable features in many applications. We show that in this constrained setting one can still design provably efficient algorithms that produce accurate clusterings. We also show that our algorithms perform well on real-world data.
originalAbstract: We study the design of interactive clustering algorithms for data sets satisfying natural stability assumptions. Our algorithms start with any initial clustering and only make local changes in each step; both are desirable features in many applications. We show that in this constrained setting one can still design provably efficient algorithms that produce accurate clusterings. We also show that our algorithms perform well on real-world data.

paragraphs: The paper studies interactive clustering under a practical restriction: each step may make only local changes to the current clustering. The algorithms can begin from any initial clustering. Together, these properties describe a process that improves an existing grouping incrementally, without requiring a specially prepared starting arrangement.

The theoretical question is whether these restrictions still permit efficient and accurate clustering. The authors show that they do for datasets satisfying the stability assumptions used in their analysis. Stability is therefore part of the setting supporting the result. The guarantee concerns datasets with that structure, rather than every possible collection of points.

The authors also report good performance on real-world data. This complements the theoretical result with empirical evidence for the algorithms' usefulness. The contribution establishes that arbitrary initialization and local updates can coexist with provable efficiency and accuracy under the stated assumptions. That combination matters for interactive workflows because the algorithm can work from a current clustering and revise it through a sequence of limited changes.
summary.tldr: Under stability assumptions, interactive clustering can start from any grouping and reach accurate results through efficient local changes.

title: Local algorithms for interactive clustering

abstract: Standard sparse pseudo-input approximations to the Gaussian process (GP) cannot handle complex functions well. Sparse spectrum alternatives attempt to answer this but are known to over-fit. We suggest the use of variational inference for the sparse spectrum approximation to avoid both issues. We model the covariance function with a finite Fourier series approximation and treat it as a random variable. The random covariance function has a posterior, on which a variational distribution is placed. The variational distribution transforms the random covariance function to fit the data. We study the properties of our approximate inference, compare it to alternative ones, and extend it to the distributed and stochastic domains. Our approximation captures complex functions better than standard approaches and avoids over-fitting.

The random covariance function has a posterior, on which a variational distribution is placed. The variational distribution transforms the random covariance function to fit the data. We study the properties of our approximate inference, compare it to alternative ones, and extend it to the distributed and stochastic domains. Our approximation captures complex functions better than standard approaches and avoids over-fitting.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process approximations face a tension between representing complex functions and fitting the data too closely. The paper identifies difficulties with standard sparse pseudo-input methods on complex functions and overfitting in sparse-spectrum alternatives. It proposes a variational treatment of sparse spectra to address both issues within the same approximation.

The covariance function is represented by a finite Fourier-series approximation and treated as a random quantity. Instead of relying on a single fixed covariance function, the method places a variational distribution over its posterior. Fitting this distribution adapts the random covariance function to the observations while explicitly representing uncertainty in the spectral approximation.

The authors investigate the approximation’s properties, compare it with other inference approaches, and extend it to distributed and stochastic settings. They report better capture of complex functions than standard approaches while avoiding overfitting. The contribution is the combination of a compact spectral representation and uncertainty-aware inference, with extensions that make the approach relevant to more than one computational training setting.
summary.tldr: Variational uncertainty over a sparse Fourier covariance approximation helps Gaussian processes capture complex functions while avoiding overfitting.

title: Improving the Gaussian Process Sparse Spectrum Approximation by Representing Uncertainty in Frequency Inputs

abstract: Training of large-scale deep neural networks is often constrained by the available computational resources. We study the effect of limited precision data representation and computation on neural network training. Within the context of low-precision fixed-point computations, we observe the rounding scheme to play a crucial role in determining the network’s behavior during training. Our results show that deep networks can be trained using only 16-bit wide fixed-point number representation when using stochastic rounding, and incur little to no degradation in the classification accuracy. We also demonstrate an energy-efficient hardware accelerator that implements low-precision fixed-point arithmetic with stochastic rounding

Our results show that deep networks can be trained using only 16-bit wide fixed-point number representation when using stochastic rounding, and incur little to no degradation in the classification accuracy. We also demonstrate an energy-efficient hardware accelerator that implements low-precision fixed-point arithmetic with stochastic rounding

paragraphs: Training large neural networks can be constrained by the computing resources available. This paper studies whether training can use limited numerical precision while retaining classification performance. It examines both how numbers are represented and how computations are performed, concentrating on low-precision fixed-point arithmetic.

A central finding is that the rounding rule strongly affects training behavior. When arithmetic produces values that the chosen representation cannot express exactly, the way those values are rounded becomes part of the learning procedure. The authors find that stochastic rounding enables deep networks to train with 16-bit fixed-point numbers while showing little or no degradation in classification accuracy in their results.

The paper also demonstrates an energy-efficient hardware accelerator implementing this arithmetic and rounding combination. That connects the training experiments to a concrete computing design. The contribution is therefore both an empirical result about learning with restricted precision and a hardware demonstration of how the successful numerical approach can be implemented.
summary.tldr: Stochastic rounding enables 16-bit fixed-point neural-network training with little or no reported accuracy loss and supports an energy-efficient accelerator.

title: Deep Learning with Limited Numerical Precision

abstract: Variants of max-product (MP) belief propagation effectively find modes of many complex graphical models, but are limited to discrete distributions. Diverse particle max-product (D-PMP) robustly approximates max-product updates in continuous MRFs using stochastically sampled particles, but previous work was specialized to tree-structured models. Motivated by the challenging problem of protein side chain prediction, we extend D-PMP in several key ways to create a generic MAP inference algorithm for loopy models. We define a modified diverse particle selection objective that is provably submodular, leading to an efficient greedy algorithm with rigorous optimality guarantees, and corresponding max-marginal error bounds. We further incorporate tree-reweighted variants of the MP algorithm to allow provable verification of global MAP recovery in many models. Our general-purpose Matlab library is applicable to a wide range of pairwise graphical models, and we validate our approach using optical flow benchmarks. We further demonstrate superior side chain prediction accuracy compared to baseline algorithms from the state-of-the-art Rosetta package.
