Motivated by the challenging problem of protein side chain prediction, we extend D-PMP in several key ways to create a generic MAP inference algorithm for loopy models. We define a modified diverse particle selection objective that is provably submodular, leading to an efficient greedy algorithm with rigorous optimality guarantees, and corresponding max-marginal error bounds. We further incorporate tree-reweighted variants of the MP algorithm to allow provable verification of global MAP recovery in many models. Our general-purpose Matlab library is applicable to a wide range of pairwise graphical models, and we validate our approach using optical flow benchmarks. We further demonstrate superior side chain prediction accuracy compared to baseline algorithms from the state-of-the-art Rosetta package.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable joint configuration in a graphical model is a difficult inference problem. Particle-based max-product methods approximate continuous possibilities using sampled candidates, but earlier diverse particle max-product work focused on tree structures. Motivated by protein side-chain prediction, this paper extends the approach to models containing loops.

The authors modify the objective for selecting diverse particles and prove that it is submodular. This property supports an efficient greedy selection algorithm with rigorous optimality guarantees and associated max-marginal error bounds. They also incorporate tree-reweighted max-product variants, enabling verification of global maximum-probability recovery in many models. That verification capability is qualified; it is not a guarantee of global recovery for every loopy model.

The resulting method is implemented in a general-purpose Matlab library for a broad range of pairwise graphical models. Evaluation includes optical flow benchmarks and protein side-chain prediction. For the latter, the method achieves better prediction accuracy than baseline algorithms from Rosetta. The work combines a broader continuous-inference method with guarantees for key approximation and verification steps.
summary.tldr: Submodular particle selection extends continuous max-product inference to loopy models and improves protein side-chain prediction in experiments.

title: Proteins, Particles, and Pseudo-Max-Marginals: A Submodular Approach

abstract: Non-negative matrix factorization models based on a hierarchical Gamma-Poisson structure capture user and item behavior effectively in extremely sparse data sets, making them the ideal choice for collaborative filtering applications. Hierarchical Poisson factorization (HPF) in particular has proved successful for scalable recommendation systems with extreme sparsity. HPF, however, suffers from a tight coupling of sparsity model (absence of a rating) and response model (the value of the rating), which limits the expressiveness of the latter. Here, we introduce hierarchical compound Poisson factorization (HCPF) that has the favorable Gamma-Poisson structure and scalability of HPF to high-dimensional extremely sparse matrices. More importantly, HCPF decouples the sparsity model from the response model, allowing us to choose the most suitable distribution for the response. HCPF can capture binary, non-negative discrete, non-negative continuous, and zero-inflated continuous responses. We compare HCPF with HPF on nine discrete and three continuous data sets and conclude that HCPF captures the relationship between sparsity and response better than HPF.

This separation allows the response distribution to be chosen to suit the data. The model can represent binary outcomes, non-negative discrete values, non-negative continuous values, and continuous responses with an excess of zeros.

The authors compare the new model with hierarchical Poisson factorization on nine discrete and three continuous datasets. They conclude that the compound model better captures the relationship between sparsity and response. The practical significance is a more adaptable treatment of values in extremely sparse data, while preserving the computational structure that makes the original model useful.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical compound Poisson factorization separates sparsity from response modeling, supporting more varied data distributions while retaining scalability.

title: Hierarchical Compound Poisson Factorization

abstract: In the online false discovery rate (FDR) problem, one observes a possibly infinite sequence of $p$-values $P_1,P_2,…$, each testing a different null hypothesis, and an algorithm must pick a sequence of rejection thresholds $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,…$ in an online fashion, effectively rejecting the $k$-th null hypothesis whenever $P_k \leq \alpha_k$. Importantly, $\alpha_k$ must be a function of the past, and cannot depend on $P_k$ or any of the later unseen $p$-values, and must be chosen to guarantee that for any time $t$, the FDR up to time $t$ is less than some pre-determined quantity $\alpha \in (0,1)$. In this work, we present a powerful new framework for online FDR control that we refer to as “SAFFRON”. Like older alpha-investing algorithms, SAFFRON starts off with an error budget (called alpha-wealth) that it intelligently allocates to different tests over time, earning back some alpha-wealth whenever it makes a new discovery. However, unlike older methods, SAFFRON’s threshold sequence is based on a novel estimate of the alpha fraction that it allocates to true null hypotheses. In the offline setting, algorithms that employ an estimate of the proportion of true nulls are called “adaptive”, hence SAFFRON can be seen as an online analogue of the offline Storey-BH adaptive procedure. Just as Storey-BH is typically more powerful than the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure under independence, we demonstrate that SAFFRON is also more powerful than its non-adaptive counterparts such as LORD.

The goal is to control the false discovery rate up to every time point, even when the sequence of tests may continue indefinitely.

SAFFRON manages an error budget, called alpha-wealth, allocating it across tests and earning some back when it makes discoveries. Its adaptive component estimates how much of the allocated budget goes to true null hypotheses. That estimate informs the thresholds, distinguishing it from earlier non-adaptive budget-allocation methods.

They demonstrate greater power than non-adaptive counterparts such as LORD, meaning improved ability to make discoveries within the false-discovery-control framework. The contribution combines sequential budget management with an estimate of where the budget is spent, while respecting the requirement that each threshold use only past information.
summary.tldr: SAFFRON adaptively allocates an online testing error budget and demonstrates greater discovery power than non-adaptive counterparts.

title: SAFFRON: an Adaptive Algorithm for Online Control of the False Discovery Rate

abstract: Autoencoders are a deep learning model for representation learning. When trained to minimize the distance between the data and its reconstruction, linear autoencoders (LAEs) learn the subspace spanned by the top principal directions but cannot learn the principal directions themselves. In this paper, we prove that $L_2$-regularized LAEs are symmetric at all critical points and learn the principal directions as the left singular vectors of the decoder. We smoothly parameterize the critical manifold and relate the minima to the MAP estimate of probabilistic PCA. We illustrate these results empirically and consider implications for PCA algorithms, computational neuroscience, and the algebraic topology of learning.

When trained to minimize the distance between the data and its reconstruction, linear autoencoders (LAEs) learn the subspace spanned by the top principal directions but cannot learn the principal directions themselves. In this paper, we prove that $L_2$-regularized LAEs are symmetric at all critical points and learn the principal directions as the left singular vectors of the decoder. paragraphs: A linear autoencoder learns to reconstruct its input through a linear representation. With reconstruction error alone, it learns the subspace spanned by the leading principal directions, but it does not identify those directions themselves. The distinction is between finding the relevant space and identifying particular principal directions within that space.

This paper studies what changes when L2 regularization is added. The authors prove symmetry at every critical point and show that the principal directions can be obtained as the decoder's left singular vectors. Regularization therefore affects the mathematical structure of the learned solution, beyond the reconstruction subspace that an unregularized linear autoencoder identifies.

The authors also give a smooth parameterization of the critical manifold and connect minima to the maximum a posteriori estimate in probabilistic PCA. Empirical illustrations accompany these theoretical results. The paper considers implications for PCA algorithms, computational neuroscience, and the algebraic topology of learning, using linear autoencoders as a setting where the relationship among regularization, representation, and optimization geometry can be characterized.
summary.tldr: L2 regularization gives linear autoencoders a structured loss landscape and makes principal directions recoverable from the decoder's singular vectors.

title: Loss Landscapes of Regularized Linear Autoencoders

abstract: Adaptive Multi-hyperplane Machine (AMM) is an online algorithm for learning Multi-hyperplane Machine (MM), a classification model which allows multiple hyperplanes per class. AMM is based on Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), with training time comparable to linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) and significantly higher accuracy. On the other hand, empirical results indicate there is a large accuracy gap between AMM and non-linear SVMs. In this paper we show that this performance gap is not due to limited representability of the MM model, as it can represent arbitrary concepts. We set to explain the connection between the AMM and Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ) algorithms, and introduce a novel Growing AMM (GAMM) classifier motivated by Growing LVQ, that imputes duplicate hyperplanes into the MM model during SGD training. We provide theoretical results showing that GAMM has favorable convergence properties, and analyze the generalization bound of the MM models. Experiments indicate that GAMM achieves significantly improved accuracy on non-linear problems, with only slightly slower training compared to AMM. On some tasks GAMM comes close to non-linear SVM, and outperforms other popular classifiers such as Neural Networks and Random Forests.

paragraphs: A multi-hyperplane machine classifies data using multiple hyperplanes for each class. Its existing online training algorithm, AMM, offers training time comparable to a linear support vector machine with substantially higher accuracy. However, empirical performance still falls well below nonlinear support vector machines. The paper investigates whether the model itself causes that gap.

The authors show that the model can represent arbitrary concepts, so limited representational capacity does not explain the gap. They connect AMM to Learning Vector Quantization and introduce Growing AMM, or GAMM. Inspired by a growing version of vector quantization, GAMM inserts duplicate hyperplanes into the model during stochastic gradient training.

The paper provides favorable convergence results for GAMM and analyzes generalization bounds for multi-hyperplane models. Experiments show substantially improved accuracy on nonlinear problems with only slightly slower training than AMM. On some tasks, GAMM approaches nonlinear support vector machines and outperforms neural networks and random forests. These results suggest that changing how the model grows during training can unlock capabilities that its previous training procedure did not realize.
summary.tldr: Growing AMM adds hyperplanes during training to improve nonlinear classification accuracy with a modest training-time increase.

title: Growing Adaptive Multi-hyperplane Machines

abstract: The goal of compressed sensing is to learn a structured signal $x$ from a limited number of noisy linear measurements $y \approx Ax$. In traditional compressed sensing, “structure” is represented by sparsity in some known basis. Inspired by the success of deep learning in modeling images, recent work starting with Bora-Jalal-Price-Dimakis’17 has instead considered structure to come from a generative model $G: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n$. We present two results establishing the difficulty and strength of this latter task, showing that existing bounds are tight: First, we provide a lower bound matching the Bora et.al upper bound for compressed sensing with $L$-Lipschitz generative models $G$ which holds even for the more relaxed goal of \emph{non-uniform} recovery. Second, we show that generative models generalize sparsity as a representation of structure by constructing a ReLU-based neural network with $2$ hidden layers and $O(n)$ activations per layer whose range is precisely the set of all $k$-sparse vectors.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a structured signal from relatively few noisy linear measurements. Traditionally, the structure is sparsity in a known basis. This paper examines the alternative of defining plausible signals through the output range of a generative model, asking both how difficult recovery is and how expressive that representation can be.

The first result supplies a lower bound matching an existing upper bound for Lipschitz generative models. It holds even for the more relaxed non-uniform recovery objective. This establishes tightness of the existing bound in the stated setting, showing that the corresponding recovery difficulty is not merely an artifact of the earlier analysis.

The second result constructs a ReLU network with two hidden layers and a number of activations per layer proportional to the ambient signal dimension. Its range is exactly the collection of k-sparse vectors. Generative models therefore include sparsity as a representable special case, providing a precise expressiveness result alongside the recovery lower bound.
summary.tldr: Matching recovery lower bounds and an exact sparse-signal network construction establish both limits and expressiveness of generative compressed sensing.

title: On the Power of Compressed Sensing with Generative Models

abstract: When predictions support decisions they may influence the outcome they aim to predict. We call such predictions performative; the prediction influences the target. Performativity is a well-studied phenomenon in policy-making that has so far been neglected in supervised learning. When ignored, performativity surfaces as undesirable distribution shift, routinely addressed with retraining. We develop a risk minimization framework for performative prediction bringing together concepts from statistics, game theory, and causality. A conceptual novelty is an equilibrium notion we call performative stability. Performative stability implies that the predictions are calibrated not against past outcomes, but against the future outcomes that manifest from acting on the prediction. Our main results are necessary and sufficient conditions for the convergence of retraining to a performatively stable point of nearly minimal loss. In full generality, performative prediction strictly subsumes the setting known as strategic classification. We thus also give the first sufficient conditions for retraining to overcome strategic feedback effects.
originalAbstract: When predictions support decisions they may influence the outcome they aim to predict. We call such predictions performative; the prediction influences the target. Performativity is a well-studied phenomenon in policy-making that has so far been neglected in supervised learning. When ignored, performativity surfaces as undesirable distribution shift, routinely addressed with retraining. We develop a risk minimization framework for performative prediction bringing together concepts from statistics, game theory, and causality. A conceptual novelty is an equilibrium notion we call performative stability. Performative stability implies that the predictions are calibrated not against past outcomes, but against the future outcomes that manifest from acting on the prediction. Our main results are necessary and sufficient conditions for the convergence of retraining to a performatively stable point of nearly minimal loss. In full generality, performative prediction strictly subsumes the setting known as strategic classification. We thus also give the first sufficient conditions for retraining to overcome strategic feedback effects.

paragraphs: A prediction can affect the decisions people make and thereby change the outcome being predicted. The paper calls this performative prediction. If a learning system ignores that feedback, the resulting changes can appear as distribution shift, prompting retraining without explicitly accounting for how the model helped create the new data.

The authors develop a risk-minimization framework that combines ideas from statistics, game theory, and causality. Its central equilibrium concept is performative stability. At such a point, predictions are calibrated against the future outcomes produced by acting on those predictions. This shifts attention from fitting a historical distribution to the relationship between a deployed predictor and the outcomes it induces.

The main results give necessary and sufficient conditions for retraining to converge to a performatively stable point with nearly minimal loss. These are conditional convergence results, so retraining is not asserted to succeed under arbitrary feedback. The framework also strictly includes strategic classification, and the paper supplies sufficient conditions under which retraining can overcome strategic feedback effects.
summary.tldr: Performative prediction formalizes how deployed predictions change outcomes and establishes conditions for retraining to reach a stable, nearly optimal predictor.

title: Performative Prediction

abstract: Group invariant and equivariant Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP), also known as Equivariant Networks and Group Group Convolutional Neural Networks (G-CNN) have achieved remarkable success in learning on a variety of data structures, such as sequences, images, sets, and graphs. This paper proves the universality of a broad class of equivariant MLPs with a single hidden layer. In particular, it is shown that having a hidden layer on which the group acts regularly is sufficient for universal equivariance (invariance). For example, some types of steerable-CNN’s become universal. Another corollary is the unconditional universality of equivariant MLPs for all Abelian groups. A third corollary is the universality of equivariant MLPs with a high-order hidden layer, where we give both group-agnostic bounds and group-specific bounds on the order of the hidden layer that guarantees universal equivariance.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the output; invariant networks keep the output unchanged. Such structures are useful across sequences, images, sets, and graphs. This paper asks how expressive these constrained networks can be, focusing on multilayer perceptrons with a single hidden layer.

The main theorem establishes universality for a broad class of these networks. In particular, a regular group action on the hidden layer is sufficient for universal equivariance or invariance. This provides a structural condition under which respecting a symmetry still permits universal approximation of the corresponding symmetry-respecting functions.

Several consequences follow. Some steerable convolutional networks become universal, and equivariant multilayer perceptrons have unconditional universality for Abelian groups. The authors also establish universality using high-order hidden layers, giving both general and group-specific bounds on the required order. These are expressiveness guarantees: they clarify which architectural structures suffice to represent the desired class of functions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves sufficient structural conditions for single-hidden-layer equivariant networks to achieve universal approximation.

title: Universal Equivariant Multilayer Perceptrons

abstract: Sample selection approaches are popular in robust learning from noisy labels. However, how to properly control the selection process so that deep networks can benefit from the memorization effect is a hard problem. In this paper, motivated by the success of automated machine learning (AutoML), we model this issue as a function approximation problem. Specifically, we design a domain-specific search space based on general patterns of the memorization effect and propose a novel Newton algorithm to solve the bi-level optimization problem efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm, which ensures a good approximation to critical points. Experiments are performed on both benchmark and real-world data sets. Results demonstrate that the proposed method is much better than the state-of-the-art noisy-label-learning approaches, and also much more efficient than existing AutoML algorithms.

paragraphs: Selecting which examples to learn from is a common response to noisy labels. The difficult part is controlling selection so that a deep network benefits from its memorization behavior during training. This paper treats that control problem as something to learn automatically, drawing on ideas from automated machine learning.

The authors formulate the selection problem as function approximation and build a specialized search space around general patterns of the memorization effect. They then introduce a Newton algorithm to solve the resulting bilevel optimization efficiently. This couples the search for a useful selection function with the learning process that the function is intended to improve, rather than leaving selection control entirely to manual design.

The theoretical analysis guarantees a good approximation to critical points of the optimization problem. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets report substantially better results than state-of-the-art noisy-label approaches, together with greater efficiency than existing AutoML algorithms. The contribution combines a search space informed by training behavior with an optimization method designed to make searching that space practical.
summary.tldr: The method automatically searches for sample-selection functions that exploit memorization patterns, improving reported noisy-label learning and search efficiency.

title: Searching to Exploit Memorization Effect in Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: Stochastic convex optimization over an $\ell_1$-bounded domain is ubiquitous in machine learning applications such as LASSO but remains poorly understood when learning with differential privacy. We show that, up to logarithmic factors the optimal excess population loss of any $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially private optimizer is $\sqrt{\log(d)/n} + \sqrt{d}/\epsilon n.$ The upper bound is based on a new algorithm that combines the iterative localization approach of Feldman et al. (2020) with a new analysis of private regularized mirror descent. It applies to $\ell_p$ bounded domains for $p\in [1,2]$ and queries at most $n^{3/2}$ gradients improving over the best previously known algorithm for the $\ell_2$ case which needs $n^2$ gradients. Further, we show that when the loss functions satisfy additional smoothness assumptions, the excess loss is upper bounded (up to logarithmic factors) by $\sqrt{\log(d)/n} + (\log(d)/\epsilon n)^{2/3}.$ This bound is achieved by a new variance-reduced version of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm that requires just a single pass over the data. We also show that the lower bound in this case is the minimum of the two rates mentioned above.

paragraphs: This paper characterizes the achievable accuracy of differentially private stochastic convex optimization over an l1-bounded domain. Up to logarithmic factors, the optimal excess population loss is sqrt(log(d)/n) + sqrt(d)/(epsilon n), where d is dimension and n is sample size. The rate separates a statistical term from a privacy-dependent term.

The upper bound comes from combining iterative localization with a new analysis of private regularized mirror descent. The algorithm also applies to lp-bounded domains for p between 1 and 2. It uses at most n^(3/2) gradient queries, improving on the stated previous n^2 requirement for the l2 case.

A new variance-reduced Frank–Wolfe algorithm achieves this bound in a single pass over the data. For that smooth setting, the authors also establish a lower bound given by the minimum of the two stated rates. The results connect privacy, domain geometry, smoothness, and computational effort.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes near-optimal private optimization rates in l1 geometry and develops efficient algorithms, including a single-pass method under additional smoothness.

title: Private Stochastic Convex Optimization: Optimal Rates in L1 Geometry

abstract: A Random Utility Model (RUM) is a distribution on permutations over a universe of items. For each subset of the universe, a RUM induces a natural distribution of the winner in the subset: choose a permutation according to the RUM distribution and pick the maximum item in the subset according to the chosen permutation. RUMs are widely used in the theory of discrete choice. In this paper we consider the question of the (lossy) compressibility of RUMs on a universe of size $n$, i.e., the minimum number of bits required to approximate the winning probabilities of each slate. Our main result is that RUMs can be approximated using $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ bits, an exponential improvement over the standard representation; furthermore, we show that this bound is optimal. En route, we sharpen the classical existential result of McFadden and Train (2000) by showing that the minimum size of a mixture of multinomial logits required to can approximate a general RUM is $\tilde{\Theta}(n)$.

In this paper we consider the question of the (lossy) compressibility of RUMs on a universe of size $n$, i.e., the minimum number of bits required to approximate the winning probabilities of each slate. Our main result is that RUMs can be approximated using $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ bits, an exponential improvement over the standard representation; furthermore, we show that this bound is optimal. paragraphs: A random utility model describes uncertainty over rankings of a collection of items. To select a winner from any offered subset, it samples a ranking and chooses the highest-ranked available item. The model therefore defines choice probabilities for every subset, linking a distribution over complete preferences to observable decisions among available options.

This paper asks how compactly those choice probabilities can be represented when approximation is allowed. The target is lossy compression of the model’s winning probabilities across all subsets. For a universe of n items, the authors prove that roughly n² bits suffice, up to the factors suppressed by their notation. They also prove optimality of this bound.

This is an exponential improvement over the standard representation. Along the way, the authors sharpen an earlier existence result concerning mixtures of multinomial logit models. They show that the required mixture size for approximating a general random utility model has order n, again up to suppressed factors. The contribution characterizes both the achievable compression and the representation size needed for this alternative family.
summary.tldr: Random utility models admit an optimal approximately quadratic-bit representation of choice probabilities, exponentially smaller than their standard representation.

title: Light RUMs

abstract: To cope with high annotation costs, training a classifier only from weakly supervised data has attracted a great deal of attention these days. Among various approaches, strengthening supervision from completely unsupervised classification is a promising direction, which typically employs class priors as the only supervision and trains a binary classifier from unlabeled (U) datasets. While existing risk-consistent methods are theoretically grounded with high flexibility, they can learn only from two U sets. In this paper, we propose a new approach for binary classification from $m$ U-sets for $m\ge2$. Our key idea is to consider an auxiliary classification task called surrogate set classification (SSC), which is aimed at predicting from which U set each observed sample is drawn. SSC can be solved by a standard (multi-class) classification method, and we use the SSC solution to obtain the final binary classifier through a certain linear-fractional transformation. We built our method in a flexible and efficient end-to-end deep learning framework and prove it to be classifier-consistent. Through experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over state-of-the-art methods.
originalAbstract: To cope with high annotation costs, training a classifier only from weakly supervised data has attracted a great deal of attention these days. Among various approaches, strengthening supervision from completely unsupervised classification is a promising direction, which typically employs class priors as the only supervision and trains a binary classifier from unlabeled (U) datasets. While existing risk-consistent methods are theoretically grounded with high flexibility, they can learn only from two U sets. In this paper, we propose a new approach for binary classification from $m$ U-sets for $m\ge2$. Our key idea is to consider an auxiliary classification task called surrogate set classification (SSC), which is aimed at predicting from which U set each observed sample is drawn. SSC can be solved by a standard (multi-class) classification method, and we use the SSC solution to obtain the final binary classifier through a certain linear-fractional transformation. We built our method in a flexible and efficient end-to-end deep learning framework and prove it to be classifier-consistent. Through experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper addresses binary classification when individual examples have no class labels, but class proportions provide weak supervision. Existing risk-consistent approaches discussed in the abstract can use only two unlabeled datasets. The authors develop a method that can incorporate any number of such datasets starting from two, broadening the available source of training information.

The central move is to first predict dataset membership. Each example’s source dataset supplies a label for an auxiliary multiclass task called surrogate set classification. A standard classifier can learn this task even though the desired binary labels remain unavailable. The resulting solution is then converted into a binary classifier using a linear-fractional transformation.

The authors place this construction inside an efficient, end-to-end deep learning framework and prove classifier consistency. That theoretical result concerns recovering the desired classifier through the surrogate task, rather than merely succeeding at identifying datasets. Experiments report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a way to turn known dataset membership and class-prior supervision into a usable route for binary learning across multiple unlabeled sets.
summary.tldr: Predicting which unlabeled dataset an example comes from provides a route to binary classification using class-prior supervision.

title: Binary Classification from Multiple Unlabeled Datasets via Surrogate Set Classification

abstract: Existing deep learning methods for solving mean-field games (MFGs) with common noise fix the sampling common noise paths and then solve the corresponding MFGs. This leads to a nested loop structure with millions of simulations of common noise paths in order to produce accurate solutions, which results in prohibitive computational cost and limits the applications to a large extent. In this paper, based on the rough path theory, we propose a novel single-loop algorithm, named signatured deep fictitious play (Sig-DFP), by which we can work with the unfixed common noise setup to avoid the nested loop structure and reduce the computational complexity significantly. The proposed algorithm can accurately capture the effect of common uncertainty changes on mean-field equilibria without further training of neural networks, as previously needed in the existing machine learning algorithms. The efficiency is supported by three applications, including linear-quadratic MFGs, mean-field portfolio game, and mean-field game of optimal consumption and investment. Overall, we provide a new point of view from the rough path theory to solve MFGs with common noise with significantly improved efficiency and an extensive range of applications. In addition, we report the first deep learning work to deal with extended MFGs (a mean-field interaction via both the states and controls) with common noise.

paragraphs: Mean-field games with common noise involve uncertainty shared across the population of players. Existing deep-learning approaches described in this paper fix sampled common-noise paths and solve the associated games. That creates nested computation requiring millions of simulations for accurate solutions, making the shared uncertainty particularly expensive to handle.

The proposed signatured deep fictitious play algorithm, Sig-DFP, uses rough path theory to work with unfixed common noise in a single loop. These examples support the reported efficiency and demonstrate the approach across several game settings. The work also addresses extended mean-field games, where interaction depends on both states and controls, under common noise; the authors identify this as the first deep-learning treatment of that combination.
summary.tldr: Sig-DFP uses rough path theory to solve mean-field games with common noise in one loop and handle uncertainty changes without retraining.

title: Signatured Deep Fictitious Play for Mean Field Games with Common Noise

abstract: Transformer-based models are popularly used in natural language processing (NLP). Its core component, self-attention, has aroused widespread interest. To understand the self-attention mechanism, a direct method is to visualize the attention map of a pre-trained model. Based on the patterns observed, a series of efficient Transformers with different sparse attention masks have been proposed. From a theoretical perspective, universal approximability of Transformer-based models is also recently proved. However, the above understanding and analysis of self-attention is based on a pre-trained model. To rethink the importance analysis in self-attention, we study the significance of different positions in attention matrix during pre-training. A surprising result is that diagonal elements in the attention map are the least important compared with other attention positions. We provide a proof showing that these diagonal elements can indeed be removed without deteriorating model performance. Furthermore, we propose a Differentiable Attention Mask (DAM) algorithm, which further guides the design of the SparseBERT. Extensive experiments verify our interesting findings and illustrate the effect of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Attention maps show how positions in a sequence attend to one another. Earlier analyses often inspected already pretrained models and used the observed patterns to design sparse attention masks. This paper instead examines the importance of attention positions during pretraining, asking which connections matter while the model is being learned.

The authors find that diagonal attention entries, which connect a position to itself, are the least important compared with other positions. They also provide a proof supporting removal of these entries without deterioration in model performance. This challenges the inference that a connection’s appearance in a trained attention map necessarily establishes its importance during training.

The paper introduces a Differentiable Attention Mask algorithm to guide the design of SparseBERT. Its experiments support the reported findings about attention positions and demonstrate the effect of the masking algorithm. The contribution combines an analysis of attention during pretraining with a method for designing sparse attention, grounding architectural choices in the importance of connections as learning takes place.
summary.tldr: SparseBERT studies attention importance during pretraining and uses differentiable masks, finding diagonal attention entries least important.

title: SparseBERT: Rethinking the Importance Analysis in Self-attention

abstract: Dictionary learning is a key tool for representation learning, that explains the data as linear combination of few basic elements. Yet, this analysis is not amenable in the context of graph learning, as graphs usually belong to different metric spaces. We fill this gap by proposing a new online Graph Dictionary Learning approach, which uses the Gromov Wasserstein divergence for the data fitting term. In our work, graphs are encoded through their nodes’ pairwise relations and modeled as convex combination of graph atoms, i.e. dictionary elements, estimated thanks to an online stochastic algorithm, which operates on a dataset of unregistered graphs with potentially different number of nodes. Our approach naturally extends to labeled graphs, and is completed by a novel upper bound that can be used as a fast approximation of Gromov Wasserstein in the embedding space. We provide numerical evidences showing the interest of our approach for unsupervised embedding of graph datasets and for online graph subspace estimation and tracking.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning represents data using combinations of a small set of basic elements. Applying that idea to graphs is difficult because graphs can occupy different metric spaces, lack corresponding nodes, and contain different numbers of nodes. This paper proposes an online dictionary-learning method that accommodates those differences through a graph-specific fitting objective.

Each graph is described by pairwise relations between its nodes and modeled as a convex combination of graph atoms, the learned dictionary elements. The fitting term uses Gromov Wasserstein divergence. An online stochastic algorithm learns the atoms from unregistered graphs, including datasets whose graphs vary in size, and the approach also extends to labeled graphs.

The authors additionally derive an upper bound that provides a fast approximation of Gromov Wasserstein in the embedding space. Numerical results support the method's usefulness for unsupervised graph embeddings and for estimating and tracking graph subspaces online. The contribution makes dictionary-style representations available for graph collections where direct correspondence between the original objects is absent.
summary.tldr: The method learns graph dictionaries online using Gromov Wasserstein fitting, accommodating graphs with unmatched nodes and different sizes.

title: Online Graph Dictionary Learning

abstract: Gaussian processes (GP) are a widely-adopted tool used to sequentially optimize black-box functions, where evaluations are costly and potentially noisy. Recent works on GP bandits have proposed to move beyond random noise and devise algorithms robust to adversarial attacks. This paper studies this problem from the attacker’s perspective, proposing various adversarial attack methods with differing assumptions on the attacker’s strength and prior information. Our goal is to understand adversarial attacks on GP bandits from theoretical and practical perspectives. We focus primarily on targeted attacks on the popular GP-UCB algorithm and a related elimination-based algorithm, based on adversarially perturbing the function f to produce another function f whose optima are in some target region. Based on our theoretical analysis, we devise both white-box attacks (known f) and black-box attacks (unknown f), with the former including a Subtraction attack and Clipping attack, and the latter including an Aggressive subtraction attack. We demonstrate that adversarial attacks on GP bandits can succeed in forcing the algorithm towards the target region even with a low attack budget, and we test our attacks’ effectiveness on a diverse range of objective functions.

paragraphs: Gaussian process bandits guide sequential searches for good inputs to functions whose evaluations are expensive or noisy. This paper examines what happens when an adversary deliberately interferes with that search. It takes the attacker's perspective, studying how manipulation can steer an optimizer toward a chosen region rather than merely making its observations less reliable.

The attacks primarily target GP-UCB and a related elimination-based algorithm. They perturb the objective so that the resulting function has its optima in the attacker's target region. The authors distinguish attackers who know the original function from those who do not. Their theoretical analysis motivates Subtraction and Clipping attacks for the former setting and an Aggressive subtraction attack for the latter.

Experiments across diverse objective functions show that targeted steering can succeed even with a small attack budget. The contribution is both analytical and practical: it connects different levels of attacker knowledge and strength to concrete attacks. The findings demonstrate possible vulnerabilities under the studied conditions, rather than establishing that every Gaussian process optimizer can always be redirected.
summary.tldr: Targeted attacks can steer Gaussian process bandit algorithms toward an adversary's chosen region, sometimes with a small attack budget.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Gaussian Process Bandits

abstract: One of the most important and challenging application areas for complex machine learning methods is to predict, characterize and model rich, multi-dimensional, neural data. Recent advances in neural recording techniques have made it possible to monitor the activity of a large number of neurons across different brain regions as animals perform behavioural tasks. This poses the critical challenge of establishing links between neural activity at a microscopic scale, which might for instance represent sensory input, and at a macroscopic scale, which then generates behaviour. Predominant modeling methods apply rather disjoint techniques to these scales; by contrast, we suggest an end-to-end model which exploits recent developments of flexible, but tractable, neural network point-process models to characterize dependencies between stimuli, actions, and neural data. We apply this model to a public dataset collected using Neuropixel probes in mice performing a visually-guided behavioural task as well as a synthetic dataset produced from a hierarchical network model with reciprocally connected sensory and integration circuits intended to characterize animal behaviour in a fixed-duration motion discrimination task. We show that our model outperforms previous approaches and contributes novel insights into the relationships between neural activity and behaviour.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons across brain regions creates an opportunity to connect detailed neural activity with observable behavior. It also creates a modeling challenge: sensory signals, neural events, and actions operate at different scales. This paper aims to model their dependencies together, where predominant approaches use relatively separate techniques for those scales.

The authors propose an end-to-end model based on flexible, computationally tractable neural-network point processes. The framework characterizes relationships among stimuli, actions, and neural data within a shared model. Its purpose is to connect the microscopic activity captured in neural recordings to the larger-scale processes associated with behavior, making those relationships accessible to joint analysis.

The model is applied to public Neuropixel recordings from mice performing a visually guided task. It is also tested on synthetic data from interacting sensory and integration circuits modeling motion discrimination. The authors report better performance than previous approaches and new insights into neural activity's relationship with behavior. These findings support joint modeling across the two evaluated data settings.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end neural point-process model jointly captures stimulus, neural-activity, and behavior dependencies, outperforming prior approaches in the reported evaluations.

title: Neural Network Poisson Models for Behavioural and Neural Spike Train Data

abstract: Training graph neural networks (GNNs) is extremely time consuming because sparse graph-based operations are hard to be accelerated by community hardware. Prior art successfully reduces the computation cost of dense matrix based operations (e.g., convolution and linear) via sampling-based approximation. However, unlike dense matrices, sparse matrices are stored in the irregular data format such that each row/column may have different number of non-zero entries. Thus, compared to the dense counterpart, approximating sparse operations has two unique challenges (1) we cannot directly control the efficiency of approximated sparse operation since the computation is only executed on non-zero entries; (2) sampling sparse matrices is much more inefficient due to the irregular data format. To address the issues, our key idea is to control the accuracy-efficiency trade off by optimizing computation resource allocation layer-wisely and epoch-wisely. For the first challenge, we customize the computation resource to different sparse operations, while limit the total used resource below a certain budget. For the second challenge, we cache previous sampled sparse matrices to reduce the epoch-wise sampling overhead. Finally, we propose a switching mechanisms to improve the generalization of GNNs trained with approximated operations. To this end, we propose Randomized Sparse Computation. In practice, rsc can achieve up to 11.6X speedup for a single sparse operation and 1.6X end-to-end wall-clock time speedup with almost no accuracy drop.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks spend substantial training time on sparse graph operations. Approximating these operations through sampling is difficult because sparse matrices have irregular numbers of nonzero entries. A sampling choice therefore does not directly translate into a predictable computation cost, and sampling the irregular representation can itself be expensive.

Randomized Sparse Computation manages the accuracy–efficiency trade-off by allocating computation across layers and training epochs. It assigns resources to different sparse operations while keeping total use within a budget. It also caches previously sampled sparse matrices to reduce repeated sampling overhead, and introduces a switching mechanism to improve generalization when training uses approximated operations.

The reported results reach up to an 11.6-fold speedup for an individual sparse operation and a 1.6-fold reduction in end-to-end training time, with almost no accuracy loss. Distinguishing these measurements matters: faster sparse kernels translate into a smaller overall training gain. The approach targets both the arithmetic cost and the overhead involved in making sparse approximation practical.
summary.tldr: RSC accelerates graph neural-network training through budgeted sparse approximations, cached sampling, and a switching mechanism that supports generalization.

title: RSC: Accelerate Graph Neural Networks Training via Randomized Sparse Computations

abstract: Cross-validation (CV) is one of the most popular tools for assessing and selecting predictive models. However, standard CV suffers from high computational cost when the number of folds is large. Recently, under the empirical risk minimization (ERM) framework, a line of works proposed efficient methods to approximate CV based on the solution of the ERM problem trained on the full dataset. However, in large-scale problems, it can be hard to obtain the exact solution of the ERM problem, either due to limited computational resources or due to early stopping as a way of preventing overfitting. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm to efficiently approximate CV when the ERM problem is solved via an iterative first-order algorithm, without running until convergence. Our new method extends existing guarantees for CV approximation to hold along the whole trajectory of the algorithm, including at convergence, thus generalizing existing CV approximation methods. Finally, we illustrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of our method through a range of empirical studies.

paragraphs: Cross-validation helps assess and select predictive models, but its computational cost grows when many folds are used. Existing approximation methods can reduce this cost by starting from the solution obtained on the full dataset. That starting point becomes problematic when obtaining an exact training solution is itself expensive or undesirable.

This paper develops approximate cross-validation for models trained with iterative first-order optimization, without requiring training to reach convergence. This accommodates both limited computational resources and deliberate early stopping to prevent overfitting. The approach makes the intermediate states of training part of the approximation problem, instead of depending solely on the final optimized model.

The authors extend cross-validation approximation guarantees across the optimization trajectory, with convergence included as a special case. Their framework consequently generalizes methods built around a completed empirical risk minimization solution. Empirical studies illustrate accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution is especially relevant to evaluating models as they are actually trained: a stopped iterate can be the model of interest even when the underlying optimization problem has not been solved exactly.
summary.tldr: Iterative approximate cross-validation extends approximation guarantees to intermediate training steps, including models stopped before convergence.

title: Iterative Approximate Cross-Validation

abstract: For offline reinforcement learning (RL), model-based methods are expected to be data-efficient as they incorporate dynamics models to generate more data. However, due to inevitable model errors, straightforwardly learning a policy in the model typically fails in the offline setting. Previous studies have incorporated conservatism to prevent out-of-distribution exploration. For example, MOPO penalizes rewards through uncertainty measures from predicting the next states, which we have discovered are loose bounds of the ideal uncertainty, i.e., the Bellman error. In this work, we propose MOdel-Bellman Inconsistency penalized offLinE Policy Optimization (MOBILE), a novel uncertainty-driven offline RL algorithm. MOBILE conducts uncertainty quantification through the inconsistency of Bellman estimations under an ensemble of learned dynamics models, which can be a better approximator to the true Bellman error, and penalizes the Bellman estimation based on this uncertainty. Empirically we have verified that our proposed uncertainty quantification can be significantly closer to the true Bellman error than the compared methods. Consequently, MOBILE outperforms prior offline RL approaches on most tasks of D4RL and NeoRL benchmarks.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning uses learned dynamics to generate additional experience from a fixed dataset. Errors in those dynamics can mislead policy learning, so previous methods introduce conservatism to discourage unsupported exploration. This paper examines whether uncertainty about predicted next states measures the uncertainty that matters most for learning values.

The authors identify Bellman error as the ideal uncertainty target and show that next-state uncertainty measures used by MOPO give loose bounds on it. Their MOBILE algorithm instead compares Bellman estimates across an ensemble of learned dynamics models. Disagreement among these estimates supplies an uncertainty measure used to penalize the Bellman estimation.

Empirically, this measure can be significantly closer to the true Bellman error than the alternatives compared. MOBILE also outperforms earlier offline reinforcement-learning approaches on most tasks in the D4RL and NeoRL benchmarks. The findings support assessing model uncertainty through its consequences for value estimation, with the reported advantage applying to most, rather than all, evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: MOBILE uses disagreement in Bellman estimates to measure model uncertainty and improve offline reinforcement learning on most evaluated benchmark tasks.

title: Model-Bellman Inconsistency for Model-based Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Hypergraphs are a powerful abstraction for representing higher-order interactions between entities of interest. To exploit these relationships in making downstream predictions, a variety of hypergraph neural network architectures have recently been proposed, in large part building upon precursors from the more traditional graph neural network (GNN) literature. Somewhat differently, in this paper we begin by presenting an expressive family of parameterized, hypergraph-regularized energy functions. We then demonstrate how minimizers of these energies effectively serve as node embeddings that, when paired with a parameterized classifier, can be trained end-to-end via a supervised bilevel optimization process. Later, we draw parallels between the implicit architecture of the predictive models emerging from the proposed bilevel hypergraph optimization, and existing GNN architectures in common use. Empirically, we demonstrate state-of-the-art results on various hypergraph node classification benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/yxzwang/PhenomNN.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent interactions involving groups of entities, making them useful when relationships extend beyond pairs. Many hypergraph neural networks adapt architectures from ordinary graph neural networks. This paper develops a different starting point: a family of learnable energy functions that incorporate hypergraph structure.

Minimizing one of these energies produces representations for the nodes. A parameterized classifier then uses those representations to make predictions. The energy function and classifier are trained together through supervised bilevel optimization, meaning that the prediction-learning process includes an inner optimization that determines the node representations. This connects the representations directly to both the hypergraph and the supervised prediction objective.

The authors also explain parallels between the architecture implicit in this optimization process and commonly used graph neural networks. Their experiments report state-of-the-art results on several hypergraph node classification benchmarks. The work therefore contributes both a way to construct predictive models from energy minimization and evidence that the resulting models can perform strongly on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Learnable hypergraph energy functions generate node representations through optimization, producing models with strong reported node-classification results.

title: From Hypergraph Energy Functions to Hypergraph Neural Networks

abstract: Despite the success of equivariant neural networks in scientific applications, they require knowing the symmetry group a priori. However, it may be difficult to know which symmetry to use as an inductive bias in practice. Enforcing the wrong symmetry could even hurt the performance. In this paper, we propose a framework, LieGAN, to automatically discover equivariances from a dataset using a paradigm akin to generative adversarial training. Specifically, a generator learns a group of transformations applied to the data, which preserve the original distribution and fool the discriminator. LieGAN represents symmetry as interpretable Lie algebra basis and can discover various symmetries such as the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, restricted Lorentz group $\mathrm{SO}(1,3)^+$ in trajectory prediction and top-quark tagging tasks. The learned symmetry can also be readily used in several existing equivariant neural networks to improve accuracy and generalization in prediction.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks build symmetry into their predictions, but using them normally requires deciding in advance which symmetry applies. That choice can be difficult in scientific applications, and enforcing an inappropriate symmetry can hurt performance. LieGAN addresses this problem by learning candidate symmetries directly from a dataset.

Its training resembles a generative adversarial setup. A generator learns a group of transformations and applies them to the data, while a discriminator tries to distinguish the transformed distribution from the original. The generator seeks transformations that preserve the distribution and fool the discriminator. Learned symmetries are expressed as an interpretable Lie algebra basis, making the discovered transformation structure explicit.

The paper demonstrates discovery of symmetries including rotation groups and the restricted Lorentz group in trajectory prediction and top-quark tagging tasks. It also shows that learned symmetries can be incorporated into several existing equivariant networks to improve prediction accuracy and generalization. This connects symmetry discovery to models that can use the discovered structure.
summary.tldr: LieGAN learns interpretable symmetry groups from data through adversarial training and uses them to improve equivariant prediction models.

title: Generative Adversarial Symmetry Discovery

abstract: This work considers the category distribution heterogeneity in federated learning. This issue is due to biased labeling preferences at multiple clients and is a typical setting of data heterogeneity. To alleviate this issue, most previous works consider either regularizing local models or fine-tuning the global model, while they ignore the adjustment of aggregation weights and simply assign weights based on the dataset size. However, based on our empirical observations and theoretical analysis, we find that the dataset size is not optimal and the discrepancy between local and global category distributions could be a beneficial and complementary indicator for determining aggregation weights. We thus propose a novel aggregation method, Federated Learning with Discrepancy-Aware Collaboration (FedDisco), whose aggregation weights not only involve both the dataset size and the discrepancy value, but also contribute to a tighter theoretical upper bound of the optimization error. FedDisco can promote utility and modularity in a communication- and computation-efficient way. Extensive experiments show that our FedDisco outperforms several state-of-the-art methods and can be easily incorporated with many existing methods to further enhance the performance. Our code will be available at https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/FedDisco.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines contributions from clients whose datasets may contain very different proportions of categories. This paper argues, through empirical observations and theoretical analysis, that size alone is not optimal when local category distributions differ from the global distribution.

FedDisco adjusts aggregation weights using both dataset size and a measure of the discrepancy between local and global category distributions. These two signals provide complementary information: the quantity of local data and how its category mix differs from the overall mix. The resulting weights also contribute to a tighter theoretical upper bound on optimization error.

Experiments show FedDisco outperforming several leading methods and improving performance when incorporated into existing approaches. The authors describe the method as efficient in communication and computation, with a modular design. Its contribution is to make the aggregation rule itself responsive to category imbalance, providing another way to address heterogeneity alongside changes to local training or global fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: FedDisco improves federated aggregation by weighting clients using both dataset size and category-distribution discrepancy.

abstract: In complex environments with large discrete action spaces, effective decision-making is critical in reinforcement learning (RL). Despite the widespread use of value-based RL approaches like Q-learning, they come with a computational burden, necessitating the maximization of a value function over all actions in each iteration. This burden becomes particularly challenging when addressing large-scale problems and using deep neural networks as function approximators. In this paper, we present stochastic value-based RL approaches which, in each iteration, as opposed to optimizing over the entire set of $n$ actions, only consider a variable stochastic set of a sublinear number of actions, possibly as small as $\mathcal{O}(\log(n))$. The presented stochastic value-based RL methods include, among others, Stochastic Q-learning, StochDQN, and StochDDQN, all of which integrate this stochastic approach for both value-function updates and action selection. The theoretical convergence of Stochastic Q-learning is established, while an analysis of stochastic maximization is provided. Moreover, through empirical validation, we illustrate that the various proposed approaches outperform the baseline methods across diverse environments, including different control problems, achieving near-optimal average returns in significantly reduced time.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning often requires finding the highest-valued action among every available choice. With a large discrete action space, that repeated search can become expensive, particularly when a neural network approximates the value function. This paper reduces the search burden by considering a changing random subset of actions at each iteration.

The proposed subset sizes grow sublinearly with the total number of actions and can be as small as logarithmic in that number. The approach is applied to both value updates and action selection. The resulting methods include Stochastic Q-learning, StochDQN, and StochDDQN, extending the same computational idea across several value-based learning algorithms.

The paper establishes theoretical convergence for Stochastic Q-learning and analyzes stochastic maximization. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments, including control tasks, show the proposed approaches outperforming the compared baselines and achieving near-optimal average returns in substantially less time. The theoretical convergence claim specifically concerns Stochastic Q-learning, while the broader family receives experimental support for reducing computation without losing strong returns in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Stochastic value-based reinforcement learning searches small random action subsets, reducing computation while achieving strong empirical returns.

title: Stochastic Q-learning for Large Discrete Action Spaces

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLM), but our theoretical understanding of LoRA has been limited. In this work, we theoretically analyze LoRA fine-tuning in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime with $N$ data points, showing: (i) full fine-tuning (without LoRA) admits a low-rank solution of rank $r\lesssim \sqrt{N}$; (ii) using LoRA with rank $r\gtrsim \sqrt{N}$ eliminates spurious local minima, allowing gradient descent to find the low-rank solutions; (iii) the low-rank solution found using LoRA generalizes well.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, fine-tunes a model through low-rank parameter changes. This paper examines why that restriction can still permit effective optimization and generalization. Its theoretical analysis takes place in the neural tangent kernel regime and expresses the required rank in terms of N, the number of training data points.

The first result establishes that full fine-tuning admits a solution whose rank is at most roughly proportional to the square root of N. The second shows that choosing a LoRA rank at least roughly proportional to the square root of N removes spurious local minima. Within the analyzed regime, this enables gradient descent to find the low-rank solutions.

The third result establishes that the solution found through LoRA generalizes well. Together, the results address whether a suitable low-rank solution exists, whether optimization can reach it, and whether it performs beyond the training data. The square-root rank condition is a sufficient condition from the analysis, not a claim that smaller ranks must fail. All three conclusions retain the paper's stated NTK-regime scope.
summary.tldr: In the NTK regime, LoRA with sufficiently large rank has no spurious local minima and finds low-rank solutions that generalize well.

title: LoRA Training in the NTK Regime has No Spurious Local Minima

abstract: Variational logistic regression is a popular method for approximate Bayesian inference seeing wide-spread use in many areas of machine learning including: Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning and multi-instance learning to name a few. However, due to the intractability of the Evidence Lower Bound, authors have turned to the use of Monte Carlo, quadrature or bounds to perform inference, methods which are costly or give poor approximations to the true posterior. In this paper we introduce a new bound for the expectation of softplus function and subsequently show how this can be applied to variational logistic regression and Gaussian process classification. Unlike other bounds, our proposal does not rely on extending the variational family, or introducing additional parameters to ensure the bound is tight. In fact, we show that this bound is tighter than the state-of-the-art, and that the resulting variational posterior achieves state-of-the-art performance, whilst being significantly faster to compute than Monte-Carlo methods.

paragraphs: Variational logistic regression approximates Bayesian inference by optimizing a tractable distribution in place of the full posterior. A difficulty is that its evidence lower bound contains an intractable expectation. Existing approaches use Monte Carlo sampling, numerical quadrature, or mathematical bounds, with tradeoffs between computational expense and the quality of the resulting posterior approximation.

The paper introduces a new bound for the expected softplus function and applies it to variational logistic regression and Gaussian-process classification. Unlike other bounding approaches, it does not require expanding the variational family or adding parameters specifically to make the bound tight. This keeps the approximation from acquiring those additional modeling or optimization components.

The authors show that their bound is tighter than the state of the art and report state-of-the-art performance for the resulting variational posterior. They also find computation significantly faster than Monte Carlo methods. The contribution targets a specific mathematical bottleneck in Bayesian classification, improving the bound used for inference while supporting both posterior quality and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: A tighter softplus-expectation bound improves variational Bayesian classification without additional variational parameters and computes significantly faster than Monte Carlo methods.

title: Logistic Variational Bayes Revisited

abstract: Attribution methods correspond to a class of explainability methods (XAI) that aim to assess how individual inputs contribute to a model’s decision-making process. We have identified a significant limitation in one type of attribution methods, known as “white-box" methods. Although highly efficient, as we will show, these methods rely on a gradient signal that is often contaminated by high-frequency artifacts. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new approach called "FORGrad". This simple method effectively filters out these high-frequency artifacts using optimal cut-off frequencies tailored to the unique characteristics of each model architecture. Our findings show that FORGrad consistently enhances the performance of already existing white-box methods, enabling them to compete effectively with more accurate yet computationally demanding "black-box" methods. We anticipate that our research will foster broader adoption of simpler and more efficient white-box methods for explainability, offering a better balance between faithfulness and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Attribution methods estimate how individual inputs contribute to a model’s decision. White-box methods can do this efficiently by using internal gradient information. This paper identifies a problem with that signal: high-frequency artifacts often contaminate the gradients used to construct the explanations.

The proposed method, FORGrad, filters out these artifacts. It uses cutoff frequencies tailored to the characteristics of each model architecture, making the filtering sensitive to the model being explained. The approach improves the signal supplied to existing white-box attribution methods, allowing those methods to retain their computational advantages while producing better explanations.

The authors report consistent improvements across the existing white-box methods they evaluate. With filtering, these methods compete effectively with more accurate but more computationally demanding black-box approaches. The findings connect explanation quality to the frequency content of the gradient signal and support a better balance between faithfulness and computation. Broader adoption of white-box methods is presented as a hoped-for consequence of that improvement.
summary.tldr: FORGrad filters high-frequency gradient artifacts to improve existing white-box explanations while preserving their computational appeal.

title: Saliency strikes back: How filtering out high frequencies improves white-box explanations

abstract: Recent studies on online reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated the advantages of learning multiple behaviors from a single task, as in the case of few-shot adaptation to a new environment. Although this approach is expected to yield similar benefits in offline RL, appropriate methods for learning multiple solutions have not been fully investigated in previous studies. In this study, we therefore addressed the problem of finding multiple solutions from a single task in offline RL. We propose algorithms that can learn multiple solutions in offline RL, and empirically investigate their performance. Our experimental results show that the proposed algorithm learns multiple qualitatively and quantitatively distinctive solutions in offline RL.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether offline reinforcement learning can recover several distinct ways to solve one task. Its starting point is evidence from online reinforcement learning that learning multiple behaviors can be useful, including for adapting to a new environment with few examples. The authors identify the corresponding offline problem as insufficiently explored by existing methods.

They propose algorithms aimed specifically at learning multiple solutions from a single task and investigate their behavior experimentally. The objective makes diversity among solutions a central part of the learning problem. Success therefore involves obtaining meaningfully different behaviors, rather than treating several learned outputs as interchangeable instances of the same solution.

The experiments show solutions that differ both qualitatively and quantitatively. That finding supports the feasibility of discovering behavioral variety in the offline setting examined. The motivation includes potential adaptation benefits suggested by online learning, but the stated empirical result concerns discovery of distinct solutions itself. The paper thus establishes a basis for studying how a collection of solutions can be learned within offline reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: The proposed offline reinforcement-learning algorithms discover multiple qualitatively and quantitatively distinct solutions to a single task.

title: Discovering Multiple Solutions from a Single Task in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite the impressive performance of deep learning models across diverse tasks, their complexity poses challenges for interpretation. This challenge is particularly evident for audio signals, where conveying interpretations becomes inherently difficult. To address this issue, we introduce Listenable Maps for Audio Classifiers (L-MAC), a posthoc interpretation method that generates faithful and listenable interpretations. L-MAC utilizes a decoder on top of a pretrained classifier to generate binary masks that highlight relevant portions of the input audio. We train the decoder with a loss function that maximizes the confidence of the classifier decision on the masked-in portion of the audio while minimizing the probability of model output for the masked-out portion. Quantitative evaluations on both in-domain and out-of-domain data demonstrate that L-MAC consistently produces more faithful interpretations than several gradient and masking-based methodologies. Furthermore, a user study confirms that, on average, users prefer the interpretations generated by the proposed technique.

paragraphs: L-MAC aims to make an audio classifier’s decisions understandable through explanations that people can listen to. Audio poses a communication challenge for interpretability: identifying relevant evidence is useful only if that evidence can also be conveyed meaningfully. The method adds a decoder on top of a pretrained classifier to produce binary masks selecting relevant portions of the input.

The decoder learns through a two-sided objective. The selected audio should preserve strong confidence in the classifier’s decision, while the excluded audio should reduce the probability of that output. This tests both what the explanation retains and what it leaves behind, tying the mask to the behavior of the classifier being explained.

Quantitative evaluations on data both within and outside the original domain show more faithful interpretations than several gradient-based and masking-based methods. A user study also finds that participants prefer L-MAC’s explanations on average. These results address complementary goals: representing the classifier’s decision faithfully and producing an explanation whose audible form users find preferable.
summary.tldr: L-MAC learns audio masks that produce listenable explanations with stronger measured faithfulness and higher average user preference than the compared methods.

title: Listenable Maps for Audio Classifiers

abstract: Explainable machine learning significantly improves the transparency of deep neural networks. However, existing work is constrained to explaining the behavior of individual model predictions, and lacks the ability to transfer the explanation across various models and tasks. This limitation results in explaining various tasks being time- and resource-consuming. To address this problem, we introduce a Transferable Vision Explainer (TVE) that can effectively explain various vision models in downstream tasks. Specifically, the transferability of TVE is realized through a pre-training process on large-scale datasets towards learning the meta-attribution. This meta-attribution leverages the versatility of generic backbone encoders to comprehensively encode the attribution knowledge for the input instance, which enables TVE to seamlessly transfer to explaining various downstream tasks, without the need for training on task-specific data. Empirical studies involve explaining three different architectures of vision models across three diverse downstream datasets. The experiment results indicate TVE is effective in explaining these tasks without the need for additional training on downstream data.
