summary.tldr: SymSpectra combines spectral information and functional-group dependencies to improve molecular substructure recognition under class imbalance.

title: SymSpectra: Symmetric Information Bottleneck Framework for Molecular Structure Recognition under Imbalanced Settings

abstract: Federated learning often face both data and model heterogeneity, with the latter often more challenging. Architectural differences yield incompatible representation, making the knowledge-sharing carrier central to heterogeneous collaboration. Using proxy model enables distillation-based collaboration but incurs high communication and computation costs. Prototype-based carriers are lighter yet cause semantic confusion when incompatible features are mixed. Therefore, we propose rule-based federated learning (RFL) that shares interpretable, class-discriminative rules to enable heterogeneous collaboration, avoid feature confusion, and keep communication lightweight. RFL uses a rule network to unify clients’ decision features and collaborates at the rule level, avoiding forcible averaging of incompatible representations. RFL selects sparse, high-coverage, beneficial rules for broadcasting, compressing shared knowledge into an interpretable class-rule set and reducing communication and computation costs. Each client selectively activates only rules relevant to its local classes, mitigating negative transfer while preserving personalization. Across heterogeneous settings, RFL achieves a better accuracy–communication trade-off.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participants use different model architectures as well as different data. Their internal representations may be incompatible, making direct knowledge exchange confusing. Proxy models can support collaboration through distillation but add computation and communication, while lighter prototype representations can mix features with different meanings.

Rule-based federated learning changes the form of shared knowledge to interpretable rules that distinguish classes. A rule network unifies clients’ decision features, allowing collaboration at the rule level. The system selects a sparse collection of useful rules with broad coverage and broadcasts a compact class-rule set, reducing the amount of knowledge that must be communicated and processed.

Each client activates only the rules relevant to its local classes. This selective use is intended to reduce negative transfer while preserving personalization. Experiments across heterogeneous settings report a better balance between accuracy and communication cost. The contribution makes the knowledge-sharing format central to collaboration: clients exchange decision-relevant rules without requiring their incompatible internal features to be forcibly averaged.
summary.tldr: Rule-based federated learning shares compact, interpretable class rules to improve collaboration among clients with different model architectures.

title: Towards Rule-Based Knowledge Sharing in Federated Learning

abstract: Scientific computing has long relied on double precision (64-bit floating point) arithmetic to guarantee accuracy in simulations of real-world phenomena. However, the growing availability of hardware accelerators such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) has made low-precision formats attractive due to their superior performance, reduced memory footprint, and improved energy efficiency. In this work, we investigate the role of mixed-precision arithmetic in neural-network based Variational Monte Carlo (VMC), a widely used method for solving computationally otherwise intractable quantum many-body systems. We first derive general analytical bounds on the error introduced by reduced precision on Metropolis-Hastings MCMC, and then empirically validate these bounds on the use-case of VMC. We demonstrate that significant portions of the algorithm, in particular, sampling the quantum state, can be executed in half precision without loss of accuracy. More broadly, this work provides a theoretical framework to assess the applicability of mixed-precision arithmetic in machine-learning approaches that rely on MCMC sampling. In the context of VMC, we additionally demonstrate the practical effectiveness of mixed-precision strategies, enabling more scalable and energy-efficient simulations of quantum many-body systems.

title: Neural Quantum States in Mixed Precision

abstract: Decision-based image attacks commonly rely on zeroth-order (ZO) Monte Carlo probing to estimate decision-boundary normals and iteratively refine adversarial perturbations to minimize the $\ell_2$ norm. We theoretically analyze and empirically demonstrate an intrinsic inefficiency arising from heterogeneous input sensitivity, where only a small subset of coordinates strongly affects the target model’s predictions. Empirically, with one-bit feedback and a limited query budget, updates on low-sensitivity coordinates are overwhelmed by initialization and sampling noise, preventing their perturbations from exhibiting consistent improvement. By modeling ZO refinement as a stochastic dynamical system, we formally characterize its asymptotic behavior: the optimization enters a stationary regime, where the perturbation aligns (in expectation) with the normal and its coordinate-wise magnitudes encode a local sensitivity ranking. However, this stationarity does not generally yield $\ell_2$-optimal perturbations under nonlinear boundaries. Building on this observation, we propose a novel and effective algorithm, Sensitivity-Aware Rescaling (SAR), that leverages this sensitivity signal to infer an importance map from the current best perturbation, then progressively suppresses low-importance regions through a coarse-to-fine schedule to reduce the $\ell_2$ norm. Extensive experiments show that SAR achieves consistent improvements in perturbation norm, attack success rate, and visual imperceptibility. The code is available at https://github.com/Flyingssheep/SAR.

This paper identifies an inefficiency when sensitivity varies across input coordinates: with limited queries and one-bit feedback, noise can overwhelm improvements in coordinates that barely influence the prediction.

Their analysis characterizes a stationary regime in which the perturbation aligns with the boundary normal in expectation, and its coordinate magnitudes reveal a local ranking of sensitivity. The contribution connects a theoretical account of stalled refinement to a practical way of reducing unnecessary image changes.
summary.tldr: Sensitivity-Aware Rescaling uses information left in noisy attack perturbations to suppress unimportant regions and improve decision-based attacks.

title: Bias in Zeroth-Order Normal Estimation for Decision-Based Attacks

abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) facilitates few-step image generation by aligning a distilled student with a reference multi-step teacher. In practice, however, optimizing DMD can reduce sample diversity in few-step synthesis, and existing remedies typically rely on perceptual or adversarial regularization, leading to stability and scalability challenges during training. Here, we describe diversity-preserved DMD (DP-DMD), a role-separated distillation method inspired by the complementary roles of early and late denoising steps. Specifically, the first distillation step is trained with a teacher-derived target-prediction objective (e.g., v-prediction) to preserve sample diversity, while the remaining steps are optimized with the standard DMD loss to refine perceptual quality. DP-DMD, with no perceptual or adversarial regularization, no additional modules, and no teacher-generated reference samples, preserves sample diversity while maintaining competitive visual quality under few-step sampling, providing a simple and stable alternative to other DMD variants.

paragraphs: Distribution matching distillation trains a fast image generator to approximate a teacher that uses many generation steps. A recurring problem is that optimizing this match can narrow the variety of images the student produces. Existing attempts to restore diversity often add perceptual or adversarial training objectives, bringing additional stability and scaling challenges.

DP-DMD separates the jobs assigned to different generation steps. The first step learns through a target-prediction objective derived from the teacher, such as velocity prediction, with the aim of preserving diversity. Subsequent steps use the usual distribution matching loss to improve perceptual quality. This division follows the idea that early and late denoising stages play complementary roles.

The reported result is preserved sample diversity alongside competitive visual quality with few sampling steps. The method requires no extra modules, perceptual or adversarial regularizers, or teacher-generated reference samples. Its contribution is a change in how training objectives are distributed across steps, offering a simple and stable alternative to other DMD variants without adding those auxiliary components.
summary.tldr: DP-DMD assigns diversity preservation to the first generation step and perceptual refinement to later steps for fast, varied image synthesis.

title: Diversity-Preserved Distribution Matching Distillation for Fast Visual Synthesis

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have shown remarkable performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. Despite this progress, they are still prone to hallucination, generating responses that are inconsistent with visual content. In this work, we find that LVLMs tend to hallucinate when they pay insufficient attention to the correct visual evidence and gradually forget it during the generation process. We empirically find that although LVLMs overall attend insufficiently to visual evidence, they exhibit sensitivity to the correct visual evidence in specific layers, with notable inter-layer discrepancy. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel hallucination mitigation method that enhances visual evidence based on Inter-Layer Visual Attention Discrepancy (ILVAD). Specifically, we obtain the attention weights from early generated tokens to visual tokens across layers and identify the tokens that are repeatedly activated as visual evidence, forming a saliency map. We then enhance attention to visual evidence during generation through the saliency map to reduce visual forgetting. In addition, we leverage the saliency map to obtain attention scores of generated text to visual evidence, in order to select and emphasize text tokens that are strongly grounded in visual evidence. Our method is training-free and plug-and-play. Multiple benchmark evaluations conducted on five recently released models show that our method can consistently mitigate hallucinations in different LVLMs over various architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/ytx-ML/ILVAD.

This paper finds that sensitivity to the correct evidence varies across layers. Even when overall visual attention is weak, particular layers can still identify useful image information.

ILVAD uses this discrepancy to construct a saliency map. It examines attention from early generated tokens to visual tokens across layers, identifying visual tokens that are repeatedly activated. The map then increases attention to that evidence during subsequent generation, aiming to reduce the model’s tendency to forget what it saw.

ILVAD requires no training and is designed as a plug-in intervention. Evaluations on multiple benchmarks and five models report consistent hallucination mitigation across architectures, supporting the usefulness of preserving visual evidence throughout generation.
summary.tldr: ILVAD uses differences in attention across layers to identify visual evidence and keep generated responses grounded in it without additional training.

title: Finding the Correct Visual Evidence Without Forgetting: Mitigating Hallucination in LVLMs via Inter-Layer Visual Attention Discrepancy

abstract: Multi-turn, multi-agent LLM game evaluations exhibit substantial run-to-run variance. In long-horizon interactions, small deviations compound across turns and are amplified by multi-agent coupling, biasing win rate estimates and destabilizing comparative rankings across repeated tournaments. Prompt choice exacerbates this by inducing different effective policies and interaction dynamics. We address both instability and underperformance in games with MEMO: (Memory-augmented MOdel context optimization), a self-play framework that treats inference-time context as an optimizable, agentic object by coupling retention and exploration. Retention distills self-play trajectories into a persistent memory bank of structured insights that act as priors; exploration combines tournament-style prompt evolution under TrueSkill with prioritized replay over decisive states. Across five text-based games and a 2,000-game budget per task, MEMO raises mean win rate from 25.1% to 49.5% for GPT-4o-mini and from 20.9% to 45.0% for Qwen-2.5-7B, while sharply reducing run-to-run dispersion. These results suggest substantial headroom in multi-agent LLM game performance and robustness can be unlocked through memory, with MEMO achieving gains in negotiation and imperfect-information settings, while RL remains more effective in perfect-information settings. Project website: https://yunfeixie233.github.io/MEMO/.

paragraphs: MEMO addresses both weak performance and unstable evaluation in multi-agent language-model games. Small differences can accumulate across turns and spread through interactions between agents, producing variable win rates and rankings. Prompt choices add another source of variation because they change how agents behave throughout a game.

The framework optimizes the context used at inference through self-play. Its retention component condenses gameplay trajectories into persistent, structured insights that guide later decisions. Its exploration component evolves prompts through tournaments using TrueSkill and prioritizes replay of decisive states. This combines keeping useful experience with searching for better strategies expressed through context.

summary.tldr: MEMO combines persistent self-play memory and prompt evolution to raise game win rates and reduce run-to-run variability.

title: MEMO: Memory-Augmented Model Context Optimization for Robust Multi-Turn Multi-Agent LLM Games

abstract: Sparse optimization is a fundamental challenge in various practical applications. A popular approach to sparse optimization is Lp regularization. However, it may encounter optimization instability due to the unbounded gradients when 0$<$p$<$1. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to sparse optimization termed ReWA, based on Reparameterization, Weight decay, and Adaptive learning rate. ReWA is closely connected to lp-regularization, yet it unveils a distinct optimization landscape that helps mitigate instability issues. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with ResNets demonstrate that ReWA leads to significant sparsity improvements over the L1-regularization approach while preserving test accuracy.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization seeks solutions in which many parameters are zero. A common strategy encourages sparsity through an Lp penalty, but when p lies between zero and one, its gradients can become unbounded. That behavior can make optimization unstable, creating tension between a penalty's sparsity-promoting effect and the difficulty of optimizing it.

The paper introduces ReWA, which combines reparameterization, weight decay, and an adaptive learning rate. The approach remains closely connected to Lp regularization while producing a different optimization landscape. Its purpose is to retain a useful connection to sparsity-promoting regularization while mitigating the instability associated with the conventional formulation.

Experiments use ResNet models on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. The authors report significant sparsity improvements over L1 regularization while preserving test accuracy. These findings support ReWA as a practical alternative in the evaluated image-classification settings. The broader contribution is to connect the way parameters are represented and updated with the stability of sparse optimization, rather than considering the regularization penalty in isolation.
summary.tldr: ReWA combines reparameterization, weight decay, and adaptive learning rates to improve sparsity while mitigating optimization instability.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Sparse Optimization with Reparameterization, Weight Decay, and Adaptive Learning Rate

abstract: Proactive and real-time interactive experiences are essential for human-like AI companions, yet face three key challenges: (1) achieving low-latency inference under continuous streaming inputs, (2) autonomously deciding when to respond, and (3) controlling both quality and quantity of generated content to meet real-time constraints. In this work, we instantiate AI companions through two gaming scenarios—commentator and guide—selected for their suitability for automatic evaluation. We introduce the Live Gaming Benchmark, a large-scale dataset with three representative scenarios: solo commentary, co-commentary, and user guidance, and present Proact-VL, a general framework that shapes multimodal language models into proactive, real-time interactive agents capable of human-like environment perception and interaction. Extensive experiments show Proact-VL achieves superior response latency and quality while maintaining strong video understanding capabilities, demonstrating its practicality for real-time interactive applications.

paragraphs: An AI companion watching a continuous video stream needs to do more than answer individual questions. It must process incoming information quickly, decide for itself when a response is useful, and control how much it says. Proact-VL addresses these connected requirements for proactive interaction under real-time constraints, where both response timing and response quality matter.

The authors study companions in gaming roles as commentators and guides, choosing these settings because they support automatic evaluation. They introduce the Live Gaming Benchmark, a large-scale dataset covering solo commentary, co-commentary, and user guidance. These scenarios provide a concrete setting for evaluating an agent that must perceive an evolving environment and interact without relying solely on explicit response requests.

Proact-VL is presented as a general framework for shaping multimodal language models into such agents. Experiments show superior response latency and quality while retaining strong video understanding. The results demonstrate practicality in the evaluated real-time interactions. The contribution links a benchmark for proactive behavior with a framework that treats deciding when and how much to speak as part of the interactive task.
summary.tldr: Proact-VL supports proactive, low-latency video interaction and introduces a gaming benchmark for commentary and guidance.

title: Proact-VL: A Proactive VideoLLM for Real-Time AI Companions

abstract: Few-shot time series forecasting is fundamentally challenged by the scarcity of high-quality training data and the risk of severe overfitting. To address this issue, we propose ReAugment, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that explicitly learns where and how to augment time series data. ReAugment maintains a zoo of forecasting models and measures prediction diversity across them to identify training samples that are most prone to overfitting. These samples serve as anchor points and are used as inputs to the data augmentation process. We then employ an RL approach to learn transformation policies, using a model zoo-guided reward function to bias the transformed data to overfit-prone regions of the training distribution that are most beneficial for generalization. A key advantage of the RL formulation is that it avoids backpropagating gradients through the forecasting models, thereby mitigating gradient vanishing. Experiments across diverse forecasting architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of ReAugment in both few-shot and standard time series forecasting.

paragraphs: Forecasting from few time-series examples creates a risk that a model memorizes limited training data instead of learning patterns that generalize. ReAugment addresses this by learning both where augmentation is most useful and how to transform the selected examples. Its augmentation process is targeted using information from several forecasting models.

The framework maintains a model zoo and measures diversity among its predictions to identify samples considered especially prone to overfitting. Those samples become anchors for augmentation. A reinforcement-learning policy then chooses transformations, guided by a reward derived from the model zoo. The reward steers generated data toward overfit-prone regions where augmentation is expected to help generalization.

Using reinforcement learning avoids the need to backpropagate gradients through the forecasting models, mitigating vanishing-gradient problems in the augmentation process. Experiments across diverse forecasting architectures demonstrate effectiveness in both few-shot and standard forecasting settings. The results support using model disagreement to focus augmentation effort and a learned transformation policy to make that effort useful across different predictors.
summary.tldr: ReAugment uses forecasting-model disagreement and reinforcement learning to target data augmentation where it can improve generalization.

title: ReAugment: Targeted Few-Shot Time Series Augmentation via Model Zoo-Guided Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Autonomous data science has been a long-standing challenge, and is now becoming feasible with the emergence of powerful large language models (LLMs). Recent workflow-based data agents have shown promising results on specific data tasks but remain fundamentally limited in achieving full autonomy due to their reliance on predefined workflows. In this paper, we introduce DeepAnalyze, the first agentic LLM for autonomous data science, capable of automatically completing the end-to-end data science from raw data to research reports. To tackle high-complexity data science tasks, we propose a curriculum-based agentic training paradigm that emulates the learning trajectory of human data scientists, enabling LLMs to progressively acquire and integrate multiple capabilities in real-world environments. Accordingly, we contribute a data-grounded trajectory synthesis framework to constructs high-quality data science training data. Through training in real-world environment, DeepAnalyze learns to perform a broad spectrum of data tasks, ranging from data question answering to open-ended data research. Experiments on 13 benchmarks demonstrate that, with only 8B parameters, DeepAnalyze outperforms workflow-based agents built on advanced proprietary LLMs. DeepAnalyze is fully open-sourced, paving the way toward autonomous data science.

paragraphs: DeepAnalyze targets data science that runs from raw data through analysis to a research report. The paper identifies predefined workflows as a constraint on existing data agents: a fixed sequence can support particular tasks but restrict the flexibility needed for more open-ended work. DeepAnalyze instead trains an agentic language model to acquire and combine the relevant capabilities.

Its training curriculum introduces capabilities progressively, following a learning trajectory inspired by human data scientists. A data-grounded trajectory synthesis framework creates the training examples used for this process. Training in real-world environments allows the model to integrate those skills across tasks ranging from answering questions about data to conducting open-ended data research.

Across 13 benchmarks, the 8-billion-parameter model outperforms workflow-based agents built on advanced proprietary language models. The reported comparison supports the value of training the agent's own data-science behavior, alongside the capabilities of its underlying model. DeepAnalyze is also fully open-sourced, making the presented system available for further work on agents that coordinate an entire data-science process.
summary.tldr: DeepAnalyze trains an 8B agent through a data-science curriculum and outperforms tested proprietary-model workflow agents across 13 benchmarks.

title: DeepAnalyze: Agentic Large Language Models for Autonomous Data Science

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding in large language models but suffers from substantial latency due to synchronous retrieval. While recent work explores asynchronous retrieval, existing approaches rely on heuristic coordination between retrieval and generation and assume stable information demands during decoding that often break in complex, multi-domain settings. In this paper, we propose an advanced asynchronous retrieval framework that enables predictive prefetching aligned with evolving information needs. The framework explicitly predicts when retrieval should be triggered and what information should be retrieved using three components, a retrieval predictor, a context monitor, and a query generator, by exploiting semantic precursors in generation dynamics that emerge several tokens before uncertainty becomes critical. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate up to 43.5% end-to-end latency reduction and 62.4% improvement in time-to-first-token, while maintaining answer quality comparable to synchronous RAG baselines.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in external information, but waiting synchronously for retrieval adds latency. Retrieving asynchronously can reduce waiting, yet coordination becomes difficult when information needs change during generation. This paper proposes predicting those needs early enough to fetch relevant material before uncertainty becomes critical.

The framework combines a retrieval predictor, a context monitor, and a query generator. Together, they determine when to initiate retrieval and what information to request. Their decisions use semantic precursors in the generation process that emerge several tokens before the critical point. Monitoring the evolving context is central to keeping prefetching aligned with changing information demands.

Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report end-to-end latency reductions of up to 43.5% and a 62.4% improvement in time to first token, while retaining answer quality comparable to synchronous retrieval baselines. These findings support predictive coordination as a way to reduce retrieval-related waiting. The result connects anticipation of future information needs with faster responses, while evaluating quality against the synchronous approach.
summary.tldr: The framework predicts when and what to retrieve, reducing response latency while maintaining answer quality comparable to synchronous RAG.

title: Predictive Prefetching for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Hyperspectral image change detection (HSI-CD) suffers from severe annotation scarcity and complex change patterns, which fundamentally limit the effectiveness of directly fine-tuning pre-trained foundation models. Although semi-supervised learning provides a promising direction, existing approaches mainly rely on confidence-based pseudo-label selection, leading to limited data diversity or severe error propagation. In this paper, we propose Influence-Aware Semi-supervised Fine-tuning (IA-SFT), a novel framework that evaluates the influence of pseudo-labels on model decision behavior to identify truly valuable supervision signals. Instead of confidence-based selection, IA-SFT evaluates each low-confidence pseudo-label by measuring its impact on labeled data, enabling reliable filtering of high-value pseudo-labels with minimal noise. To further adapt foundation models to HSI-CD, we design an Adaptive Fusion Change Decoder (AFCD) that jointly models global semantic consistency and local change details. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that IA-SFT consistently improves pseudo-label quality and detection performance, achieving superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additional analyses validate the transferability of IA-SFT when integrated into different frameworks in a plug-and-play manner. Code will be released.

paragraphs: Hyperspectral change detection faces scarce annotations and complex patterns of change. Semi-supervised learning can expand supervision using model-generated labels, but selecting those labels by confidence creates a difficult tradeoff: strict selection limits diversity, while permissive selection can propagate errors. This paper examines whether low-confidence labels can still provide valuable training signals.

IA-SFT evaluates a low-confidence pseudo-label through its influence on model decision behavior, measured by its impact on labeled data. That provides a basis for filtering useful supervision with minimal noise beyond the model's confidence alone. The framework also introduces an Adaptive Fusion Change Decoder that jointly handles global semantic consistency and local change details.

Additional analyses demonstrate transferability when IA-SFT is integrated into different frameworks. The findings support assessing uncertain labels by their training value: uncertainty does not automatically make a label unhelpful, and influence-based filtering can recover useful supervision from that pool.
summary.tldr: IA-SFT selects useful low-confidence pseudo-labels by their influence on labeled data, improving hyperspectral change detection.

title: Rethinking Low-Confidence Pseudo Labels: Influence-Aware Semi-Supervised Fine-Tuning for Hyperspectral Change Detection

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) often has a hierarchical structure, where an upper-level (UL) learner selects model parameters and a lower-level (LL) decision-making process responds, naturally leading to a bilevel optimization problem. Most existing bilevel RL methods assume a single-policy LL Markov decision process (MDP), and therefore fail to capture competitive structures arising in applications such as incentive design, where multiple policies interact. We study bilevel optimization problems in which the LL problem is a regularized min–max zero-sum Markov game and the UL objective is optimized through the saddle-point equilibrium induced by the LL game. In this work, we propose penalty-augmented Nikaido–Isoda descent–ascent (PANDA), a penalty-based first-order policy-gradient method based on the Nikaido–Isoda function. By exploiting the min–max game structure, PANDA avoids computing UL hypergradients and does not require second-order information. We prove that PANDA converges to stationary points without convexity assumptions on either the UL or LL objectives. Moreover, PANDA reaches an $\epsilon$-stationary point in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1})$ iterations with sample complexity $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3})$, matching the best-known rates for bilevel RL with single-policy LL MDPs. Experiments demonstrate the superior performance of PANDA over closely related baselines.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning problems involve two linked decisions: an upper-level learner chooses parameters, and a lower-level process responds. Existing approaches often model that response as a single policy. This paper instead considers competing policies in a regularized zero-sum Markov game, allowing the upper-level objective to depend on the equilibrium produced by their interaction.

The proposed method, PANDA, uses a penalty formulation based on the Nikaido–Isoda function and updates policies using first-order gradients. Its use of the game's min–max structure avoids upper-level hypergradient calculations and second-order information. This makes the competitive lower-level problem approachable without those additional derivative computations.

The authors prove convergence to stationary points without assuming convexity of either objective. They report iteration and sample complexity rates matching the best known for bilevel reinforcement learning with a single lower-level policy. Stationarity is the stated guarantee, rather than global optimality. Experiments also show stronger performance than closely related baselines, supporting the method's practical value alongside its theoretical results.
summary.tldr: PANDA optimizes hierarchical reinforcement learning problems with competing lower-level policies using first-order updates and provable convergence to stationary points.

title: Bilevel Optimization over Saddle Points of Zero-Sum Markov Games

abstract: Despite high semantic alignment, modern text-to-image (T2I) generative models still struggle to synthesize diverse images from a given prompt. In this work, we enhance the T2I diversity through a geometric lens. Unlike most existing methods that rely primarily on entropy-based guidance to increase sample dissimilarity, we introduce Geometry-Aware Spherical Sampling (GASS) to enhance diversity by explicitly controlling both prompt-dependent and prompt-independent sources of variation. Specifically, we decompose the diversity measure in CLIP embeddings using two orthogonal directions: the text embedding, which captures semantic variation related to the prompt, and an identified orthogonal direction that captures prompt-independent variation (e.g., backgrounds). Based on this decomposition, GASS increases the geometric projection spread of generated image embeddings along both axes and guides the T2I sampling process via expanded predictions along the generation trajectory. Our experiments on different frozen T2I backbones (U-Net and DiT, diffusion and flow) and benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of disentangled diversity enhancement with minimal impact on image fidelity and semantic alignment.
originalAbstract: Despite high semantic alignment, modern text-to-image (T2I) generative models still struggle to synthesize diverse images from a given prompt. In this work, we enhance the T2I diversity through a geometric lens. Unlike most existing methods that rely primarily on entropy-based guidance to increase sample dissimilarity, we introduce Geometry-Aware Spherical Sampling (GASS) to enhance diversity by explicitly controlling both prompt-dependent and prompt-independent sources of variation. Specifically, we decompose the diversity measure in CLIP embeddings using two orthogonal directions: the text embedding, which captures semantic variation related to the prompt, and an identified orthogonal direction that captures prompt-independent variation (e.g., backgrounds). Based on this decomposition, GASS increases the geometric projection spread of generated image embeddings along both axes and guides the T2I sampling process via expanded predictions along the generation trajectory. Our experiments on different frozen T2I backbones (U-Net and DiT, diffusion and flow) and benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of disentangled diversity enhancement with minimal impact on image fidelity and semantic alignment.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can follow a prompt accurately yet produce a narrow range of images for it. GASS approaches this diversity problem through the geometry of image and text representations. Its aim is to control variation associated with the prompt separately from variation that is independent of the prompt.

The method decomposes diversity in CLIP embedding space along two perpendicular directions. The text-embedding direction represents prompt-related semantic variation, while an identified orthogonal direction represents variation such as backgrounds. GASS increases the spread of projected image embeddings along both directions and uses expanded predictions throughout the generation trajectory to guide sampling.

Experiments test the approach on frozen image-generation backbones spanning U-Net and Transformer architectures, as well as diffusion and flow models. The authors report improved diversity with minimal effects on image fidelity and semantic alignment. These findings suggest that explicitly separating sources of variation can broaden generated outputs while largely retaining their relevance to the prompt. The contribution is a sampling intervention that works across the evaluated model families without retraining those backbones.
summary.tldr: GASS guides image sampling along separate prompt-related and prompt-independent directions to increase diversity with minimal reported quality impact.

title: GASS: Geometry-Aware Spherical Sampling for Disentangled Diversity Enhancement in Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Evaluations of generative models are now ubiquitous, and their outcomes critically shape public and scientific expectations of AI’s capabilities. Yet skepticism about their reliability continues to grow. How can we know that a reported accuracy genuinely reflects a model’s underlying performance? Although benchmark results are often presented as direct measurements of capability, in practice they are inferences: treating a score as evidence of capability already presupposes a theory of what it means to be capable at a task. We argue that AI evaluations should instead be framed as inference tasks grounded on an explicit theory of capability. While this perspective is standard in fields like psychometrics, it remains underdeveloped in AI evaluation, where core assumptions are often left implicit. As a proof-of-concept, we empirically show that reported performance can depend strongly on the evaluator’s modeling assumptions, underscoring the need for transparent, theory-driven evaluation practices. We conclude by offering an Evaluation Card to help researchers document, justify, and scrutinize the modeling decisions underlying AI evaluations.

paragraphs: A benchmark score does not explain itself. This paper argues that interpreting accuracy as evidence of an AI capability requires assumptions about what that capability means and how the test reveals it. Those assumptions often remain unstated, even though evaluation results strongly influence scientific and public expectations.

The authors propose treating evaluation as an inference problem grounded in an explicit theory of capability. They draw attention to psychometrics, where this perspective is established. The practical change is to make the reasoning connecting observed answers to claims about underlying performance visible and open to scrutiny.

As an empirical proof of concept, the paper shows that reported performance can depend strongly on an evaluator’s modeling assumptions. This supports its call for an Evaluation Card that records and justifies those decisions. The intended benefit is greater transparency about what a score supports, enabling researchers to examine the assumptions behind an evaluation instead of treating its numerical result as a direct reading of capability.
summary.tldr: AI evaluations should explicitly state the assumptions that connect benchmark scores to claims about capability.

title: Position: AI Evaluations Should be Grounded on a Theory of Capability

abstract: Generative AI agents equate understanding with resolving explicit queries, an assumption that confines interaction to what users can articulate. This assumption breaks down when users themselves lack awareness of what is missing, risky, or worth considering. In such conditions, proactivity is not merely an efficiency enhancement, but an epistemic necessity. We refer to this condition as epistemic incompleteness: where progress depends on engaging with unknown unknowns for effective partnership. Existing approaches to proactivity remain narrowly anticipatory, extrapolating from past behavior and presuming that goals are already well defined, thereby failing to support users meaningfully. However, surfacing possibilities beyond a user’s current awareness is not inherently beneficial. Unconstrained proactive interventions can misdirect attention, overwhelm users, or introduce harm. Proactive agents, therefore, require behavioral grounding: principled constraints on when, how, and to what extent an agent should intervene. We advance the position that generative proactivity must be grounded both epistemically and behaviorally. Drawing on the philosophy of ignorance and research on proactive behavior, we argue that these theories offer critical guidance for designing agents that can engage responsibly and foster meaningful partnerships.

paragraphs: An agent that only answers explicit questions is limited by what its user already knows to ask. This paper examines situations where progress depends on recognizing missing knowledge, overlooked risks, or possibilities outside the user’s awareness. It calls this epistemic incompleteness and argues that proactivity becomes necessary under those conditions.

The authors criticize approaches that anticipate requests mainly by extrapolating from past behavior and assuming established goals. Such approaches may miss situations where users need help discovering what matters in the first place. The paper draws on the philosophy of ignorance to frame this problem of engaging with unknown unknowns.

However, bringing up additional possibilities can also distract, overwhelm, or harm users. The authors therefore pair epistemic grounding with behavioral grounding, drawing on research into proactive behavior to constrain when an agent intervenes, how it does so, and how far it goes. Their proposal treats responsible proactivity as both a knowledge problem and an interaction problem, requiring attention to the value and consequences of intervention.
summary.tldr: Proactive agents should help users engage with unknown unknowns while following principled constraints on when and how to intervene.

abstract: Temporal difference (TD) algorithms are attractive for reinforcement learning due to their ease-of-implementation and use of ``bootstrapped'' return estimates to make efficient use of sampled data. In particular, TD(lambda) methods comprise a family of reinforcement learning algorithms that often yield fast convergence by averaging multiple estimators of the expected return. However, TD(lambda) chooses a very specific way of averaging these estimators based on the fixed parameter lambda, which may not lead to optimal convergence rates in all settings. In this paper, we derive an automated Bayesian approach to setting lambda that we call temporal difference Bayesian model averaging (TD-BMA). Empirically, TD-BMA always performs as well and often much better than the best fixed lambda for TD(lambda) (even when performance for different values of lambda varies across problems) without requiring that lambda or any analogous parameter be manually tuned.

paragraphs: Temporal difference learning uses bootstrapped return estimates to learn efficiently from sampled experience. TD(lambda) combines multiple estimators of expected return, with the parameter lambda determining a particular averaging scheme. The paper addresses the possibility that a fixed choice of this parameter may give suboptimal convergence rates in some settings.

The authors derive temporal difference Bayesian model averaging, or TD-BMA, as an automated Bayesian approach to setting lambda. The method addresses how return estimators should be combined without requiring a manually tuned lambda or an analogous parameter. This connects a practical tuning decision with a model-averaging perspective on the estimators involved.

In the reported empirical evaluation, TD-BMA performs at least as well as the best fixed lambda and often substantially better. This remains the reported pattern when the performance of different lambda values varies across problems. The result is empirical, rather than a universal convergence guarantee, but it supports automatic adaptation as a way to obtain strong performance without manually searching for a fixed setting.
summary.tldr: TD-BMA automatically adapts temporal-difference averaging and empirically matches or exceeds the best fixed lambda without manual tuning.

title: Temporal Difference Bayesian Model Averaging: A Bayesian Perspective on Adapting Lambda

abstract: Fisher kernels provide a commonly used vectorial representation of structured objects. The paper presents a technique that exploits label information to improve the object representation of Fisher kernels by employing ideas from metric learning. In particular, the new technique trains a generative model in such a way that the distance between the log-likelihood gradients induced by two objects with the same label is as small as possible, and the distance between the gradients induced by two objects with different labels is as large as possible. We illustrate the strong performance of classifiers trained on the resulting object representations on problems in handwriting recognition, speech recognition, facial expression analysis, and bio-informatics.

paragraphs: Fisher kernels turn structured objects into vector representations using a generative model. The paper investigates how class labels can improve those representations themselves. Its goal is to make the vectors reflect distinctions relevant to classification, so that the representation carries useful label information before a classifier is trained on it.

The method draws on metric learning and changes how the generative model is trained. Each object's representation involves gradients of its log-likelihood. Training seeks to bring these gradient vectors closer together for objects with the same label and move them farther apart for objects with different labels. Labels therefore influence the geometry induced by the model, rather than only the classifier that uses its output.

The authors illustrate strong classifier performance using the learned representations in handwriting recognition, speech recognition, facial expression analysis, and bioinformatics. These applications demonstrate the approach across several kinds of structured objects. The central contribution is a way to train a generative representation with a discriminative purpose: organize its gradient features around the categories that the eventual prediction task must distinguish.
summary.tldr: Label-guided training makes Fisher-kernel representations bring same-class objects together and separate objects from different classes.

title: Learning Discriminative Fisher Kernels

abstract: Much of current machine learning (ML) research has lost its connection to problems of import to the larger world of science and society. From this perspective, there exist glaring limitations in the data sets we investigate, the metrics we employ for evaluation, and the degree to which results are communicated back to their originating domains. What changes are needed to how we conduct research to increase the impact that ML has? We present six Impact Challenges to explicitly focus the field’s energy and attention, and we discuss existing obstacles that must be addressed. We aim to inspire ongoing discussion and focus on ML that matters.

paragraphs: This paper argues that much machine learning research has become disconnected from problems important to science and society. It directs attention to how research is conducted: which datasets are studied, which metrics define success, and whether findings are communicated back to the fields that supplied the original problems.

These concerns connect research choices to impact. A dataset determines the problem a study actually investigates, while an evaluation metric shapes what counts as progress. Communicating results back to an originating domain is another part of that connection. The paper treats shortcomings across these areas as obstacles to making machine learning useful beyond its own research community.

The authors present six Impact Challenges intended to focus the field's attention and discuss obstacles that must be addressed. Their stated aim is to inspire continued discussion and research with greater external relevance. The contribution is an agenda for reconsidering research priorities and evaluation practices, centered on the relationship between technical work and consequential problems in the wider world.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes six Impact Challenges to reconnect machine learning research practices with consequential scientific and societal problems.

title: Machine Learning that Matters
